10365-precaution-a-novel:
James Fenimore Cooper published this novel in 1820, his first book, set among English country society rather than American frontier life. The story follows young women and men through calls, balls, and courtships, where rank, wealth, and reputation shape every choice. Cooper writes in the manner of Jane Austen's age, with moral care.

Love, flattery, and false friends test the heroines, who must learn caution before trusting a suitor's fine words. The title itself warns against haste in matters of the heart. Readers get Cooper's early, polite social novel, interesting as the start of a great American career.
10369-memoir-and-diary-of-john-yeardley-:
Charles Tylor edited this memoir and diary of John Yeardley, a Quaker minister, published in Philadelphia in 1860. Yeardley's own words frame the book: he hoped to die in peace with God and in love for all people, holding every nation his nation. The memoir traces a life of plain faith and wide travel.

Yeardley joins the Society of Friends, enters business, marries, and is recorded as a minister in 1815. Later chapters follow his work in Germany and his preaching journeys. Readers get a detailed, devout portrait of Quaker ministry in the early nineteenth century.
10621-birthright-a-novel:
T. S. Stribling published Birthright in 1922, a novel about a Black man educated at Harvard who returns to the rural South. Peter Siner steps off the train at Cairo, Illinois, and is directed into the Jim Crow car, a sharp reminder that his degree changes little in the world he left. The village he comes home to still runs on old customs and sharp color lines.

Through Peter, his family, and Cissie, Stribling shows the clash between schooling, hope, and the daily facts of segregation. The novel follows work, love, and standing in a small Black community under white rule. Readers get a frank, early portrait of race in America, written before the civil rights era gave it a new language.
10667-snake-and-sword-a-novel:
Percival Christopher Wren, best known for Beau Geste, wrote Snake and Sword as a novel of a soldier's soul in three parts: its welding, its searing, and its saving. Colonel Matthew Devon de Warrenne of the Queen's Own Bombay Lancers stands at its center, with Lucille and a shadowy enemy called the Snake. Troopers, campaigns, and love affairs fill the chapters.

Wren writes of honor, temptation, and redemption in the empire's far stations, with adventure never far off. The Snake's agents, myrmidons, and revenges drive the plot toward its reckoning seven years on. Readers who like imperial romance with a moral pulse will find this a stirring, old-fashioned tale.
10837-the-soul-of-democracy-the-philosop:
Edward Howard Griggs published The Soul of Democracy in 1918, on the philosophy of the world war in relation to human liberty. His motto sets man for the state, meaning autocracy, against man for mankind, the soul of democracy. Twenty chapters move from the world tragedy and the conflict of ideas to the aims of the Allied nations, moral standards, and America's duty.

Later chapters weigh non-resistance, preparedness, reconstruction, education, socialism, feminism, and the menaces and dilemmas of democracy. Griggs writes as a lecturer to general readers. The book offers a wartime case for democratic ideals, and a program for keeping them after peace.
10905-phantom-fortune-a-novel:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon, author of Lady Audley's Secret, wrote this long Victorian novel of fortune, love, and secrets. Penelope and Lesbia, two young women of very different temper, move between country houses and London society, where balls, garden parties, and shopping fill days that run from morning to dawn. An old man on the fell, a letter bag, and a fortune refused or pursued drive the plot.

Braddon keeps mysteries unfolding across forty-six chapters, with mistaken identities, hidden pasts, and a day of reckoning. The novel shows high society from inside, sharp on manners and money. Readers who enjoy sensation fiction will find its mix of romance, suspense, and social observation still engaging, despite its length.
10943-elusive-isabel:
Jacques Futrelle set this 1908 spy romance in Washington, where diplomats dine politely while intrigue runs underneath. Isabel Thorne, a beautiful and mysterious visitor, draws the attention of Mr. Campbell, an American official. Cables, a fan's secret language, a vanished diplomat, and a safe-opening scheme carry the plot through drawing rooms, embassies, and a prison.

Futrelle keeps the question open: is Isabel a foreign agent, an innocent caught in a game, or something between the two? Campbell must test her story without breaking the law or his own code. The novel mixes romance with early spy fiction, using Washington society as a chessboard where a glance, a letter, or a slip of paper can shift the balance.
1098-the-turmoil-a-novel:
Booth Tarkington sets this novel in a booming Midwestern city, where the Sheridan family, grown rich on industry, watches its sons chase love, money, and ruin. Bibbs Sheridan, the frail, bookish son, loves a woman his family scorns, while his brothers blunder through business and marriage.

The turmoil of the title is both the city's growth and the family's own strife, as old ways give way to smoke, speed, and new wealth. Tarkington writes with humor and moral care. The book, first of his Growth trilogy, gives a vivid picture of America changing fast.
11217-the-visioning-a-novel:
Susan Glaspell's 1911 novel opens on a golf course, where Katherine Wayneworth Jones, an army girl known as Katie, is bunkered in the sand on her twenty-fifth birthday. Raised across military posts and courted by bachelor officers, Katie faces a choice: marry inside the army, as everyone expects, or imagine a different life. Captain Prescott's arrival sharpens the question.

Glaspell, later famous as a playwright, writes Katie's inner life with wit and sympathy, letting small scenes carry large decisions. The novel explores how a woman formed by one closed world begins to see beyond it. Its title points to that inward turn, and its golf-course opening sets a light tone for a serious subject.
11303-vain-fortune-a-novel:
George Moore's Vain Fortune, in a completely revised 1895 edition, centers on Emily Watson after Moore rewrote the novel to make her its principal character instead of Hubert Price. Moore's preface explains the revision frankly: the first edition was thin and insipid, and a Dutch translator's suggestion let him combine the English and American versions without altering a sentence. Illustrations by Maurice Greiffenhagen accompany the text.

The novel follows Emily through love, ambition, and social maneuvering in late Victorian London. Moore's naturalist eye gives the story its edge, observing manners and motives without moralizing. Readers interested in Moore's development will find the preface as revealing as the plot, showing a novelist revising in public.
11655-fate-knocks-at-the-door-a-novel:
Will Levington Comfort's 1912 novel, Fate Knocks at the Door, takes its title from Beethoven's words on the first notes of the Fifth Symphony: thus fate knocks at the door. Parts run from Asia, allegro con brio, through New York, andante con moto, to Equatoria.

Chapters open with a great wind, a pack train in Luzon, red pigment of service, and that Adelaide passion. Later chapters bring the long-awaited woman, two Davids, and shadowy sisters. A woman in the book names a man The Modern, after fragments brought by Vina and David Cairns. The novel is a romance of travel, war, and destiny.
11697-mare-nostrum-our-sea-a-novel:
Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's Mare Nostrum, translated by Charlotte Brewster Jordan in 1919, opens with Captain Ulysses Ferragut, whose first gallantries at ten were with an empress six hundred years old. His father, a notary near the cathedral, took wife and son to mass in a quiet chapel rather than to cardinal's pomp.

Chapters follow Mater Amphitrite, Pater Oceanus, Freya, and the aquarium of Naples, with the wiles of Circe and the sin of Ulysses. Later Ferragut is offered a short, well-paid job, supplying German Mediterranean submarines with petrol on the way back to Barcelona. The novel is a sea story of war, love, and the Mediterranean.
11901-tommy-and-grizel:
J. M. Barrie's Tommy and Grizel, published in 1900 with a 1912 edition illustrated by Bernard Partridge, follows Tommy Sandys from childhood games to adult love. Early chapters show Tommy finding a way, searching for treasure, and building a myth around himself, while Grizel, with her crooked smile, watches him with an inquiring eye.

As Tommy grows, his flights of fancy desert him when real feeling is required. His bond with Grizel deepens into a long duel of affection, pride, and misunderstanding. Barrie sets the story in a Scottish village world of dens, ghosts, and quiet houses, and treats Tommy's charm as both his gift and his flaw.
11904-ailsa-paige-a-novel:
Chambers's 1910 novel Ailsa Paige opens with an epigraph on life as a mixture of a little good with much evil. The beautiful is linked with the revolting, bathos with pathos, and the commonplace with the sublime. Published by D. Appleton and Company, with illustrations, it belongs to Chambers's popular fiction of the period.

The story is set amid the excitement of a city preparing volunteer regiments, where stocks fall but theatres grow fuller. People welcome excitement after a dreadful year of lethargy. Through Ailsa and the men around her, Chambers mixes romance with the restlessness of a society on the edge of war. One man in that circle is an odd, high-flown fellow who tries hard to win over someone he thinks dislikes him.
11987-by-advice-of-counsel:
Arthur Train's By Advice of Counsel, published in March 1921, presents adventures of the celebrated firm of Tutt and Tutt, attorneys and counsellors at law, with a frontispiece by Arthur William Brown. Contents include The Shyster, The Kid and the Camel, and Contempt of court, stories built around the firm's courtroom craft.

Train, himself a lawyer, gives his attorneys cases that turn on language, procedure, and human motive: an Arabic interpreter struggling to render a contemptuous article on marriage law. Arguments that domestic relations, not delegated to the federal government, remain with the states. The stories entertain while showing how law, in practice, depends on words, witnesses, and the temper of a judge.
12016-the-merchant-of-berlin-an-historic:
L. Mühlbach's historical novel The Merchant of Berlin, translated from German by Amory Coffin, M.D., appeared in this edition in 1910. Its contents open with a festival and a workman's holiday, then move through brother and sister, Feodor von Brenda, Mr. Kretschmer of the Vossian Gazette, and the cowards' race.

The plot turns on invasion and civic courage: an interrupted festival, a leader of the people. The Russian at the gates, with a chapter urging the reader to be prudent. Mühlbach, a popular German novelist, writes history as melodrama, using a Berlin merchant and his circle to show how ordinary citizens faced occupation, rumor, and the demands of patriotism.
12024-bred-in-the-bone-or-like-father-li:
Bred in the Bone, or Like Father, Like Son, a novel published in New York in 1872, opens with Carew of Crompton. Its author also wrote A Beggar on Horseback, Gwendoline's Harvest, and Carlyon's Year. The first chapter insists that anyone who lived in Breakneckshire twenty years earlier, or anywhere in the Midlands, would know Carew's name without being told.

The title states the book's theme: character inherited, for better or worse, from father to son. Through the Carew family and their neighbors, the novel explores how a son repeats, resists, or redeems a father's faults. It does so in the manner of Victorian sensation fiction, with country houses, family secrets, and strong feeling.
12177-the-precipice-a-novel:
Elia W. Peattie published this novel in 1914, at the height of debate over women roles, work, and marriage. Its heroine, Kate Barrington, leaves college with honors and returns to a small Illinois town full of plans.

Kate tries teaching, charity work, and friendship with women who have chosen very different lives, while suitors and family press her toward marriage. Peattie frames the story with a fanfare image: women everywhere hearing a call to new lives, whether they answer or not. The novel avoids easy triumph, showing gains that cost comfort and safety. It reads as a thoughtful, middlebrow feminist novel of its moment, sympathetic to ambition and honest about its price.
12243-round-the-block-an-american-novel:
John Bell Bouton published Round the Block in 1864, an American novel of New York life, with illustrations. Bouton sets the story on a single city block, following neighbors through a year of social climbing, speculation, and romance.

Book first opens on New Year Day with three bachelors, peeps, and a character named Quigg, while later books follow Mrs. Slapman at home and a set of humbugs called Metropoliganians, tarred and feathered in a back lot for sixteen dollars damage. The novel satirizes city manners, boarding houses, and money schemes. Bouton writes in the lively, episodic manner of mid-century American humor. The book gives a vivid street-level view of Civil War New York.
12279-the-maid-at-arms-a-novel:
Robert W. Chambers published The Maid-at-Arms in 1902, a novel of the American Revolution in New York, illustrated by Howard Chandler Christy. Chambers, known for romantic histories, sets the story among patroons, cousins, and soldiers.

Chapters run from the road to Varick house through a night at the patroon and riding the bounds. Later come hidden fire, the ghost ring, and the maid-at-arms herself, on duty, on scout, and at Oriskany. A mid-book scene has Cecile toss her head over a minuet invitation from a Half-moon officer, while Harry begs a lace handkerchief. The novel mixes love, espionage, and battle. Chambers writes with color and pace, favoring brave girls and gallant officers.
12303-fated-to-be-free-a-novel:
Jean Ingelow published Fated to be Free in 1875, a novel connected to her earlier Off the Skelligs. Ingelow, a popular Victorian poet and novelist, writes in her preface that authors who explain works that should explain themselves make the case no better.

The novel follows two stories linked by fate and family, with characters like Johnnie and Crayshaw trading threats and lisped promises about ponies sold at Easter. Ingelow themes are providence, duty, and the freedom that comes from accepting one lot. The style is earnest and domestic, with long moral reflections. The book shows a Victorian woman writer wrestling with determinism and faith, in a romance that values character over plot.
12304-nancy-a-novel:
Rhoda Broughton published Nancy as a novel in 1874 with D. Appleton in New York. Broughton, author of Good-bye, Sweetheart and Red as a Rose is She, wrote sensation fiction with a sharp eye for young women choices.

Nancy, the heroine, narrates her own courtship and marriage, opening with a verse about a couple who fell out at eve and kissed again with tears. The plot follows quarrels, reconciliations, and the small decisions that shape a marriage, with Broughton usual wit and frankness about feeling. A mid-book scene has Nancy chasing a departing figure through mist, resolved to speak truth after all. The novel is a lively Victorian romance, less scandalous than Broughton reputation suggests.
12335-overland-a-novel:
J. W. De Forest published Overland in 1871, a novel of New Mexico and the Southwest. De Forest, author of Kate Beaumont and Miss Ravenel Conversion, sets the story in Santa Fe, then an undergrown, decrepit, out-at-elbows ancient hidalgo of a town.

Santa Fe, two hundred and seventy years old, held fewer than five thousand people, yet served as metropolis of a vast country. The plot follows travelers, soldiers, and settlers across deserts and mountains, with a mid-book heroine rushing toward a man in a fissure, crying out to save him. De Forest writes with realism about frontier hardship, race, and law. The novel is an early American western, more sober than the dime novels of its day.
12345-friday-the-thirteenth-a-novel:
Thomas W. Lawson published Friday, the Thirteenth in 1907, a novel of Wall Street panic and manipulation, with a frontispiece by Sigismond de Ivanowski. Lawson, a Boston stock operator turned reformer, wrote from inside the market he attacked.

The plot follows brokers, promoters, and a heroine whose great blue eyes lose something as the panic builds. A mid-book scene has Bob dwell on the number twenty, tantalizing traders into sticking by their guns, while Barry Conant nerve returns with a piercing take it. Lawson exposes pools, corners, and the power of exchanges to ruin small investors. The novel is a muckraking thriller, part romance, part indictment of American finance.
12347-the-morgesons-a-novel:
Elizabeth Stoddard published The Morgesons in 1901, a novel of village and domestic life that later critics praised as ahead of its time. Stoddard preface says environment caused her to write these novels, though she never dreamed imagination would lead her back to her native village.

The story follows the Morgeson women through love, marriage, and disappointment, with a heroine who declares herself changed and eager to begin life when she might have felt done with it. Ben, Veronica, and other kin circle through the narrative. Stoddard writes with irony and psychological candor unusual for her era. The novel is now read as a pioneering American work about women inner lives.
12348-richard-vandermarck-a-novel:
Mrs. Sidney S. Harris published Richard Vandermarck in 1871, a novel dedicated to S. S. H. Harris, author of Rutledge and St. Philip, writes of New York society and family secrets.

Chapters run from Varick Street and very good luck through Kilian, companions, and a tutor, to three weeks too late, Sunday, a dance, and every day from six to seven. A mid-book voice declares itself a child no longer, in the flush and strength of manhood, with half a century of suffering yet in frame and brain. The novel follows Richard through love, duty, and inheritance. Harris writes domestic romance with moral earnestness, in the manner of her popular novels.
12385-the-italians-a-novel:
Frances Elliot's 1875 novel is set in Lucca, in Tuscany, and opens with crowds pressing toward the city for the feast of the Holy Countenance, its carved relic. Peasants, priests, carts and holiday crowds fill the roads, and the Marchesa Guinigi, the young Enrica, Count Marescotti and Count Nobili move through that vivid social world.

Calumny, passion, a trial and burned papers drive later parts, as Enrica faces judgment and the marchesa's power is tested. Elliot uses church, salon and street to show Italian society after unification, with its old rank, new talk and sharp gossip. The novel reads as a portrait of a place as much as a plot, Lucca itself standing close to the centre.
12442-in-the-days-of-my-youth-a-novel:
Amelia B. Edwards's 1874 novel opens at Saxonholme, a quaint hamlet in a warm hollow among hills, woods and parks. Red-brick mansions, turreted and gabled, peer through green vistas, and a silver thread of streamlet runs below. The narrator recalls birthplace and parentage in a voice steeped in place.

From that English beginning the story widens to youth, love and travel, as the heroine leaves home and learns the world. Edwards, later famed for Egyptian travel writing, writes here as a novelist of feeling and scene. The book offers a Victorian coming-of-age tale, fond of landscape and manners, and told with the confidence of a writer who loved old houses and young hopes.
12452-fort-lafayette-or-love-and-secessi:
Benjamin Wood's 1862 novel, Fort Lafayette, or Love and Secession, opens at a pleasant villa on the southern bank of the James River, below Richmond. A white stone mansion, ringed by veranda, elms and old oaks, houses a family soon divided by secession. Epigraphs from Shakespeare, Thomson and Venice Preserved plead for peace.

Love crosses the political divide as war presses on the household, and Fort Lafayette itself, a prison for political suspects, shadows the tale. Wood writes as a wartime novelist, earnest about union and affection. The book remains a contemporary Civil War romance, written while its events were still unfolding.
12453-miriam-monfort-a-novel:
Published in New York in 1873, this novel is told by a daughter looking back at her parents' lives. Her mother, Miriam Harz, was cut off by her own people for marrying outside her faith, then crossed the Atlantic to a new life. Her father, Reginald Monfort, was a younger son of a noble house and an army officer with little money of his own.

The narrative follows the costs of that marriage: pride, poverty, illness and the care of a small child left without near kin. Monfort Hall, family rank and old wounds shape the daughter's own story as she grows up. The book treats faith, class and family loyalty as forces that bind and break households, told in the measured voice of a woman judging the past.
1262-the-heritage-of-the-desert-a-novel:
Zane Grey sends Jack Hare, a sick young Easterner, to the Utah desert, where the Mormon rancher August Naab nurses him back to strength. Hare learns to ride and shoot, falls in love, and stands with Naab's family against rustlers and a villainous elder in a land of red cliffs and hidden water.

Grey writes the desert as both beauty and trial, and the novel's action runs from stampedes to gunfights. The book, one of his earliest successes, fixed his formula of the tenderfoot made whole by the West. It remains a sturdy, sunlit western.
12642-the-lady-s-album-of-fancy-work-for:
The Lady's Album of Fancy Work for 1850 offers novel, elegant and useful designs in knitting, netting, crochet, braiding and embroidery, with clear directions for working patterns. Publishers, encouraged by the welcome for former efforts, issued a similar production for 1850, anxious to preserve favour so flatteringly accorded.

Every care, they say, was taken to make the album as attractive and useful as possible for ladies of the United Kingdom. Patterns, diagrams and instructions fill the volume, for parlour work and household decoration. The album survives as a charming record of Victorian women's craft, and as a practical book still usable by makers today.
12656-the-boy-allies-at-lie-ge-or-throug:
Clair W. Hayes's 1915 Boy Allies at Liège, or Through Lines of Steel, opens in Berlin, where Hal Paine dashes into a great hotel with Chester Crawford, shouting that war has been declared. Mrs. Paine, rising, steadies herself on a chair, face pale, asking if millions of men will again fly at each other's throats.

The Kaiser has declared war on France, Hal confirms, after years of peace. Boys, mothers and a continent on the brink fill the opening, before Hal and Chester slip through lines of steel toward Liège. Hayes writes brisk wartime adventure for boys, patriotic and immediate. The book launches a series that followed its heroes across the Great War's fronts.
12764-the-forty-niners-a-chronicle-of-th:
Stewart Edward White's 1918 history follows California from Spanish rule to the gold rush and its rough new cities. It starts with missions and Mexican rule, then tracks the rush of 1849 across the plains, by Panama, and into the diggings. Camps, towns, law courts, and fire all shape the fast growth he describes.

Much of the book turns on order breaking down and being rebuilt, from vigilante groups in 1851 and 1856 to San Francisco finding its feet as a real city. White stresses speed: in a few years California passed through stages that took other lands centuries. The result reads as a vivid, plain account of how gold, migration, and violence forged a new state.
12972-people-like-that-a-novel:
Kate Langley Bosher's 1916 novel People Like That follows a twenty-six-year-old woman of modest means who chooses to live in Scarborough Square. Friends and kin call the choice amazing and inexplicable, and heated criticism follows her refusal to explain. She holds that what a person does matters to only three or four people.

A later talk with Jack Peebles turns on her creed: if people of all sorts knew one another better, there would be less injustice, less indifference, and greater friendship. Bosher writes with warmth about class, kindness, and independence. The novel suits readers who like gentle social fiction with a moral centre.
13017-five-nights-a-novel:
Victoria Cross's 1908 novel is built in five parts, each named for a night: gold, violet, black, crimson, and white. The parts run from the Taku Inlet and a tea-shop to a studio, Mayfair, San Francisco, and the shadow of a volcano. A narrator tells of a love that changes color with each night it passes through.

Cross writes with frank, heated detail, and the novel's scenes turn on desire, loss, and freedom sought at high cost. One night brings a posed, revealing moment in a studio; later nights bring separation and a search for the beloved. The book is a bold Edwardian romance, more concerned with feeling than with plot, and it does not shy from its own heat.
13178-broken-to-the-plow-a-novel:
Charles Caldwell Dobie's novel Broken to the Plow, published by Harper and Brothers, opens at four in the afternoon with Fred Starratt sent for oyster cocktails and cigars. Fred must touch old Wetherbee for money, meaning to ask five dollars but deciding on twenty-five, since more demands will come before month's end. The cashier grows crustier with each draft, and Fred's life is a round of small debts.

Helen, his wife, figures the office politics coldly, seeing that Brauer holds his own job while others do the work. She wonders if her efficiency came from Red Cross service in wartime. Ginger, another woman in Fred's orbit, knows his deceitful bravado and takes what he offers without pride. Dobie's novel is a study of a man broken to routine, and of women who see clearer than he does.
13212-the-wild-olive-a-novel:
Published in May 1910 by Harper and Brothers, The Wild Olive, by the author of The Inner Shrine, opens with a fugitive in the Adirondacks at twilight. A tall young man, hatless, coatless, and barefoot, pauses on a wood road as wind plays through forest and crag. A hundred men, the frontispiece says, beat the mountain to find him.

Later, Ford meets an English couple who scorn firms that ask what a man can do, and a woman who talks of wool and wheat with feverish pride. An envelope addressed to Miss Strange bears tiny words in a corner: The Wild Olive. Miriam claims a clerk wrote it by accident. The novel is a romance of flight, identity, and love, set between wild country and city talk.
13257-the-american-baron-a-novel:
James De Mille's 1872 American Baron, published by Harper in New York, is a comic novel of Americans abroad and English society. Minnie and Kitty, two sisters, meet a solemn stranger who follows them to the Hermitage, and a baron who fetches Hawbury to explain himself. De Mille, author of The Dodge Club, writes with light, farcical energy.

Lady Dalrymple, hearing Hawbury travels with a friend, takes it as fresh proof of his infatuation with Minnie, and wonders how he can befriend a man she counts her persecutor. The baron proceeds to explain the matter and ask Hawbury's opinion. The novel turns on mistaken identity, courtship, and the clash of American bluntness with English manners.
13716-a-trip-to-venus-a-novel:
John Munro's 1897 novel sends a small party from Earth to Venus by means of a new force and an electric orrery, a device that models the planets. The travellers debate how life might arise on a cooling world, with mists condensing into seas and life appearing in due course, before they set out across space.

On Venus they find crater lands, luminous frogs and moths, singing birds, and a people who live in family households under a father's rule, with the mother placed between man and child. The story mixes hard speculation about planets with a gentle utopia, and it ends with the return home. It is an early British work of space travel fiction, written when electricity still seemed full of wonders.
13812-sir-mortimer-a-novel:
Mary Johnston published Sir Mortimer in 1904, a romance of Elizabethan adventure. Sir Mortimer, a gentleman adventurer, sails with Baldry's ship, the little Star, and faces charges of treason. Damaris, a heroine who envies and loves in turn, stands at the story's heart. Friars, duels, and sea fights fill the chapters.

Johnston mixes history with romance, using maps, ships, and court intrigue. A scene of glittering rock, debated as marcasite or mother of gold, shows the lure of treasure. Sir John thrusts himself between foes in one illustration. The novel follows Johnston's earlier successes To Have and to Hold and Prisoners of Hope. It offers swashbuckling history with a strong heroine.
14039-through-stained-glass-a-novel:
George Agnew Chamberlain published Through Stained Glass in 1915, a novel of Brazil, Kentucky, and war's aftermath. In 1866, the American minister at Rio turns from Kentucky colonels wandering the capital to a nightmare despatch for Seward. Agents of Southern states, the minister fears, plot distant chimeras while Reconstruction grips Washington.

Later scenes follow children jumping and clapping, with little Natalie clutching her mother's skirts. Shenton shouts that they are coming. Chamberlain weaves family, politics, and exotic setting into romance. The novel suits readers of early twentieth-century adventure. Its title image, light through coloured glass, fits its layered plot.
14263-katrine-a-novel:
Elinor Macartney Lane's 1909 novel Katrine opens under southern pines, where a meeting in the woods and a kindness with mixed motives set the story moving. A promise in the pines, a Paris preface, and a dedication to Grant B. Schley frame a heroine who waits years, as the frontispiece caption declares. Chapters carry her from southern woods to Paris drawing rooms and back again.

Grief and business tangle in the middle. Katrine hides in a leafy lodge room by a brook, throwing herself on pine needles while remembered endearments burn like a wound. Later, Dermott discusses Ravenel, railroads, and compromises with Mademoiselle Dulany, insisting no stage play or newspaper work will follow and Mrs. Ravenel need never know the facts. Lane writes romantic fiction with a firm hand, and Katrine's loyalty, tested by love and money, holds the novel together.
14303-queed-a-novel:
Henry Sydnor Harrison's 1911 novel Queed introduces a young man in spectacles whose cosmos, a frontispiece warns, is all ego. Contents tease the plot: a citizen meets Behemoth the great pleasure-dog, Mrs. Paynter's boarding house, Charlotte Lee Weyland as landlady's agent, and Doctor Queed refusing board. Colonel Cowles, military political economist, offers remunerative employment, while two stars fight for Queed's future.

Sharlee, as friends call Charlotte, dominates the social scenes. She stifles a yawn with gloved fingertips, rings for water, drinks slowly before a mantel mirror, and keeps a young man waiting past his promised half hour. An old man later thanks Queed in the dark for friendship in his remaining time, gripping his chair arms while lamplight shows a rakish cap and mismatched eyes. Queed learns, slowly, that intellect without affection leaves a life thin. Comic, sharp, and humane, the novel charmed a wide audience.
14469-the-english-novel:
George Saintsbury's 1913 history traces the English novel from medieval romance through Lyly, Swift, Fielding, Scott, Austen, and Thackeray to the late Victorians. Saintsbury, a professor at Edinburgh, wrote as a critic of wide reading and strong opinions.

Chapters weigh the rise of prose fiction, the four great eighteenth-century novelists, and the mid-Victorian masters, with digressions on inset tales and moral license in Fielding. The book is learned and opinionated, sometimes quaint in judgment, but it maps the form's growth with energy and remains a landmark of early novel criticism.
14681-the-art-of-travel:
Francis Galton's 1872 handbook teaches travellers how to manage in wild countries, from first enquiries and organising an expedition to the close of the journey. Outfit, medicine, surveying instruments and log-books are treated as seriously as courage, because small failures far from help can turn fatal.

Practical chapters cover climbing, cattle and harness, carriages, swimming, rafts and boats, fords and bridges, clothing, bedding, tents, fire, food and drinking water. Guns, signals, compass bearings, caches, knots, timber, metals and leather follow. Galton writes for explorers, soldiers and settlers, and his advice still shows how nineteenth-century travel depended on craft, foresight and repair.
14867-oriental-religions-and-christianit:
Frank F. Ellinwood's 1892 lectures, given on the Ely Foundation to students of Union Seminary in New York in 1891, compare eastern faiths with the Christian faith. Ellinwood, secretary of the Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions and a lecturer on comparative religion, writes for future missionaries.

His first lecture urges a clear grasp of other faiths. It warns that the new study of religion needs care, and that study of eastern systems had too long been left to hostile scholars. Later lectures weigh mission work, timid believers' fears and the claims of other faiths. The book is a period work of comparative religion, earnest, partisan and learned.
15073-the-colossus-a-novel:
Opie Read's novel The Colossus opens looking back at early life. A sleepy village and a fussy old man appear, then all was darkness and a strange request. Read also wrote The Carpetbagger, Old Ebenezer and A Kentucky Colonel. Dissecting a motive, waiting at the station and a mother's affection follow.

Domain of a great merchant, interviewers and romping with a girl follow. Acknowledgement by society, a democracy, butting against a wall and a different handwriting lead to a story told, an arouser of the sleepy and more. Read writes Southern and American life with humour and size, and his colossus is a man, a business or a town grown too large for the village that made it.
15135-the-three-black-pennys-a-novel:
Joseph Hergesheimer's 1917 novel follows three generations of a Pennsylvania iron family, each marked by a black penny, through furnace, forge, and metal. The book opens in October twilight, with frost gilding maples and sumach turning wine red in wooded hills. A dedication recalls June nights and winter dusks at Dower House.

Each part traces a man shaped by iron work, wealth, and will, as the family firm rises and changes. Hergesheimer writes in rich, sensory prose, lingering on houses, fields, and mills. Readers of American family sagas will find the novel atmospheric, ambitious, and deeply tied to place.
15185-quiet-talks-on-john-s-gospel:
S. D. Gordon's 1915 devotional book talks through the Gospel of John as a story of a lover wooing his beloved. Chapters move from John's own story to closer wooing at a supper and a moonlit walk, then to a night and day of hardening hearts. A tryst kept by surprise and a breakfast by Galilee close the arc.

Gordon opens with Francis Thompson's Hound of Heaven, a poem of a soul fleeing and pursued. His talks are plain, warm, and meant for quiet reading rather than scholarship. Christians who like devotional prose will find the book gentle, personal, and focused on Christ's love.
15265-the-quest-of-the-silver-fleece-a-n:
W. E. B. Du Bois's 1911 novel follows Zora, a Black Southern girl, through school, town, and cotton fields in a quest for a silver fleece. Chapters move from dreams and Miss Mary Taylor to planting, flowering, promise, and the rape of the fleece. A cotton corner, a dying mother, and a weaving close the arc.

Du Bois blends romance with a sharp portrait of race, labor, and education in the South, as Zora and Alwyn learn and campaign. The novel's later chapters take her to Congress and a vision of her own. Readers will find the book ambitious, earnest, and central to Du Bois's fiction.
15275-bessie-s-fortune-a-novel:
Mary Holmes's 1888 novel Bessie's Fortune, dedicated to her nephew Walter Twichell, opens with the Jerrolds of Boston and Grey Jerrold's park. Thanksgiving, an old man and a boy, Miss Betsey McPherson, and a dinner introducing Bessie follow. A horror at a farmhouse and a secret story drive the plot.

Later parts take Bessie to Stoneleigh, Monte Carlo, and Penrhyn Park, through seven years and a fortune's twists. Holmes writes in her popular domestic style, with sentiment and moral warmth. Fans of Victorian domestic novels will find Bessie earnest, eventful, and full of family feeling.
15278-the-ramrodders-a-novel:
Holman Day's 1910 political novel opens in Fort Canibas, where war and peace have swapped corners between two meeting-houses. Chapters trace the baiting of an ancient lion, a line-up for a fight, Dennis Kavanagh's girl, and a duke at bay. Caucuses planned and run, deals, and ideals follow.

Day, author of King Spruce, writes of Maine politics with humor, dialect, and a keen eye for bosses, converts, and mule teams. A governor and a maid, a girl's heart, and a truce close the tangle. Fans of political fiction will enjoy the novel's bustle and its affection for small-state democracy.
15293-influences-of-geographic-environme:
Ellen Churchill Semple's large study, dedicated to Friedrich Ratzel, builds a system of anthropo-geography from his work. A Milton motto on stars drawing light fronts the book. Chapters treat geographic barriers, nature-made highways, climate, and the interplay of factors that shape peoples, colonies, and religions.

Semple argues that humans are products of the earth's surface, though responses vary by time, habitat, and history. Her book shaped American geography, even where later scholars reject its determinism. Readers of geography and intellectual history will find it ambitious, learned, and very much of its era.
15321-tracy-park-a-novel:
Mary Holmes's 1886 novel Tracy Park opens with a telegram from the Brevoort House in New York, sent by Arthur Tracey to Frank Tracy at Shannondale. Arthur has landed from the Scotia and will take the afternoon train, asking for someone to meet him at the station. The quiet town story starts from that wire.

Frank Tracy, Tracy Park, and Shannondale society then unfold through love, secrets, and family claims, in Holmes's popular domestic style. A Dickens motto on pressing forward fronts the book. Fans of Victorian domestic novels will find Tracy Park earnest, plot-rich, and full of period manners.
15414-the-littlest-rebel:
Edward Peple's novel, published in 1914, is set in Virginia during the American Civil War. Its center is seven-year-old Virginia Cary, called Virgie, a bold and charming child in a household worn thin by war. Her mother struggles to clothe her from scraps while soldiers, shortages, and danger press close around their home.

Virgie's high spirits carry much of the story, but the plot turns on a hard wartime errand: a pass meant to carry mother and daughter through Federal lines toward Richmond. The child meets officers from both sides and wins them over with frank talk and nerve. Beneath the humor sits a portrait of a Southern family trying to keep its dignity and its bonds intact while war remakes daily life.
15430-the-lever-a-novel:
William Dana Orcutt published this novel in 1911, opening with an Archimedes motto about a lever long enough to move the world. The dedication praises justice and right as woman's creed. The story opens on the maple-lined road from Washington to Chevy Chase. A girl in a carriage looks back at a young man in an automobile, then blushes at her own notice of him.

Alice, her companion Eleanor, and ten-year-old Patricia give the opening its social sparkle, and Allen, the young man, soon enters Alice's orbit in offices and drawing rooms. Business papers, managers, and talk of power run through later scenes, as Alice learns how influence works. Orcutt's novel mixes romance with a study of leverage: who moves whom, in Washington society and beyond it.
15431-success-a-novel:
Samuel Hopkins Adams published this novel in 1921, in three parts titled Enchantment, Vision, and Fulfillment. It opens at a lonely desert station called Manzanita, a mile from a small frame town on a railroad line. Cactus blooms after rare rain, scrub pine spreads north, and storm clouds gather in the southwest.

The story follows a search for success in the American West, tracing how early hopes harden into a plan and then into a life's work. Adams sets ambition against a harsh, beautiful landscape, where towns are thin and the railroad cuts a hard line through the waste. The novel's interest lies in that slow change: a young dreamer learning what success costs, and what it leaves behind, in a new country.
15596-bressant-a-novel:
Julian Hawthorne published this novel in 1873, with page images from Michigan State University Libraries and the Making of America Collection. Thirty-two chapters or more run from Professor Valeyon losing his handkerchief and signs of a thunder-shower to Sophie and Cornelia entering into a covenant. A business transaction, a tea-rose, and Cornelia undoing a knot follow.

Later chapters bring great expectations, a daguerreotype, nursing, and an untimely reminiscence. Parting an anchor, Sophie's confession, and a flank movement lead to Bressant confiding a secret to the fountain. Locked up, armed neutrality, and another intermission follow. Bressant takes a vacation, fact meets fancy, and found and lost close the set. Hawthorne writes a romance of love, secrets, and moral trial in the shadow of his father's name.
15709-the-christmas-angel:
A children's Christmas story by Abbie Farwell Brown, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1910. Reginald Birch supplied the pictures. Miss Terry, a stern old lady, opens a play box of childhood toys and finds her past waiting inside. Brown writes with warmth for young readers and for adults who recall old toys.

Jack-in-the-box, a flannel dog, Noah's ark, and a doll named Miranda each take a turn before the fire. The paper angel, Angelina, hangs on the tree and stirs memories of Miss Terry's brother Tom, fifty years before. By Christmas Day the old toys have softened a hard heart. The tale endures as a gentle fable on memory, kindness, and second chances.
15730-a-short-history-of-a-long-travel-f:
A spiritual allegory by Stephen Crisp, a Quaker writer of the seventeenth century. Crisp tells of a youth who hears of the house of God, where all happiness waits, and longs to enter it. No one can tell him where the house stands, yet the desire burns in him. The tale follows his long travel from Babylon, the world, toward Bethel, the house of God.

On the road the traveller meets guides, false and true, and learns to test talk against inner light. Crisp writes in plain, earnest prose, close to Bunyan's manner but with a Quaker voice. Temptation, doubt, and steady hope mark each stage. The book still moves readers who know a search for faith: short, direct, and full of quiet fire.
15956-vellenaux-a-novel:
A novel by E. W. Forrest, author of The Blue Jacket and Ned Fortesque, issued in 1874. Forrest's preface thanks a generous public for favour to his former works, which led him to try a novel. Vellenaux blends truth and imagination so closely that readers can scarcely tell where one begins and the other ends. History and fiction share the pages.

Scenes from the Sikh wars fill the book: the siege of Mooltan and the battle of Chillianwalla, never to be forgotten. Soldiers, sieges, and Indian landscapes carry the plot. Forrest writes with a veteran's eye for battle. The novel stands as a stirring war romance: a hero, a war, and history told as adventure.
16053-the-haunted-chamber-a-novel:
Published in 1888 under the pen name The Duchess, this novel opens at dusk around an old castle by the sea. Twilight lies on flowers, fountains, and elms, while ivy climbs the ancient walls past mullioned windows toward an old tower. There, in the haunted chamber, shadows lie heaviest, as if to hide the scene of some terrible crime.

Romance and mystery grow from that gloomy room, with love, fear, and old secrets driving the plot. The Duchess, Mrs. Hungerford, was a best-selling writer of society romance, and her castle setting gives the tale a gothic edge. Readers who enjoy Victorian romance with a touch of the supernatural will find this an atmospheric escape.
16092-the-wharf-by-the-docks-a-novel:
Florence Warden sets this novel among the wharves and back streets of London's East End, where dock life shapes work, gossip, and courtship. The story centers on a proud young woman with light-blue eyes and a haughty air, whose looks draw men even as she seems to push them away. A visitor named Max watches her draw water in an outhouse yard, and their guarded flirtation opens the tale.

Warden builds her plot from such small meetings, misunderstandings, and the secrets of houses thought empty. The docks give the book its rough, busy backdrop, while romance and suspicion drive the action. Readers of Victorian popular fiction will find a fast, atmospheric story of love and intrigue by the Thames.
16186-a-little-rebel:
Published in Montreal in 1891 by John Lovell and Son, A Little Rebel is a novel by The Duchess, author of Her Last Throw and April's Lady. Chapter one finds a professor before an untasted breakfast, the very picture of dismay, with two letters open before him. One tells of an old friend's death, its opening lines all he has read, while the other, written by that friend a week before dying, he has already read three times through.

The second letter is urgent and pleading, and its contents fill the professor with ever-growing consternation. From that morning of letters grows a story of duty, rebellion, and affection in the Duchess's popular style. Readers of Victorian romance will enjoy its brisk, emotional opening and its lively heroine.
16366-the-workingman-s-paradise-an-austr:
William Lane's Workingman's Paradise, first published in 1892 under the pen name John Miller, is an Australian labour novel in two parts. Part one, The Woman Tempted Him, runs from Nellie showing Ned round. Sweating in the Sydney slums, shorn like sheep, and Saturday night in Paddy's Market follow. Chapters ask were they conspirators and where the evil really lies. This is socialism, one chapter declares.

Part two, He Knew Himself Naked, follows the slaughter of an innocent, the road to Queensland, a woman's whim, the waning moon, and unemployment. Lane writes as a socialist organizer for working readers, earnest about wages, faith, and love. The novel remains a key document of Australia's early labour movement and its dreams.
16371-bluebell-a-novel:
Mrs. G. C. Huddleston's 1875 novel Bluebell follows a young heroine through Canadian social life, from sweet seventeen and tobogganing to sleigh clubs, woodland walks, and a perilous sail. Later chapters carry Bluebell to the old country, with letters, proposals, and rough weather along the way. Some pages of the source scan are marked unreadable.

The novel mixes romance with lively Canadian scenes: garrison fun, lake roads, and northern lights. Huddleston keeps the tone light and the plot moving. For readers of Victorian domestic romance, the book offers a rare Canadian setting and a heroine whose debut spans two worlds.
16559-the-life-story-of-an-old-rebel:
John Denvir tells his life as an old rebel in this 1910 Dublin memoir. Early chapters recall coming over from Ireland, the Nation newspaper, and the Hibernians, then O'Connell in Liverpool, the famine, and the No-Popery mania. The Irish Revolutionary Brotherhood, the rising of 1867, the Manchester martyrdom, and the Home Rule movement follow.

Denvir writes as a participant, naming Stephens, Davitt, and the men of the rescue plots. The memoir mixes personal memory with movement history. Readers of Irish nationalism will find a first-hand account from a lifelong fighter, frank and full of names.
16574-the-twins-a-domestic-novel:
Martin Farquhar Tupper sets this 1851 domestic novel at Burleigh-Singleton, a pleasant little watering-place on England's south coast, fit for small incomes and good consciences. The town boasts cheap meat and drink but preeminent dullness in men and manners. Breezy Heights, water-meadows by the dark Mullet, and Pacton Park give the scene its variety.

Tupper, author of Proverbial Philosophy, writes a quiet tale of twins, neighbors, and domestic life. The opening chapter fixes place, time, and circumstance with care. Readers of Victorian domestic fiction will find a gentle, old-fashioned novel of a seaside town and its people.
16703-a-comedy-of-masks-a-novel:
Ernest Dowson and Arthur Moore set this 1893 novel in the tarry docklands between Tower and Poplar, where Rainham's Dock, called Blackpool, once built wooden leviathans. Models of those ships still ornament its antique office, but iron ships and the Clyde and Tyne have ended Thames building. Fewer ships put in for repair, and the yard fades.

Dowson and Moore write with decadent grace, in the London of artists, docks, and masks. The novel's opening fixes place with loving detail. Readers of 1890s fiction will find a moody, elegant tale of a riverside world slipping away.
16730-mike-fletcher-a-novel:
George Moore wrote this 1889 novel of London night life, art, and restless youth. It opens at a famed restaurant, where diners, drinkers, and hangers-on crowd the bar and the long gallery. Mike Fletcher moves through that gay, loud world, chasing art, love, and a place of his own.

Moore paints the scene in thick detail: silk, light, noise, and talk that never quite says what it means. Beneath the glitter lies a young man's wish to matter and his fear of being used up by the town. The novel is a sharp, early naturalist portrait of a city that feeds on its young and spits them out changed.
16798-elster-s-folly-a-novel:
Mrs. Henry Wood wrote this novel, here in a 1916 edition, best known as the author of East Lynne and The Channings. Chapters move from an early train and a countess-dowager, through jealousy, an inquest, fever, weddings, strangers, and cross-questioning, to a shed razed and a dowager's alarm. Val, Maude, and Mr. Carr carry much of the plot.

Wood builds a long domestic mystery from small town talk, secrets, and sudden turns. Jealousy, money, and marriage press on each house, and the truth comes out in stages. Readers who like long Victorian family novels will find plenty of plot, feeling, and moral weight in this tale of folly and its costs.
16946-kitty-canary-a-novel:
Kate Langley Bosher's 1913 novel follows Kitty Canary, a young woman boarding for the summer and sure, at last, that she is in love. The man she favors was once engaged to Elizabeth Hamilton Carter, and the break between them hangs over the house. Kitty watches her rival with sharp, funny eyes, and she speaks in a bright first-person voice from the opening page.

Much of the fun comes from Kitty's blunt judgments and her muddled hopes, set against small-town visits, talk, and courtship. Under the jokes, the book asks what real love looks like when pride, old ties, and showy charm get in the way. It is a light, warm romance with a heroine who thinks aloud and learns as she goes.
16968-the-bad-man-a-novel:
Charles Hanson Towne wrote this 1921 novel, based on Porter Emerson Browne's play, issued by Putnam's Sons in New York and London and dedicated to Holbrook Blinn, who played the bad man. Chapters show a young American with courage in a new country, a neighbor eyeing his ranch, whispers of border wealth, Uncle Henry speaking his mind, and Red revealing his heart.

Towne turns a stage hit into a western tale of ranch, border, and a bad man whose charm hides danger. The plot moves fast, with talk, threats, and a fight for land and love. Readers who like old western melodramas will find a brisk, theatrical novel, full of border color and a villain who steals the show.
17062-the-crock-of-gold-a-rural-novel:
Martin Farquhar Tupper, author of Proverbial Philosophy, wrote this 1851 rural novel, The Crock of Gold, issued by Silas Andrus in Hartford. It opens with Roger Acton, a laborer, waking at five on a raw March morning, dark and bitterly cold, rain beating on a crazy cottage window. Roger must rise, for open weather comes by sunrise, his work lies two miles off, and Master Jennings shows no favor to late men.

Tupper tells of honest Roger, a fair specimen of a class Britain once boasted, much neglected and much enduring, just, industrious, and patient, true to altar and home. The crock of gold tempts him from that path. Readers who like Victorian rural novels will find a moral, earnest tale of labor, temptation, and content.
17094-the-story-of-the-red-cross-as-told:
Annie Fellows Johnston tells the story of the Red Cross as a tale for the Little Colonel, her beloved child heroine of Kentucky. The book sits in a long series that follows the Little Colonel through house parties, holidays, Arizona, and boarding school, each volume sold in cloth with pictures. Here the famous child listener hears how the Red Cross came to aid the hurt in war.

Johnston wraps history in a cozy story frame, so young readers learn through a child they know. The tone is warm, clear, and earnest, with the Red Cross ideal of care for friend and foe alike. Families who love the series will find a gentle history lesson inside a favorite story world.
1752-el-dorado-an-adventure-of-the-scarl:
Baroness Orczy returns to the Scarlet Pimpernel in this adventure set during the French Revolution, when the daring Englishman risks his life to save French aristocrats from the guillotine. The foreword clears up a confusion between the Pimpernel and the real royalist plotter Baron de Batz, so readers know which hero they are following.

The plot turns on a rescue from Paris by night, with the Pimpernel slipping through the Villette gate and outwitting agents of the Republic. Orczy keeps the romance and the disguises at full strength. The novel works as pure swashbuckling: a masked hero, a cause worth dying for, and an enemy who is always one step behind.
17698-bella-donna-a-novel:
Robert Hichens, author of The Call of the Blood and A Spirit in Prison, wrote this novel, published in New York in October 1908 by A. L. Burt Company, copyright held by J. B. Lippincott Company, in a fifth edition. The novel opens with Doctor Meyer Isaacson, a London man who rose with alarming speed, arriving at success as suddenly as a shot finds its mark.

Readers get a society novel of Egypt, London, and dangerous attraction, in Hichens's lush, popular style. The book suits readers of Edwardian bestsellers and of Hichens's Oriental romances. Its fame rests on its heroine and its Egyptian colour.
17800-wych-hazel:
Susan Warner and Anna Warner, authors of The Wide, Wide World, wrote this novel, Wych Hazel, first published in 1876 and issued in Putnam's edition of 1888. A contemporary Atlantic Monthly review, quoted in the file, questioned whether the Warners had added to their fame by the new novel. It called the story one of no marked merit or originality, told in a crabbed and unintelligible way, with pertness in every speaker.

The review adds that the story is told almost entirely by means of conversation. Readers get a Warner sisters' novel as its own age judged it, for better and worse. The book suits readers of the Warners and of American domestic fiction.
17981-under-handicap-a-novel:
Jackson Gregory wrote Under Handicap in 1914, issued in New York by A. L. Burt, by arrangement with Harper and Brothers. Gregory, author of The Outlaw, dedicates the novel to his lady, Lotus McGlashan Gregory.

The tale opens in desert heat and thirsty sand, where the Overland Limited rushes past telegraph poles and rails of burning steel. Conniston finds a huddled heap at his feet, and a story of love, pride, and the West unfolds. Gregory writes big, outdoor romance with a sure hand. It is a rousing western tale, full of sand, steel, and stubborn hearts.
18002-a-canadian-heroine-volume-1-a-nove:
The author of Leaves from the Backwoods wrote A Canadian Heroine in London in 1873, printed by Tinsley Brothers in three volumes. The first volume opens at sunset in early summer, when every tree stands in full, fresh leaf.

The sky over Canada glows more glorious than any English sky, with pale green depths and clouds of rose and gold. Under such a heaven the heroine's story unfolds, in a land the French verse calls fair and proud. It is a gentle, Victorian novel of Canada, full of landscape, feeling, and the pride of a new country.
18122-a-canadian-heroine-volume-2-a-nove:
The author of Leaves from the Backwoods wrote A Canadian Heroine in London in 1873, printed by Tinsley Brothers in three volumes. This text is the second volume, though its title page bears the first volume's imprint, a quirk of the old printing.

The tale opens with Mrs. Costello, who feels a reprieve when a journey can be delayed a month. Her health and spirits, strained by past anguish, make home and quiet her dearest wish. She clings to delay, hoping some cause may spare them their terrors at Cacouna. It is a gentle, Victorian Canadian novel, full of feeling, place, and quiet endurance.
18132-a-canadian-heroine-volume-3-a-nove:
The third and closing volume of a Canadian novel published in London in 1873 by the author of Leaves from the Backwoods. Its title points to a heroine in Canada, and its opening pages turn on two people, Mr. Leigh and Mrs. Costello. Leigh is low and anxious after talks with Costello, who has told him a strange and almost unbelievable story of her life.

The volume then has to work out what that story means for both of them. Costello first seeks Leigh's sympathy and help, then seems to change course, leaving him unsure how to act. Readers who reach this volume get the end of a long domestic story, told in the plain style of a nineteenth-century Canadian romance.
1840-the-financier-a-novel:
Frank Cowperwood learns the value of a dollar as a boy in Philadelphia, and grows into a financier whose charm, nerve, and other people's money build a fortune. From a boyhood in which he learns the value of a dollar, Cowperwood builds a fortune in stocks and street railways. His love affairs run alongside his deals with the same appetite.

Dreiser writes the business world as a force of nature, and Cowperwood as a man who treats law as weather to be sailed through. The novel is the first of a trilogy, and its power lies in its scale: a whole city's finance, politics, and society arranged around one man's will to have what he wants.
18418-a-crooked-path-a-novel:
Mrs. Alexander, author of The Wooing O't and A Life Interest, wrote this novel, published in New York by the F. M. Lupton Publishing Company. A Crooked Path opens in the London season, some years before the arch at Constitution Hill was swept back for traffic. On a splendid early June forenoon, two gentlemen coming from opposite directions meet at the gate of Apsley House.

The elder is a stout, florid man of military aspect, with a large gray mustache, and the meeting sets the story's gathering clouds in motion. From Hyde Park corner the novel moves into society, family, and the crooked ways by which plans bend. Readers get a Victorian society novel of London streets, calls, and consequences, where a chance meeting can turn a whole season.
18430-our-elizabeth-a-humour-novel:
Florence A. Kilpatrick wrote this humour novel, published by Thornton Butterworth in London in November 1920, with pictures by Ernest Forbes. Our Elizabeth opens with an author's note: Elizabeth is not a type, she is an individuality, and there is only one Elizabeth. Signs and omens at her birth, Kilpatrick says, fixed her sense of the superstitious, and sketches in Punch first gave her small-scale life.

Kilpatrick developed those impressions to full life size for this novel, acknowledging their use. A frontispiece shows Elizabeth Renshaw, and the chapters follow her through the humours of a life ruled by omens, habits, and strong opinions. Readers get an English comic novel of character: one woman, her superstitions, and the household that must live with them, told with the light malice of Punch at its best.
18572-the-president-a-novel:
Alfred Henry Lewis wrote this novel, published by A. S. Barnes in New York in 1904, and dedicated to Ethel Oviatt Lewis. Lewis, author of The Boss and Wolfville Days, set his story in the world of American politics, where a young man learns how power is won and held.

Chapters tell how Richard began to woo, how a president is bred, how a speakership was fought for, and how Richard was taught many things. Storri, who plots vengeance and woos Mrs. Hanway-Harley, stands as Richard's rival, and the novel follows ambition, love, and party dealing toward the highest office in the land.
18578-our-unitarian-gospel:
M. J. Savage preached these sermons in the Church of the Messiah during the season of 1897-98. He published them in Boston in 1898 as Our Unitarian Gospel, with the subtitle the good news of the blessed God. The sermons are printed as delivered, not as literature, for a larger congregation than Sunday morning could reach.

The contents ask what Unitarians do in place of what they take away, why they have no creed, and whether any creeds are wicked to question. Later sermons take up doubt and faith, sin and atonement, prayer, worship, morality, reward and punishment, and evolution, offering a gospel of life and hope rather than death and despair.
18630-the-tale-of-frisky-squirrel:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this Sleepy-Time Tale in 1915, with pictures by Eleanore Fagan. Its hero, Frisky Squirrel, lives with his mother in a hollow limb of an old hickory tree, where nuts hang close at hand in fall. Bold and restless, he leaps from branch to branch, dodges hawks and foxes, and raids Farmer Green's wheat and corn. Chapters follow his fall, a picnic, a mill visit, and a spell locked in an attic.

A weasel named Freddie, a cat, and a threshing machine add danger along the way, while Mr. Crow lends a hand. Bailey keeps the tone warm and funny, with short chapters for bedtime reading. The tale is a gentle classic of early children's animal fiction.
18739-zophiel:
Mrs. Brooks published this poem with Richardson and Lord of Boston in 1825. In her preface she explains that she first meant to build her poem on an incident from pagan history, then turned instead to a well-known story from the Jewish annals.

That story, she writes, joined extreme beauty with wide room for the imagination, holding both elevated truths and pleasing popular superstitions. She had hoped to carry a first canto to Britain for advice and publication, but events blocked the trip, so she finished the poem with the means at hand. Zophiel stands as an early American woman's ambitious verse romance, offered frankly as a work still short of her hopes.
18957-strangers-at-lisconnel:
Jane Barlow published this collection in New York in 1895, as a second series of Irish idylls set in the hamlet of Lisconnel. The village sits in wide bogland, where strangers seldom arrive and familiar faces seldom leave for long. Fourteen short pieces follow its people through small events: a basket, a cloak, a fairing, boys' wages, a flitting, and a return.

Barlow writes with warmth about country folk, their talk, their jokes, and their hardships, without turning them into simple figures of fun. Each sketch stands alone, yet together they build a portrait of a close community. Readers get gentle, observant stories of rural Ireland in the 1890s, valued for their dialect, humor, and sympathy.
19121-sword-and-gown-a-novel:
George Alfred Lawrence wrote this 1859 novel, first issued under the name of the author of Guy Livingstone. It follows Harry Molyneux, a sick young officer who lies on a Mediterranean shore, pale save for one scarlet mark of consumption. Sea air, hills, and pine woods frame his rest.

Harry's nights of wild living bring remorse by day, when he calls for his two small children and showers his wife with gifts. A stern old lady rebukes such easy pardon, yet his wife forgives without reproach. Readers get a Victorian tale of sin, sickness, love, and the soft pity that binds a flawed man to home.
19175-a-little-rebel-a-novel:
The Duchess, author of Her Last Throw and April's Lady, wrote this 1891 novel, A Little Rebel, published in Montreal. A professor sits before an untasted breakfast, dismayed by two letters: one telling of an old friend's death, the other, written a week before, pleading and urgent, read three times through. A wardship and a marriage plot follow.

The professor dreads meeting a hoyden from Australia, due on view at Bloomsbury on May 26, and hopes a man in the bush may claim her first. By May 30, sun plays over his dusty study and manuscript piles. Readers get a light Victorian romance of a shy scholar and a wilful girl.
19436-the-fifth-wheel-a-novel:
Olive Higgins Prouty wrote this novel of a young woman finding her place, published by a New York firm in the mid nineteen teens with pictures by James Montgomery Flagg. Ruth Vars comes out in society, meets Breckenridge Sewall, and soon feels herself the unimportant fifth wheel in other people's households.

When her brother Tom orders her west to live with his family, Ruth refuses. She will not be a spare part in his home, and she will make her way in New York instead. The novel's charm lies in Ruth's plain speech and her resolve to live on her own terms.
19512-kate-danton-or-captain-danton-s-da:
May Agnes Fleming wrote this novel of Captain Danton's daughters, published in Toronto in the late eighteen seventies. Three young women, fair and full of laughter, fill a green place with music and pleasant thoughts, while their father reads the news aloud by the fire.

Beneath the domestic calm run secrets, wills, and strong wills, as the novel's epigraph warns that a woman's will dies hard. Fleming was a popular writer of sensation fiction, and this book shows her domestic side: family talk, courtship, and quiet battles of temper. Two ghost chapters bookend a revelation chapter that clears up one mystery at last.
19735-phantom-wires-a-novel:
Arthur Stringer wrote this novel of wire tappers and hidden pasts, published in Boston in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures by Arthur William Brown. Its opening verses warn that bad in the best and good in the worst make up humanity's tangle.

A young inventor needs money to perfect his amplifier, while his love fears his own moods and distrust may wound her beyond forgiveness. Stringer mixes romance with the new world of wires, and the novel shows early techno-thriller writing at its most human. One figure wears an open Irish smile touched with wordless sorrow and a half-concealed restlessness.
2007-we-two-a-novel:
Edna Lyall's We Two follows two young people — a clergyman and the woman he loves — through a story of faith, doubt, and social pressure in Victorian England. The novel's title names its pair, and its plot turns on whether love can survive when belief divides a couple.

Lyall writes with earnestness and sympathy, and the book's interest lies in its treatment of religious doubt, a subject Lyall returned to often. Readers who know Derrick Vaughan will recognize the same moral seriousness here, and the novel remains a thoughtful example of the Victorian novel of conscience.
20225-the-story-of-a-play-a-novel:
A Story of a Play, from 1898, is a novel about the stage and its makers. A playwright seeks a new effect from an old notion, he explains. Familiar names in the tale will make that effect stronger, he hopes. He wants to show that the wages of sin is more sinning.

That grim phrase, he says, is the very body of death. Backstage life, actors, and authors fill novels of this theatrical kind. Success and failure on stage mirror the cast's tangled lives off it. Readers get a sharp, moody look at the 1890s theatre world.
20235-heart-a-social-novel:
Martin Farquhar Tupper wrote Heart, a social novel of love and money. Tupper was famed for proverbial verse read in countless Victorian homes. In Heart, a father speaks of judging men not by their purses. A son-in-law needs only a sufficiency on one side or the other.

That talk of money and marriage opens the novel's social world. Tupper mixes moral counsel with courtship, class, and family pride. His novels aimed to teach while they told a love tale. Readers get earnest Victorian fiction from a writer once read worldwide.
20261-the-adventures-of-harry-revel:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch wrote The Adventures of Harry Revel, a novel of a foundling boy. Twenty-five small foundlings live behind a wicket they seldom evade. A motto over their door promises training that will not depart in age. The boys read a particular and dreadful meaning in those words.

From that grim start, Harry Revel's adventures carry him far afield. Quiller-Couch, who wrote as Q, loved Cornwall and the sea. Orphan heroes in such tales seek a name, a home, and their due. Readers get a lively, humane adventure by a fine English storyteller.
20382-ranching-sport-and-travel:
Ranching, Sport and Travel is a memoir of work and adventure across ranch country and distant seas. The writer moves between cattle land, hunting grounds, and long sea voyages. Each chapter reports what he saw with his own eyes.

Near Point de Galle, off Ceylon, he watched a strange fight from his steamer. A sea serpent about fifteen feet long battled a huge ray on the surface of the water. He judged it a real fight and not play. Such episodes give the book its flavour: a working traveller's mix of sport, danger, and wonder.
20520-the-hero-of-the-humber-or-the-hist:
The Hero of the Humber tells the life of a Hull man famed for saving people from the river Humber. The book opens by praising his town. Hull, it says, has many institutions of which it is deservedly proud.

There is the Charterhouse, a monument of the practical piety of old days. There is the Literary and Philosophical Institute, with its large and valuable collections. Against that civic pride, the biography sets one working man's courage. Again and again he risked his own life in the Humber's tides to pull strangers from drowning.
20553-out-around-rigel:
Robert H. Wilson's Out Around Rigel is a science fiction story set among the stars of Rigel. Its hero fights with old weapons in a new world. Swordplay, not ray guns, settles the quarrel on the sand by the water.

As his opponent steps back to get free, the hero lunges and twists his weapon. In a beautiful arc, Garth's sword sails out into the water. Garth drops to the sand to nurse his right wrist. The scene shows the tale's mix: pulp action and dueling honor, played out under an alien sun for the magazine readers of its day.
2072-michael:
E. F. Benson follows Michael Comber, a generous young man whose gift to his cousin Francis opens a novel of money, friendship, and character. Michael gives gladly, and Francis accepts with a grace of his own. Benson, son of an archbishop, wrote society novels that mixed wit with moral judgment.

As the story widens, questions of debt, duty, and self-knowledge test Michael's easy nature. Benson writes social life with wit and close observation, and the book stands as a portrait of a man learning what generosity truly costs. Michael's generosity is tested by money, since giving gladly is easy until the gift begins to cost.
21106-bob-strong-s-holidays-adrift-in-th:
Bob Strong and his sister Nellie are sent by train to Portsmouth for the summer. Their barrister father is too busy to holiday with them. Their dog Rover rides in the guard's van. A retired sea captain shares their compartment, and at Guildford a grubby runaway boy appears at the window.

John Conroy Hutcheson lets the children take the boy in; the captain pays his fare, learning he fled a cruel stepfather. Boats, fish, seaweed, and trips to the Isle of Wight fill the holiday. Disasters follow too, including the wreck of a new excursion steamer and trouble near Alderney.
21127-the-mystics-a-novel:
Katherine Cecil Thurston, author of The Masquerader, published this novel in 1907 with Harper and Brothers. In a gaunt house on the loneliest stretch of the Scottish coast above the Irish Sea, John Henderson watches his uncle die. The dead man belonged to a strange religious sect led by a figure called the Prophet.

Illustrations show the Prophet's fixed gaze and the octagonal mark of the sect cut across his breast. Thurston builds a tale of a secretive mystic order, its rites, and the people drawn into its power. Henderson's inheritance of his uncle's world brings danger, grief, and strange devotion in its wake.
21297-cutlass-and-cudgel:
An excise patrol vessel cruises a smuggling coast in George Manville Fenn's tale. The first strange catch is a swimming cow, milked on deck to the crew's amusement. Soon the story turns serious. A curious young midshipman is taken prisoner by the smuggling gang the patrol hunts.

The son of one of the chief rogues brings the prisoner food. The two teenagers become friends, though class pride makes the midshipman hide it behind rudeness. At last the midshipman escapes, the gang is caught, and the farm boy ships aboard the excise vessel himself. Fenn mixes comedy, class feeling, and coastwise action in one fast tale.
21363-quicksilver-the-boy-with-no-skid-t:
A retired village doctor, childless, decides to adopt a boy from the local Institute for the Poor in George Manville Fenn's village tale. The boy he picks was a foundling at two and is now eleven or twelve. He is a globule of quicksilver who does cartwheels round the drawing room. The subtitle's skid is never explained in the text.

Manners are the battlefield: an Institute boy must be retrained for a doctor's household, with many slips along the way. He runs off in a stolen boat with a rougher local friend. Illness, a rented house in the Isle of Wight, and a discovery about his real parents end the story in Fenn's gentlest mode.
21641-april-s-lady-a-novel:
The Duchess, author of Molly Bawn, sets April's Lady at a breakfast table in a novel entered in Canada in 1890. Mr Monkton flings a letter from his father, Sir George, across to his wife. Her dark, pretty face flushes crimson at the news.

Joyce, the young sister, marvels that Barbara has been married eight whole years. Time is a swindler, she says, since Barbara looks barely born eight years ago. A parting verse, where a tightened finger says stay, fronts the tale. The Duchess, a famed Irish novelist, spins love and society in her known light, keen manner.
21767-agatha-s-husband-a-novel:
Agatha Bowen is as open and broad-hearted as her name in this novel by Dinah Maria Craik, author of John Halifax, Gentleman. Craik plays on the very sound of the name: three broad vowels, nothing small or mean in the girl. Agatha is nineteen, motherless, and moderately rich, with rooms of her own. Two friends sit in her drawing room talking over the man she is to marry.

He is still a figure of talk and guesswork when the story opens. The novel follows Agatha into marriage and tests what her husband, and she herself, turn out to be. Walter Crane's pictures grace this edition. Craik writes marriage as a serious moral craft, and Agatha's growth is the heart of the book.
2183-three-men-on-the-bummel:
Jerome K. Jerome sends three English friends off on a cycling holiday through Germany, and the trip goes wrong in the most cheerful ways. Three Men on the Bummel follows the party as they muddle through language, lodging, trains, and German custom, each mishap told with dry good humor. The comedy comes from ordinary travelers meeting a country they only half understand.

Along the way Jerome pauses to compare English and German habits, from beer gardens to police rules, always on the side of the baffled visitor. The book is light, episodic, and easy to dip into, with one comic set piece after another. It suits anyone who has ever felt lost abroad and laughed about it later.
21834-the-black-colonel:
An old Highland tale, heard from his mother at Balmoral country, becomes a novel in James Milne's The Black Colonel, published in 1921. Milne's mother's people were Forbeses, long planted on Deeside, and her grandfather's talk brought the tale a generation closer. Milne admits the strangest thing about his story is that it happened, though perhaps not as he tells it.

Chapters run from a meeting in the pass through traps laid by red-coats, raids in the dark, and the cards of love. Ossian's line about deeds of other years heads the book. It is a romance of the Scottish hills after the Jacobite times, mixing clan memory, war, and love in Milne's easy storyteller's style.
22013-the-lady-of-the-ice-a-novel:
James De Mille, a Canadian writer and professor, published The Lady of the Ice in New York in 1870. His narrator settles into winter quarters in a Canadian city built on Laurentian rock above a great river. There he falls in with his old friend Jack Randolph. Jack confesses a tangle of engagements, a widow, and one lady too many.

The comic courtship turns serious when the party crosses the St. Lawrence as the ice breaks up. A storm, a cracking ice ridge, and a desperate rescue give the book its title. De Mille mixes farce with real danger on the frozen river. The novel remains a lively piece of early Canadian fiction.
22089-the-liberty-minstrel:
George Washington Clark, a singing abolitionist, published The Liberty Minstrel in the 1840s. Clark travelled to anti-slavery meetings with his songs, and his songbook holds the words and tunes he used. Its hymns and ballads call slavery a sin and America to repent. One song figures freedom as the bright brow of a nation set free.

Other pieces plead for the enslaved, mock slaveholders, and praise those who fled to freedom. Singing was a weapon of the movement: a hall full of voices reached hearts that speeches missed. The Liberty Minstrel is a small, rare witness to that musical campaign. It shows abolition as ordinary people sang it, not only as orators preached it.
22115-a-fantasy-of-mediterranean-travel:
A Fantasy of Mediterranean Travel, printed in 1909, is a picture-led tour of the inland sea. Its plates catch a world in sudden change. One shows Sultan Abdul Hamid II on his last ride through Constantinople after losing his throne. Another shows his successor, Mehmed V, leaving the mosque after his investiture, and Armenian leaders hanged on the Galata Bridge.

Cairo's markets, full of rugs, tapestries, and lace, fill other pages. The captions are brief, and the photographs do the talking. Travel books of this kind sold wonder by the plate. This one preserves the Mediterranean of 1909: empires trembling, bazaars thriving, and tourists arriving by steamer.
22121-olive-a-novel:
Dinah Maria Craik, long known to readers as Miss Mulock, published her novel Olive in 1850. The story opens in a Scottish manse, where an old nurse croons over a newborn girl. The nurse shakes off a superstitious dread and blesses her charge warmly. That child is Olive, born to a hard fate and a frail, crooked body.

Olive grows up plain and overlooked beside her beautiful mother. Craik follows her through sorrow, work, and a slow winning of respect.
