The novel treats a heroine with a deformity as a full person, which was rare in its day. It made Craik's name and stayed a favourite with Victorian readers for decades.
22191-half-a-hero-a-novel:
Anthony Hope, who wrote The Prisoner of Zenda, published Half a Hero in 1893. The scene is a colonial capital, where a new premier faces a hostile society. Inside one family circle, the hostess declares her terms in advance. Let the Governor do as he would, she at least will not receive Mr. Medland in her house.

Medland, the rising politician, is the half-hero of the title. Hope mixes drawing-room war with real questions of power in a young colony. Love and ambition tangle around his ministry. The novel shows Hope's lighter political vein, the year before Zenda made him famous, and it still sparkles with his dialogue.
23097-fifty-years-of-public-service-pers:
Shelby Cullom's Fifty Years of Public Service marches by chapters through a long career. The contents run from General John M. Palmer and Governor Richard J. Oglesby to a senatorial career from 1883 to 1911. Then come Cleveland's first term, Cleveland's defeat and Harrison's term, Cleveland's second term, McKinley's presidency, and Roosevelt's presidency, year by year.

Cullom served Illinois as governor and senator across the Civil War's aftermath and into the new century. His recollections cover the Interstate Commerce Act, which he helped write, the canal question, and the Senate's foreign relations work. Political memoirs this full are sources as much as stories. Cullom names names, dates votes, and settles scores in the courteous style of his generation.
23106-helen-and-arthur-or-miss-thusa-s-s:
Reviewers greet Helen and Arthur, or Miss Thusa's Spinning Wheel, with unusual warmth in the notices printed with the book. One paper credits Hentz with excellences already proven across the country. Her tales' sound, healthy tone, it says, makes them safe and delightful at once, warmly recommended to every lover of pleasant fiction.

Caroline Lee Hentz wrote Helen and Arthur as a temperance-era domestic tale, with Miss Thusa and her spinning wheel at its moral center. Industry, drink, and household ruin turn the plot in the manner her readers loved. The bound-in reviews show how such books were sold, praise first, story after. The novel preserves the period's earnest, fireside didacticism intact.
23122-the-well-in-the-desert-an-old-lege:
Travelers prize water in The Well in the Desert, an old legend of the House of Arundel. Only desert travelers, the tale says, truly know water's worth. A well in the waste is treasure past telling when its water runs sweet. Even brackish water, though, can keep a traveler alive.

Emily Holt, to whom this legend is credited, retells a Crusades-era story tied to the great Arundel family. A well found in the desert becomes the hinge of faith, survival, and a vow remembered at home in England. Holt's historical tales taught Protestant history through romance. This short legend shows her manner in miniature, landscape first, then lineage, then the moral drawn clear.
23123-old-daniel:
Thomas Hodson's Old Daniel comes wrapped in a remarkable introduction. The introducer praises nothing blindly. Devoted missionaries assembled the pieces, he notes, mocking local gods as they went. Even so, he confesses the book fails to convince him as an argument for Christianity, and he calls himself a Christian as he says it.

That candor sets up a life of Daniel, an Indian Christian convert whose story missionaries in South India recorded. Hodson gathered the pieces into a biography meant to show conversion from the inside. The Rev. W. Arthur's introduction argues with its own book in public, a rare and honest sight. Readers get both the missionary record and an early doubt about its methods, bound in one volume.
23386-in-the-king-s-name-the-cruise-of-t:
George Manville Fenn wrote this long tale of the cutter Kestrel, a king's ship on patrol off the south coast, hunting smugglers, Jacobites, and all that looks suspect. Her crew's work soon leads ashore, into smugglers' caves and coastal villages where danger hides in plain sight.

The hero slips from one tight corner to the next, with escapes that seem hopeless until the last moment, in Fenn's best suspense style. Sea chases, land pursuits, and loyal comrades fill the pages. Young readers will find a masterclass in tension, plus a vivid picture of coastal England when smuggling was a trade, a crime, and, for some, a way of life.
23624-ride-proud-rebel:
Andre Norton wrote this nineteen sixty one Civil War novel, Ride Proud, Rebel, printed by the World Publishing Company. It is dedicated, with no apologies from a damnyankee, to reconstructed rebels Ernestine and William Donaldy. Norton thanks Gertrude Morton Parsley of the Tennessee State Library for aid with trooper John Johnson's unpublished memoirs of Morgan's company after Cynthiana.

Chapters ride with Morgan, sound guns in the night, run on the run, and follow a young Confederate horseman through raids, retreats, and divided loyalties. Norton writes the war from the saddle, with a young hero's pride and doubt in equal measure. Readers who love Civil War adventure with a sympathetic rebel view will enjoy the ride, its horses, its raids, and its hard lessons about a lost cause.
23641-the-forsaken-inn-a-novel:
Anna Katharine Green, already famous for The Leavenworth Case, built this 1890 novel around a decaying roadside inn with a dark past. A traveler stops there in a storm and is drawn into the lives of its odd household. There is a recluse, a girl named Honora, a young man called Edwin Urquhart, and a woman named Marah whose talk of wealth and birthright hints at a buried secret.

Chapter by chapter, Green peels back what happened in the inn's oak parlor, its garden, and a hidden chamber. A wedding, a catastrophe, and the arrival of a marquis bring the old crime into the open. Readers who like slow, careful mystery plots will enjoy watching each clue fall into place before the final word.
23772-devotions-upon-emergent-occasions-:
John Donne's Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, with Death's Duel, appeared in this Ann Arbor paperback in 1959 from the University of Michigan Press. The volume opens with a life of Donne taken from Izaak Walton, tracing the poet-preacher from his birth in London in 1573 to his place among England's great divines.

Donne was bred by a private tutor until age ten, then sent to Oxford in his eleventh year, already commanding French and Latin. The Devotions themselves were written in sickness, meditating on bells, illness, and mortality. Death's Duel, his last sermon, closes the book. Together they show Donne's mind at its most intimate: learned, fearful, and fiercely alive to death.
23797-a-true-friend-a-novel:
Adeline Sergeant published A True Friend in Montreal, a novel of friendship, family, and influence. Its opening chapter names the trouble at once: an unsuitable friendship. Lady Caroline's tactics, Helmsley Court, and the road that leads away from it set the story moving.

Janetta, Nora, and Margaret form the circle at its heart, with Wyvis Brand, Sir Philip, and an elder brother among the men who judge them. Chapters trace Janetta's promises, remonstrances, and failure, a bone of contention, and a big bribe, toward a decision and a cry of Free. Sergeant writes a Victorian novel of conscience, in which true friendship must survive family pressure.
24306-the-flaming-jewel:
Robert W. Chambers wrote this novel, published by A. L. Burt Company in New York in 1922, by arrangement with George H. Doran Company. It opens with verses on three guests at dinner: Wedgewood, Revere, and Duncan Phyfe. They eat fare from Paul Revere with fork and knife, amid porringers and platters of blue historic Willow-ware. Chambers calls the book, in his May 1922 envoy, a scrambled book from a plain, old-fashioned cook.

Episodes run from Eve and The Ruling Passion through On Star Peak, A Private War, and Drowned Valley to The Jewel Aflame, Clinch's Dump, Cup and Lip, The Forest and Mr. Sard, The Twilight of Mike, and The Place of Pines. Readers get a Chambers romance of a jewel, a mountain valley, and passions that rule their owners.
24312-the-minstrel:
Lennox Amott published this collection of poems at Lewes with Farncombe and Company in 1883, under a Virgil epigraph wishing for country and shaded valleys. It is dedicated to Harold Matthews, who joins true sense with true honor and unselfish principles with unselfish friendship, whose only fault is trusting natures too unlike his own. Amott offers the book as a just tribute to valued society.

In his preface, Amott calls the volume an intrusion at best, a bagatelle, and begs readers to overlook its faults. He includes the first canto of Midsummer Idylls in revised form, caring above all that the iambic measure run pure and tolerable, without sacrificing sense to sound. Readers get a modest Victorian volume of verse, careful in music and manner.
24341-reminiscences-of-a-rebel:
The Reverend Wayland Fuller Dunaway, formerly captain of Company I, 40th Virginia Regiment, Army of Northern Virginia, wrote these reminiscences, published by the Neale Publishing Company in New York in 1913. A Lucan epigraph heads the book, and a Bryant verse opens its first chapter, bidding men lay down axe, spade, and plow for rifle, bayonet, horseman's brand, and charger on the battlefield.

Dunaway tells how, in the fall of 1860, aged nineteen, he boarded the steamboat Virginia on the Rappahannock for Fredericksburg, bound for the University of Virginia to study law under John B. Minor and James P. Holcombe. The political sky darkened with John Brown's raid on Harper's Ferry and the election of Abraham Lincoln. Readers get a Confederate officer's memoir, from student to soldier.
2452-shavings-a-novel:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Shavings follows a Cape Cod jack-of-all-trades whose whittling and wisdom mend his neighbors' lives. The novel's hero, a retired seaman turned handyman, takes in a young stranger and helps the town face gossip, romance, and hard times. Lincoln's dialect humor and seaside detail give the story its flavor.

The book is episodic and warm, built from small kindnesses rather than grand drama. Readers who like Cape Cod fiction will find a cozy, good-natured tale. It ranks among Lincoln's most popular novels. Lincoln's Cape Cod novels sold widely in the early twentieth century.
24664-fairy-fingers-a-novel:
Anna Cora Ritchie wrote this novel, published at New York in 1865, with the motto Labor is Worship. Ritchie, author of The Autobiography of an Actress and Twin Roses, sets her tale among cousins, proposals, heart-beats, and an embroidered handkerchief, with chapters on Madeleine, Maurice, and the aristocrats in America.

The story follows its heroine through fashion, love, and work, as fairy fingers, a gift for fine needlework, become a path to independence. Ritchie's novel mixes romance with a plea for women's labour. Readers of Victorian popular fiction will find it lively, sentimental, and rich in period detail.
24794-the-arbiter-a-novel:
Lady F. E. E. Bell published The Arbiter in London in 1901. The novel opens on a clash of views about marriage. Miss Martin holds that no sensible woman should show her husband she adores him. Lady Gore, wed for twenty-four years, gaily claims to be an authority for doing just that. Their great-niece Rachel grows up between such lessons.

Bell writes a witty, humane novel of manners, where talk at tea and on couches shapes young lives. Questions of love, duty, and who judges a marriage run through the story. Readers of Edwardian domestic fiction will find sharp dialogue and a gentle eye for how families pass their wisdom, good and bad, down the years.
24804-the-rider-in-khaki-a-novel:
Nat Gould published The Rider in Khaki in New York in 1918, a racing novel touched by war. Alan, a young rider, moves between Trent Park, the racecourse, and the front, while Jane's love affair and her suspicions run beside his story. Spies, tips from a baron, a steeplechase, and a sudden proposal keep the plot turning.

Gould knew the turf well, and his race scenes ring true: favorites, stayers, and finishes judged by lengths. War brings a raid, a capture, and the rider's return alive and well. Readers who like horse stories with a wartime edge will find a brisk tale of love, racing luck, and courage under fire.
24881-the-tale-of-grumpy-weasel:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote The Tale of Grumpy Weasel in 1920 for his Sleepy-Time Tales, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. Grumpy Weasel, true to his name, nurses grudges and plots against his neighbors, above all Mr. Crow, whom he blames for putting a race into Jimmy Rabbit's head.

The frontispiece shows Grumpy and Jimmy Rabbit running a race, and the tale follows their rivalry to the stone wall and the woods. Grumpy hisses that he may have lost through a trick, but vows Jimmy will trouble them no more. Bailey tells it in short scenes for young listeners, with a sly moral on temper. The book pairs with his Grunty Pig and Meadow Mouse tales.
25474-the-job-an-american-novel:
Sinclair Lewis follows Una Golden from a Pennsylvania small town to a working life in the city. Her father, Captain Lew Golden of Panama, Pennsylvania, was captain of nothing but the Crescent Volunteer Fire Company, yet owned the title through rents, insurance, and lawsuits. Una leaves his world of mustache-combs and shirt-sleeves for New York rooms and offices. The novel's three parts are The City, The Office, and Man and Woman.

In the city Una trusts the want-ad page and follows its hints from house to house, though nearly every house bears a Room to Rent sign. She meets the lonely gray roomers of the city, people who never trained and lost heart. Lewis, later famous for Main Street and Babbitt, published The Job in 1917, with Harper and Brothers and Grosset and Dunlap.
25570-the-manxman-a-novel:
Hall Caine's novel The Manxman, in a second edition from Appleton in 1894, opens with boys together on the Isle of Man. Old Deemster Christian of Ballawhaine, called Iron Christian, stands as a hard man on the outside, with fire underneath and a closed soul.

People warn against turning that iron hand against you, and the Deemster cuts off for ever any man who wrenches open the dark chamber of his feelings. His elder son, an impetuous, fiery spirit, sets the family conflict going. Caine builds a Manx tale of pride, love, and judgment from that stern household.
25702-the-kingdom-round-the-corner-a-nov:
Coningsby Dawson writes this novel, The Kingdom Round the Corner, with pictures by W. D. Stevens. Dawson's earlier books include The Garden Without Walls, Slaves of Freedom, and The Raft, with war books such as Carry On and The Glory of the Trenches.

Chapters open with an altered world and retrievers of youth, then complications of Maisie, the air of conquest, and trampled roses. Some people find their kingdom, and the tale turns round the corner itself, as Tabs apologises for an unkind remark in a front picture. Dawson writes of love, youth lost, and hope regained after war.
25758-a-german-pompadour-being-the-extra:
Marie Hay, author of Dianne de Poytiers and An Unrequited Loyalty, writes this extraordinary history of Wilhelmine von Gravenitz, landhofmeisterin of Wurtemberg, as a narrative of the eighteenth century. Scribner's Sons published a second impression in New York in 1906. A portrait of Wilhelmine from Frau Anna Remshardt's collection fronts the book.

Chapters open with the intrigue, the Ave Maria, and the first step, followed by a journey and play acting. Love's springtide, fulfilment, and the ghetto follow, with she comes to stay this time and an attack. Hay dedicates the book of memories to a memory, tracing a court favourite's rise and fall.
25954-the-opened-shutters-a-novel:
Clara Louise Burnham tells a novel of faith, healing, and second sight in The Opened Shutters, printed in 1906. Judge Trent opens the tale, and chapters move through Thinkright's letter, blueberrying, misunderstanding, and reconciliation. The heroine learns to send no doubting thought into the world, and prays that every barrier to light may dissolve, so she gains what she needs.

A scene by the water shows her nest safe from gentle foam, reached only in storms, as a sailboat enters a broad path of water. Burnham, known for Jewel and The Right Princess, writes of minds opened like shutters to light and love. The book mixes New England scenes, Christian Science tones, and a romance that ends in peace after long misunderstanding.
26002-linda-tressel:
Anthony Trollope tells the sorrows of Linda Tressel in this short novel, first serialized anonymously in Blackwood's Magazine from October 1867 to May 1868, then printed in book form in 1868. Trollope's name came out only when the book was reprinted a decade later. Linda's troubles, Trollope says, spring from her closest friend's unbending virtue, unsoftened by sound sense or mercy.

That friend is her aunt, Madame Charlotte Staubach, widow in Nuremberg, whose small red house with three gables stands by the Pegnitz on the Schütt island. Linda dreads respectability in the form of marriage to Peter Steinmarc more than any disreputable life, yet fears her aunt will prevail and make him her lord and master. The novel is a sharp study of conscience and control.
26142-peat-and-its-uses-as-fertilizer-an:
Samuel W. Johnson, professor of analytical and agricultural chemistry at Yale College, published this fully illustrated volume in New York in 1866. Its first part explains what peat is and how it forms in swamps. It names chief kinds such as swamp muck and salt mud. It also covers peat's chemical makeup, including ulmic and humic acids and the mineral ash left after burning.

The second part turns to farm use. It covers peat's power to hold water and ammonia and its effect on soil warmth and texture. It also treats peat's value in composts and the plant food in its ash. The title promises fuel as well as fertilizer, and the book gives farmers and chemists of its day a careful, practical science of a humble material dug from wet ground.
26167-a-short-account-of-king-s-college-:
W. P. Littlechild, chapel clerk at King's College, Cambridge, wrote this short illustrated account, here in its second edition of 1921. It traces the college from Henry VI's foundation in 1441, through his remodelled plan of 1443, to the laying of the chapel's foundation stone on St. James's Day, July 25, 1446.

The book describes the chapel's rich perpendicular Gothic style, its screen, and its windows. It also notes carvings such as the arms of Henry VII and the rose and portcullis. The badges of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn are dated to 1533-1536. It ranks the chapel with the great royal chapels of the Tudor age, and it serves as a compact guide for visitors walking its stalls and screens.
26191-citadel:
Algis Budrys's science-fiction tale opens with Christopher Mead, Assistant Undersecretary for External Affairs, meeting an aging, nervous visitor named Martin Holliday. Holliday cannot bear closed rooms, and he calms only when Mead opens the windows to wide distances. He asks to lease a fresh planet, though his first planet did not work out.

The story's tag line says Holliday sought a privacy his strange nature needed, yet never quite found it. His efforts brought great triumphs for his race and great failures for himself. Verse quoted mid-story speaks of a people doomed to wander, break, and bleed. The tale blends space politics with a lonely portrait of a man who cannot live at ease among others.
26499-the-jucklins-a-novel:
Opie Read's novel follows Bill, a narrator whom neighbors and family laughed at for as long as he can remember. His father first seriously tells him he is too lazy to amount to anything, so they must make a schoolteacher of him. Bill defends himself: he can sit fishing all day without a bite, and he holds patience to be the very perfection of industry.

The humor stays homely and Southern, with evenings spent talking over lamps turned low. One companion reports killing a six-foot snake crossing a field on important business, and Bill answers that he knows a bigger snake, coiled about the universe and striking at hearts. The Jucklins belongs to Read's select works, beside Old Ebenezer and A Kentucky Colonel.
26651-the-flaming-jewel:
Robert W. Chambers published this jewel-thief novel with George H. Doran in 1922, in twelve episodes from Eve to Her Highness Intervenes. It opens with Mike Clinch, whose turn in the eternal sequence has come after two quiet years, and a letter from an Esthonian refugee countess to James Darragh in New York. José Quintana's band of international thieves, she writes, robbed Ricca, and a Levantine diamond broker named Emanuel Sard may know him.

Sard receives a coded letter from Rotterdam listing stones from tourmaline to star sapphire, while Darragh presents himself as a customer at Sard's office. Episodes on Star Peak, in a drowned valley, at Clinch's dump, and in the forest with Mr. Sard follow. Chambers mixes diamonds, disguise, and Adirondack adventure in a brisk thriller.
26768-ringfield-a-novel:
S. F. Harrison, writing as Seranus, published this novel with the Musson Book Company at Toronto in 1914. Harrison also wrote The Forest of Bourg-Marie and Pine, Rose and Fleure de Lis. Its first chapter, The Holy Waters, opens in a cascade country, a land of magnificent waterfalls holding Niagara and the unhackneyed splendours of Labrador.

The noble fall of St. Ignace, only second or third in size, ranks first in majestic and perfect beauty. Brown water descends by three horseshoe ledges to sparkling spray, between wooded banks of amazing solitariness, with no clearing or sign of habitation for a mile above. Later chapters follow the white peacock, the man in the chair, the house of Clairville, and the unseen hand. Pauline, a picnic, a sick seigneur, Father Rielle, a storm, revelry by night, and the quest of happiness follow.
2697-the-guardian-angel:
Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote this novel as a natural sequence to Elsie Venner, and his preface promises a new preface for readers who love a moral appended, like those of Aesop. The tale is meant for two classes of readers, those who want a story and those who want an argument.

A guardian angel, in Holmes's sense, is the inherited bent that watches over or waylays a life, and his heroine must reckon with hers. The novel mixes village romance with the doctor's theories of heredity and will. It remains a thoughtful companion to Elsie Venner, and a test of how free any of us are.
27347-appearances-being-notes-of-travel:
G. Lowes Dickinson, author of A Modern Symposium and Justice and Liberty, published these notes of travel in London and Toronto with J. M. Dent, and in New York with Doubleday, Page, in 1914. The book is arranged in four parts, each a set of short reflective essays on a region he visited, closing with a concluding essay.

India brings the Red Sea, Ajanta, a Bengal village, and Sri Ramakrishna. China brings Nanking, the Yangtze gorges, and Pekin. Japan brings a No dance, Nikko, and Fuji. America brings Niagara, the Rockies, the Adirondacks, and the religion of business. Dickinson writes as a thoughtful observer, and the essays reward readers who like travel with ideas in it.
27400-the-martian-a-novel:
George du Maurier, author of Trilby and Peter Ibbetson, published this novel with Harper and Brothers in New York in 1897, with illustrations by the author himself. Its French motto warns that after pleasure comes pain, and after pain, virtue, a hint of the moral shape du Maurier gives his story.

Illustrations follow a new boy at Institution F. Brossard, a little peace-maker, Loud Runswick and Antoinette Josselin, and school scenes in France, as boyhood passes into wider life. Du Maurier's own drawings and his gentle, observant narration carry the tale. It is a late Victorian novel of youth, friendship, and a strange influence, told with charm.
27447-mountain-blood-a-novel:
Joseph Hergesheimer, author of The Lay Anthony, The Three Black Pennys, and Java Head, published this novel with Alfred A. Knopf in New York in 1919, and dedicated it to his mother. It opens at sunrise over the city of Stenton, as the Greenstream stage rolls from its depot, a dingy frame tavern, toward its high destination.

Beyond the town a broad plain reaches to a shimmering blue silhouette of mountains. Stenton itself wakes to smoke from the waterworks, the acid odor of an ice plant, and a whistling locomotive. The novel sets industrial town life against the high country from its first pages. Hergesheimer's rich, sensory prose carries the contrast throughout.
2785-the-elusive-pimpernel:
Baroness Orczy wrote this sequel to The Scarlet Pimpernel, opening in Paris in 1793 with a retrospect and the ex ambassador Chauvelin. A Richmond gala, Sir Percy and his lady, and a mission for the poor of Paris set the stage.

Premonition, an invitation, and Lady Blakeney's rout lead to a challenge, with time, place, and conditions fixed. Orczy writes with dash and romance, and the Pimpernel eludes every trap. The novel delights as a swashbuckling tale of the Terror, and of a hero who laughs at the guillotine. Chauvelin's traps fail against wit, disguise, and daring.
27929-the-lady-of-loyalty-house-a-novel:
Justin Huntly McCarthy published The Lady of Loyalty House with Harper and Brothers in October 1904, a novel of Cavalier and Roundhead in the English Civil War. The dedication verse promises a tale in which Cavalier and Roundhead break a reed for a sacred cause, and where the royal standard flies against autumnal skies.

Chapters follow a stranger at the gates, the leaguer of Harby, a monstrous regiment, a prisoner of war, a gilded cage, and a high court of justice, with Brilliana as heroine. McCarthy's romance mixes history, love, and siege warfare in the manner of popular historical fiction.
28088-the-beth-book-being-a-study-of-the:
Sarah Grand's The Beth Book, published in New York in 1897, studies the life of Elizabeth Caldwell Maclure, a woman of genius. Grand opens with words from Shakespeare, Ruskin, and Emerson on how new ideas move through a time. Beth grows up in a grey, narrow home, where her gifts meet little welcome.

The novel follows Beth from childhood into womanhood, as she fights for learning, work, and a voice of her own. Men around her expect silence and obedience, and Beth's refusal costs her dearly. Grand's book remains a strong early feminist novel about talent thwarted by custom.
2813-the-grand-babylon-ho-tel:
Arnold Bennett wrote this thriller of the Grand Babylon Hotel, where T. Racksole and his daughter take a hand in high affairs. A millionaire and a waiter open the tale, and Mr. Racksole's dinner leads to three in the morning and the entrance of a prince.

Reginald Dimmock, a gold room, and Nella and the prince follow, in a plot of royalty, theft, and European intrigue. Bennett writes with brisk, Edwardian energy. The novel charms as a hotel mystery, where waiters know more than princes, and dinner is never just dinner.
2815-democracy-an-american-novel:
Henry Adams published Democracy anonymously in 1880, and readers spent years guessing its author and the real figures behind its characters. The novel follows Mrs. Lightfoot Lee, a wealthy widow who spends a winter in Washington to study American politics at first hand. She meets senators, lobbyists, and diplomats, and finds that power in the capital runs on charm, money, and private dealing.

Adams, who called the book's piracy the single real triumph of his life, wrote it as satire rather than romance. The Washington scenes, including a visit to Mount Vernon, test whether honest government can survive ambition. It remains the classic American novel about politics as a social world.
28162-the-invader-a-novel:
Margaret L. Woods's The Invader, published by Harper and Brothers in May 1907, is a novel of art, ghosts, and Oxford life. A professor shows guests a life-size portrait that seems to take over his small room. Experts cannot agree whether it is a Romney or a Raeburn, and one guest calls its owner a fraud for claiming the sitter as an ancestress.

The portrait, it seems, has a will of its own, and its presence unsettles the household. Woods blends a ghost story with talk of painting, taste, and old families. The novel rewards readers who like quiet, uncanny tales set among books and pictures.
28219-advice-to-young-musicians-musikali:
Advice to Young Musicians, translated by Henry Hugo Pierson and entered for copyright in 1860, gives short rules for the training of ear and hand. The book prints the English text first, then the German, under the title Musikalische Haus- und Lebens-Regeln. Its first rule stresses the ear: learn to tell each tone and key, and hear the notes of bell, glass, and cuckoo.

Later rules warn against mere finger drills, comparing hours of scales to repeating the alphabet faster and faster. Practice must serve music, not replace it. The little book suits young players and teachers who want plain, old-fashioned counsel on how to practise well.
28366-nancy-stair-a-novel:
Elinor Macartney Lane wrote Nancy Stair in 1904 as a novel set near Edinburgh in 1768. The narrator, Danvers Carmichael, goes on a cruise, finds a hidden treasure, and meets Nancy Stair, a strange child who begins to study law under his care. Tennyson and Burns verses open the book, on women as diverse, not undeveloped men. A. L. Burt published the novel.

Chapters follow Nancy to a duke's house, a proposal, a rival, and a swap of rhyming ware, as she arranges matters with wit and spirit. Lane, author of Mills of God, writes with warmth. The novel offers a charming Scottish romance of a girl's education and will.
28378-too-old-for-dolls-a-novel:
Anthony M. Ludovici wrote Too Old for Dolls in 1921 as a novel of the English flapper. Ludovici, author of Mansel Fellowes and A Defence of Aristocracy, opens with a poem on a girl too young for babes, too old for dolls. She wears a hat, with hair down her back, and frocks of mighty spell. G. P. Putnam's Sons published the book in New York and London.

The heroine, keen on love, dress, and dancing, drops botany for flounces, and reads of love time and again. Ludovici writes with a mix of fondness and censure for new womanhood after the war. The novel offers a vivid, partisan portrait of the flapper age.
28435-the-cryptogram-a-novel:
James De Mille's The Cryptogram, published by Harper and Brothers in 1872, opens at Chetwynde Castle in Monmouthshire. The grand Plantagenet mansion has fallen into picturesque ruin. Ivy covers its dark towers, walks are overgrown, and the western end stands unfurnished, while the river Wye winds below toward the Welsh mountains.

Two old friends meet in the furnished eastern rooms as twilight deepens, and the novel's title points to a coded message at the heart of the mystery that follows. De Mille, author of The Dodge Club and Cord and Creese, writes a Victorian romance of old houses, hidden papers, and secrets waiting to be read.
2845-sir-nigel:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote Sir Nigel as a prequel to The White Company, following the young squire Nigel Loring toward knighthood in fourteenth-century England. The chapters carry Nigel from the house of Loring through trials by the Abbot of Waverley. A yellow horse at Crooksbury and a bridge held at Tilford lead him toward the king's court and the road to France. Lady Ermyntrude's iron coffer and the twisted man of Shalford add mystery to the training.

Doyle writes the age with warmth, showing women enthroned high above the rough world of men in Nigel's awed eyes. The novel mixes combat, hawking, and court ceremony with a young man's fear of unworthiness. It remains a spirited historical romance for readers who enjoy chivalry told straight, without irony.
28492-the-light-of-the-star-a-novel:
Hamlin Garland's novel The Light of the Star, published in May 1904, follows a young playwright named Douglass and a famous actress, Miss Merival. Douglass waits impatiently for an appointment with her, rereading his manuscript each morning and haunting the theatre each evening to glimpse the real woman behind the shining mask.

Merival dazzles him in every role, from a bedecked coquette in blue and ermine to a soulful girl behind a grating, and the press feeds the city's adulation. Douglass insists he is not a lover but a playwright seeking his heroine. Garland's novel studies fame, theatre, and the gap between a star's image and her private self.
28585-with-hoops-of-steel:
Florence Finch Kelly's With Hoops of Steel, published by Grosset and Dunlap with copyright 1900, ranks among the first modern cow-boy novels. The publishers note it beside Owen Wister's The Virginian, and say twenty-five years of steady demand justified a new edition. Its value lies in an authentic portrait of old southwestern cattlemen, now passed into history.

The tale opens at dusk on a gray-white plain, rimmed by mountains east and west, among cactus, mesquite, and greasewood. A rider, lost with a tired horse, steers toward a distant light from a ranch or camp-fire near the White Sands. Readers get a southwestern romance of friendship gripped, as Hamlet says, with hoops of steel.
28768-the-history-of-little-king-pippin-:
This tiny chapbook tells the history of little King Pippin, printed at Wellington by F. Houlston and Son for two pence, with cuts. Peter Pippin, son of Gaffer and Gammer Pippin of the Ivy-house under the hill, earns his crown by merit alone, as the frontispiece verse declares. The book also gives the melancholy death of four naughty boys devoured by wild beasts.

A second marvel follows: the wonderful delivery of Master Harry Harmless by a little white horse. Peter's wish for a picture book, after reading Mrs. Lovechild's Golden Present so often he can repeat it by heart, opens the tale. Readers get a rare survival of early children's publishing: short, moral, and decorated, priced for a child's penny savings.
28988-jennie-gerhardt-a-novel:
Theodore Dreiser wrote this 1911 novel about Jennie Gerhardt, a young woman of the poor whose life is shaped by love, money, and social judgment. The book opens in the fall of 1880, when a middle-aged woman and her eighteen-year-old daughter come to the principal hotel in Columbus, Ohio, looking for work. The mother is helpless and fleshy, frank and diffident, with large patient eyes full of distress.

Dreiser follows Jennie through the choices poverty forces on her, and the price society exacts for them. The novel's sixty-two chapters build a portrait of a woman whose generosity outlasts her luck. Readers get a major American realist novel, compassionate and unsparing, and a landmark in Dreiser's rise after Sister Carrie.
29207-cleo-the-magnificent-or-the-muse-o:
Louis Zangwill wrote this novel, subtitled The Muse of the Real, in several books. Zangwill, already praised for clever and vital fiction, builds the story around Cleo, a magnificent figure whose presence tests the line between art and life. The subtitle points to that tension: a muse who belongs to the real world, not only to imagination.

The novel unfolds book by book, following its characters through social and artistic scenes with humor and dramatic force. Contemporary notices quoted in the volume praise its originality and spirit. Readers get a late Victorian literary novel about a striking woman, the artists around her, and the pull between real life and the roles people play.
29219-the-first-violin-a-novel:
Jessie Fothergill wrote this novel, published in New York by the Federal Book Company. Its narrator, Miss Hallam, opens on a wonderful April day, agreeing with her family about the weather but unable to enjoy the mild spring air. Sorrow, the first sorrow of her life, has laid a heavy hand on her, and the world feels disjointed and upside-down.

Miss Hallam has two sisters, a father, and a mother, yet cannot share her grief with any of them. Relief comes only as each family member leaves the house in turn. Later chapters introduce Anna Sartorius and the musical world of the title. Readers get a Victorian novel of a young woman's inner life, where music and a first sorrow shape a coming of age.
29589-rodney-the-ranger-with-daniel-morg:
John V. Lane, author of Marching with Morgan, wrote this 1911 boys' book of Rodney the Ranger, with Daniel Morgan on trail and battlefield. L. C. Page and Company of Boston printed it, with pictures by John Goss, in a new edition of May 1925. Chapters open with Rodney called a simpleton, move through troubles, friendship with Angus, a visit to Monticello, and a plunge into the forest.

Rodney rides with Morgan's riflemen through the Revolution's campaigns, learning war, loyalty, and pluck. A frontispiece shows a canoe with two savages coming up past him. Young readers and fans of historical adventure will find a brisk, patriotic tale of the frontier war for independence.
29633-the-beginnings-of-cheap-steel:
Philip W. Bishop, curator of arts and manufactures at the Museum of History and Technology, wrote this paper on the beginnings of cheap steel. It reviews the controversy over the origin of the process that, for more than thirty-five years, provided the greater part of American steel production. Other inventors claimed a part in the Bessemer process, and Bishop re-examines the contemporary technical press to judge their claims.

Sections treat steel before the 1850s, Bessemer and his competitors, Robert Mushet, Ebbw Vale, and William Kelly's air-boiling process. Bishop weighs the antagonism ironmasters showed toward Bessemer's ideas. Students of industrial history will find a precise, source-based study of how cheap steel was born.
29880-the-crimson-tide-a-novel:
Robert W. Chambers published The Crimson Tide in New York in 1919, with A. L. Burt Company, by arrangement with D. Appleton and Company. A frontispiece by A. I. Keller fronts the novel. Chambers dedicates it in verse to Margaret Illington Bowes and Edward J. Bowes, preferring to walk and talk with them, anchor in a sylvan nook, and fish Dream Lake with a magic hook, rather than sit indoors and write.

The dedication calls an author an ass for watching the world through window glass while skies are fair and pretty girls stroll outside. Its envoy asks the friends to inspect his goods, choose a few, and sink them in the Lake of Dreams. The preface opens on a door, a rush of foggy air, and altar candles blowing. Chambers's novel follows that moody opening into a tale of love, art, and the world beyond the window.
29902-changing-winds-a-novel:
St. John G. Ervine published Changing Winds with the Macmillan Company in New York in 1917. The novel is dedicated to the memory of Rupert Brooke, whose verses open the first book: waters blown by changing winds to laughter, then stayed by frost into a white, shining peace. Ervine notes that the Gaelic translations on pages 77 and 78 were made by P. H. Pearse, executed in Dublin for his part in the Easter Rebellion.

The first chapter opens with Mr. Quinn, of whom it would be absurd to say he was ill-tempered, and equally absurd to call him mild. William Henry Matier, a talker by profession and a gardener in his leisure moments, joins him. Ervine, known for Irish plays and a study of Carson and the Ulster movement, writes with care for Irish life. The novel is a full, thoughtful tale of its time.
30006-cloudy-jewel:
Grace Livingston Hill wrote Cloudy Jewel, printed in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with copyright in 1920 by the Golden Rule Company and by J. B. Lippincott Company. Hill had already written Marcia Schuyler and The Search. Chapter one opens with Ellen Robinson buttoning her long cloak forcefully. From the rocking-chair, where swaying noisily along and clicking the toes of her new shoes with high heels have pointed her remarks for half an hour, she rises with a haughty air.

Julia Cloud says nothing. Ellen calls her a very foolish woman and demands what she proposes to do if she will not accept the offer and come to live with them. Ellen's generous plan is that Julia earn her board by looking after four children and being useful about the house, relieving Ellen so she can go about with her husband.
30100-marion-fay-a-novel:
Anthony Trollope opens Marion Fay with a family quarrel over politics, as Lionel Trafford enters Parliament for Wednesbury as an advanced Radical. His uncle, the old Marquis of Kingsbury, a hyper-Tory among Tories, nearly breaks his heart at the falling-off. Volume 1 then moves through Lord Hampstead, the Marchioness, Lady Frances, Mrs. Roden, Paradise Row, and the post office, toward Castle Hautboy, the Braeside harriers, and Trafford Park.

Chapman and Hall published the London novel in 1882, in three volumes, and Trollope keeps his usual sharp eye on rank, money, and marriage. Marion Fay and her father enter beside schemes, lovers, and homecomings, as high and low London life cross. Readers of Trollope will find the familiar pleasures here: clear social comedy, strong women, and a plot that turns on who may marry whom.
30110-name-and-fame-a-novel:
Adeline Sergeant wrote Name and Fame, a novel printed in Montreal by John Lovell and Son. A handwritten note in the volume says this is the only edition of Name and Fame published in the United States and Canada with her authority. It is the only one by whose sale she shall profit.

Chapter one, Husband and Wife, opens on a brilliant day in June at Aix-les-Bains. Shade for the pedestrian comes from foliage clothing the pleasant slopes, under a cloudless and dazzlingly blue sky, with the sun's heat softened by a deliciously cool breeze. Aix is crowded and gay, with German potentates abounding, French notabilities not wanting, and English royalty rumored to be coming. A motley crowd of divers nationalities drinks the waters each morning and discusses the latest society scandal.
30191-a-critic-in-pall-mall-being-extrac:
Oscar Wilde gathers extracts from reviews and miscellanies in A Critic in Pall Mall, first published by Methuen in London in 1919, in a selection made by E. V. Lucas. Early pieces treat the tomb of Keats, Keats on blue, dinners and dishes, Shakespeare on scenery, and Henry the Fourth at Oxford. A handbook to marriage, reading or not reading, letters of a great woman, and Béranger in England follow, with the poetry of the people and The Cenci.

Later pieces cover Balzac in English, Ben Jonson, Symonds on the Renaissance, Morris on the Odyssey, Russian novelists, and Pater's imaginary portraits. A German princess, a village tragedy, Mrs. Somerville, Aristotle at afternoon tea, and early Christian art in Ireland widen the range. Henley, Swinburne, Yeats, Whitman, and Morris close the set, showing Wilde as a witty, wide-ranging critic.
30252-the-four-faced-visitors-of-ezekiel:
Arthur W. Orton reads Ezekiel's vision as something stranger than a dream, in a short tale from Analog, March 1961, with pictures by the author. Ezekiel, they say, saw the wheel, but Orton suggests he saw somewhat more, and that what he saw made good sense to modern understanding. Bible scholars long called the first chapter of Ezekiel strange and nearly unfathomable, a vision set down by a man remote from us in time.

Orton argues the chapter was not mystical in the usual sense, but a report of a subject wholly unfamiliar to men of its time. Many call the chapter the Bible's science fiction, and have tried to unravel what its author meant. Framed as a claimed reading, not a settled fact, the piece suits readers who like ancient texts tested against modern machines and minds.
30301-the-side-of-the-angels-a-novel:
Basil King tells The Side of the Angels, published by A. L. Burt in New York by arrangement with Harper and Brothers, under copyrights of 1915 and 1916, and published in February 1916, with a frontispiece by Elizabeth Shippen Green. An illustration promises the greeting, I am Claude, do not you remember me, and Disraeli supplies the epigraph: my lord, I am on the side of the angels. The difficulty, King opens, is one of date.

Not a month or a year, but a generation or a century, divides Thorley Masterman's love for Rosie Fay, since in 1760 or even 1860 little would need adjustment. By 1860 the Fays still matched the Thorleys, and nearly matched the Mastermans. A century earlier, the Fays might have ranked above the Thorleys, and the Mastermans did not yet exist. The Mastermans then kept yeoman, clergyman, and country doctor status among the hills of Derbyshire.
30318-money-magic-a-novel:
Hamlin Garland tells Money Magic, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1907, in the Sunset Edition. The clerk of the Golden Eagle opens, with Marshall Haney changing heart, Bertha yielding to temptation, Haney meeting an avenger, and Bertha's upward flight. The Haney palace follows, with Bertha repulsing an enemy, receiving an invitation, and meeting Ben Fordyce, who calls on horseback and becomes adviser to Mrs. Haney.

Alice Heath has a vision, Bertha takes a yellow cart, and a send-off follows. Mart visits his sister, with a dinner and a play, Bertha becoming a patron of art, and her portrait discussed. Bertha meets Manhattan, makes a promise, meets the serpent's coil, and flees. The Haneys return to the peaks, Bertha decides, Alice visits Haney, Marshall Haney faces sentence, virtue triumphs, and his last trail closes the novel. Sibley Junction, in Colorado, sets the scene.
30448-the-lieutenant-governor-a-novel:
Guy Wetmore Carryl writes The Lieutenant-Governor, a novel copyrighted in 1902 and published in Boston and New York in March 1903, dedicated in memory of a rescue at sea. Fourteen chapters open with a fly on the wheel, the odds against young Nisbet, a face in the crowd, and friends at odds.

Later scenes add a brand from the burning, McGrath laughing, the mirage of power, the governor unmasked, and the ninth passing in review. Young Nisbet finds his tongue, Diogenes speaks, and an instrument of fate sounds its voice. Carryl blends political intrigue with personal honor in a brisk tale of power, loyalty, and public life.
30863-a-castle-in-spain-a-novel:
James De Mille wrote this novel, illustrated by E. A. Abbey and published by Harper and Brothers in New York, with copyrights in 1878 and 1883. De Mille had already written Cord and Creese, The Cryptogram, The Dodge Club, and The American Baron. The book sold in paper for fifty cents and in cloth for one dollar, in the days when Harper sent books by mail, postage paid, across the United States.

Chapter one, How a Party of Travellers Set Out on a Journey, opens at Madrid, where a train for the north is about to start. Soldiers, priests, civilians, and peasants crowd the station, moved by steam to unwonted punctuality and activity, while two men stand apart in the busy scene. De Mille follows that party through Spain, with castles, travel, and romance in the lively style of his popular novels.
31106-brooke-s-daughter-a-novel:
Janet C. Conger's novel opens at the Convent of the Annonciades, a secluded and highly select school for young ladies on the outskirts of Paris. The first chapter is headed The End of Her Childhood. Behind high mossy walls, turreted buildings, and long garden avenues, the sisters teach girls of good family, with rare exceptions made for great wealth or birth.

From that sheltered start, the story follows its heroine out of girlhood and into the wider claims of family, faith, and adult life. Readers get a Victorian tale of convent discipline, quiet rebellion, and the slow break with childhood. It is told with close attention to place, manners, and the inner lives of women shut away from the world.
31212-the-advocate-a-novel:
Charles Heavysege's 1865 Montreal novel opens in September 1800, in a lawyer's office in that city. There, the most distinguished advocate of the place, a commanding man of some sixty years, argues with a sorrowful middle-aged woman named Mona Macdonald. He brushes her plea aside with talk of variety, assizes, and his own busy season, while she presses a disagreeable topic that has left her in tears.

An epigraph from Measure for Measure sets the tone for a tale of law, love, and moral reckoning in early Montreal. Heavysege, known for his biblical dramas Saul and Jephthah's Daughter, here turns to the novel, giving Canadian readers a story of the courts and the heart.
31242-critical-remarks-on-sir-charles-gr:
The Augustan Reprint Society's 1950 reprint, with an introduction by Alan Dugald McKillop, revives a 1754 pamphlet asking whether Samuel Richardson's novels corrupt or improve public taste and morals. Written as a letter to the author by a self-styled lover of virtue and sold in London for one shilling, the pamphlet takes up Sir Charles Grandison. It also takes up Clarissa and Pamela in turn.

Its writer grants Richardson a laudable aim, the revival of religion and virtue, then presses hard on whether his long, minute novels serve that aim or merely feed curiosity. For students of the early novel, the reprint preserves a contemporary verdict on the most debated fiction of its age.
31375-under-false-pretences-a-novel:
Adeline Sergeant's 1889 novel, published by William Bryce in Toronto, unfolds in more than forty chapters from a prologue by a loch through Hugo Luttrell. A dead man's testimony, mother and son, a farewell, and Gower Street follow. It goes on to Elizabeth's wooing, Brother Dino, a mountainside, and the heiress of Strathleckie. San Stefano, the prior's opinion, and the Villa Venturi carry the intrigue to Italy.

Later chapters bring a lost letter, mischief afoot, a flask of Italian wine, a wishing well, a covenant, Elizabeth's confession, and Percival's own way. They go on to a revelation, accuser and accused, retribution, Percival's atonement, Dino's homecoming, wreck on the Rocas Reef, and Hugo's victory. Rich in incident and moral complication, the novel is Victorian sensation fiction at full stretch.
31490-the-religion-of-politics-a-sermon-:
Ezra S. Gannett was junior pastor of the Federal Street Church in Boston. He delivered The Religion of Politics as a sermon before Governor John Davis, Lieutenant Governor George Hull, the council, and the legislature of Massachusetts at the annual election on January 5, 1842. Printed at Boston in 1842, it takes its text from First Corinthians, chapter ten, verse thirty-one. The House of Representatives thanked Gannett the next day and asked for a copy for publication.

Gannett's sermon argues that politics, like all human action, falls under religious duty. Addressed to men taking up public office, it urges them to govern as stewards answerable to God. The sermon is a clear example of the election-sermon tradition, in which clergy spoke directly to rulers. Readers of American political thought will find religion and republican duty joined in one public address.
31642-eyes-like-the-sea-a-novel:
Maurus Jókai's novel Eyes Like the Sea, translated from the Hungarian by R. Nisbet Bain, was published at New York by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1894. Its chapters open with Sea-Eyes, Monsieur Galifard, and the first needle prick, then a first distinction, a first grievance, a Damenwalzer, a frightful monster, a readjusted scarf, and a second needle prick. A masterpiece and a hut follow.

The novel is told in the first person, with chapter titles that tease the reader from one small incident to the next. Jókai's tale moves through society, mishap, and romance, with sea-eyes at its center and a hero learning his way by pricks and distinctions.
31858-ancestors-a-novel:
Gertrude Atherton's 1907 novel Ancestors was published by Harper and Brothers in September 1907. It opens in 1904 with Miss Thangue, who has never before seen her friend's hand tremble over the teacups, after two monotonous years abroad. Her friend Victoria Gwynne requires the most delicate touch of all her patron-friends.

Flora Thangue, daughter of a Yorkshire village clergyman and childhood playmate of the little girls of the nearby castle, has learned boldness without overstepping. Readers get a society novel of ancestry, money, and manners, in which an American heiress and English county families measure each other across a social divide.
31945-st-peter-s-umbrella-a-novel:
Kálmán Mikszáth's novel St. Peter's Umbrella, translated from Hungarian by B. W. Worswick with an introduction by R. Nisbet Bain and published by Harper and Brothers in 1901, opens with a legend. The schoolmaster's widow at the Haláp is dead, leaving only a goat, a fattening goose, and a tiny girl of two.

Five parts follow the legend, the Gregorics family, traces that lead to Glogova, intellectual society in Bábaszék, and a third devil. An umbrella, an earring, and a will draw a village together. Readers get a beloved Hungarian novel, comic and tender, in which a sacred umbrella joins hands under its shelter.
31981-the-eel:
Miriam Allen DeFord's short story The Eel was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in April 1958 and illustrated by Dillon. It opens with a tagline: the punishment had to fit more than just the crime, it had to suit every world in the Galaxy. Its hero is known, and disliked, everywhere in the Galaxy, above all on eight planets across three different solar systems.

They all want to try him and punish him, each by their own laws and customs, a pursuit going on for twenty-six terrestrial years. The only place that does not want him is Earth, his home planet, where he was too smart to work his schemes, though the Galactic Police seek him there too. Readers get a wry science-fiction tale of a criminal too slippery for one world's justice.
31984-a-life-sentence-a-novel:
Adeline Sergeant's novel A Life Sentence was published in Montreal in 1889 by John Lovell and Son. It opens in a crowded courtroom as a guilty verdict is returned against Andrew Westwood. A curious thrill, half sigh and half sob, runs through the court, for even the most callous cannot hear unmoved the verdict condemning a fellow-creature to a shameful death.

The spectators at Andrew Westwood's trial for Sydney Vane's murder had expected the verdict. Yet it struck with the force of a shock, after a trial already two whole days long and into the afternoon of a third. Readers get a Victorian courtroom novel of murder, guilt, and a sentence that shapes a life.
32046-tales-from-the-german-comprising-s:
Tales from the German, comprising specimens from the most celebrated authors, translated by John Oxenford and C. A. Feiling and published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1844, opens with W. Hauff's Severed Hand. Its introduction says the translators aimed to present the English public with a collection combining effectiveness with variety, containing specimens of the most celebrated writers of prose fiction Germany has produced.

The translators admit that short tales cannot often promote any very high purpose, and that amusement for a leisure hour is their principal purpose. They hope readers will find themselves amused or interested. Readers get a Victorian anthology of German tales, chosen for variety rather than length, with lengthened novels excluded by design.
32302-the-destroying-angel:
Louis Joseph Vance's The Destroying Angel, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company in October 1912 with four illustrations by Arthur I. Keller, is a melodrama of love, doom, and detection. Vance, author of The Brass Bowl, The Bronze Bell, The Bandbox, and Cynthia of the Minute, dedicates the book to Robert Hobart Davis. Its twenty-one chapters run from Doom and The Last Straw through Mrs. Morten, Mrs. Whitaker, and Wilful Missing to Curtain, The Late Extra, and A History.

Later chapters include Entr'acte, The Window, The Spy, The Mouse-Trap, Offshore, Debacle, Disclosures, The Beacon, Discovery, Blight, Capitulation, Temperamental, and Black Out. The novel opens with a lover asking whether any hope remains for him. An illustration shows Whitaker's jaw dropping, his eyes widening with wonder and pity. Readers get an Edwardian romantic thriller, where a hopeless love opens onto spies, traps, and disclosure.
32416-way-of-a-rebel:
Walter Miller junior's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in April 1954, follows Lieutenant Laskell, a one-man submarine patrol fifty miles off the Florida coast. Surfacing after dark, Laskell tunes to Miami for the eight o'clock news. He hears a grim announcement he expected: Congress has approved the Manlin Bill, declaring total emergency under the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and President Williston has resigned at once.

Executive, legislative, and judicial power now rests with the Department of Defense, and Secretary Garson issues decrees ending any shirking of duty and calling on Eurasian Soviet leaders to stop air attacks. Laskell must search his own heart for the reason of right or wrong, deep beneath a turbulent Atlantic. Miller builds a tense story of rebellion, duty, and conscience under emergency rule.
32432-fidelity-a-novel:
Susan Glaspell's novel Fidelity, published in Boston in 1915, opens in everyday talk disturbed by Cora Albright's blunt question. Neighbours move with apparent ease to news of a new hotel costing two hundred thousand dollars and a sick neighbour without a cook, yet Dr. Deane Franklin, watching from a porch vine's shadow, sees whirlpools beneath their calm. His smile at seeing through people twists one side of his face, half shutting one eye.

From that opening, Glaspell builds a novel of marriage, loyalty, and the past, as characters weigh what faithfulness means when old love and new duty collide. The title points to the book's central question: to whom, and at what cost, is fidelity owed? Glaspell writes with psychological care, making small-town talk carry large moral weight.
32446-waldfried-a-novel:
Berthold Auerbach's novel Waldfried, translated by Simon Adler Stern and published in New York in 1874, opens with a father's New Year letter. In Book First, chapter one, the narrator quotes his eldest son writing from America for New Year 1870, reporting that the family has been sorely tried of late. Wolfgang, the son's only child, stands at the centre of that early sorrow.

From that letter the novel builds a German family story spanning home and emigration, with old and young generations weighing duty, loss, and hope. Auerbach, known for village tales and moral fiction, writes with warmth about work, faith, and family bonds. The book suits readers who enjoy nineteenth-century German novels of character and domestic life.
32560-gerald-fitzgerald-the-chevalier-a-:
Charles Lever's Gerald Fitzgerald, the Chevalier, published in London in 1899, first ran in installments in the Dublin University Magazine. Its publishers explain the tardy book form: the magazine changed hands after James M'Glashan's death, Lever set the story aside, and his daughter Mrs. Nevill could not account for its omission from his collected novels.

The novel opens in Rome, at the foot of the Campidoglio, in a mean alley called the Viccolo D'Orsi, better known as the Thieves' Corner. Dwellings built from fragments of ancient temples stand amid crumbling masonry, and Lever sets his hero's story among descendants of Rome's masters, fallen into rags and want.
32668-black-diamonds-a-novel:
Maurus Jókai, translated by Frances A. Gerard, opens this novel deep in a coal mine, where black walls and a still black pool frame a lone man in a boat by lamplight. Pillars of ancient pine and palm rise from the pit, hinting at a world of light buried long ago.

From that dark start the tale widens to mines, money, and marriage, as Ivan's fortunes tangle with Angela, her grandfather Prince Theobald, and schemes for a railway. Jókai mixes mine lore, finance, and romance in a story of greed, pride, and love.
32707-anne-a-novel:
Constance Fenimore Woolson tells the story of Anne, a young woman of direct feeling and little worldly polish. Her novel appeared from Harper in 1882, illustrated by C. S. Reinhart. It opens with Anne hanging evergreen in her father's house. Later she moves into wider company, where her simplicity draws attention she does not seek.

An older woman schemes to break Anne's attachment to a boy from her island home. She places Anne among fashionable loungers at a resort, trusting that new admirers will efface the old memory. Anne's truthfulness, the claims of family, and the pull of first love shape the tale. It is a novel of character, manners, and choice.
32826-fairfax-and-his-pride-a-novel:
Marie Van Vorst tells of Antony Fairfax, a southerner who steps into the world through New York, in this novel published by Small, Maynard and Company in 1920. On a bitter January day in 1880 he arrives from New Orleans at the South Ferry, carrying a handbag and a single valise.

The cold strikes him like a blow, yet he dreams of galleries, museums, and open doors for his ambitions. In New York he walks with Molly, a collar-factory girl in worn shoes, and learns pride, class, and friendship. Later, cold and hungry in Paris on the Rue du Bac, he works alone for the art he adores, believing in himself at last.
32887-trilbyana-the-rise-and-progress-of:
Published in 1895 by the Critic Company in a limited run of 250 copies, this small book traces how George du Maurier's novel Trilby became a popular sensation. It follows the story from its serial run in Harper's Monthly, between January and August, to its success in book form, and gathers drawings, anecdotes, and commentary on the craze that followed. Du Maurier's own first drawing for Punch appears among its illustrations.

The book is less a work of criticism than a scrapbook of a literary fashion at its peak. It records how readers, artists, and the press talked about Trilby, and how a single novel could seize the public mind in a season. For students of publishing and popular taste, it preserves the noise around a hit before that noise faded.
32977-from-sea-to-sea-letters-of-travel:
Rudyard Kipling's From Sea to Sea, complete in one volume from Doubleday, Page in 1913, gathers his letters of travel in two parts. Part one, Letters of Marque, opens in India with the Taj and the globe-trotter, a young man from Manchester, and the charm of Rajputana and Jeypore, city of the globe-trotter. Later letters describe a cotton-press in detail, the temple of Mahadeo, and the dead city of Amber left undescribed by design.

Kipling writes as a young journalist with a sharp eye and a sharper pen, and the letters show India, and the wider world, as he met them on the road. His voice is confident, funny, and often provocative, and modern readers will meet the attitudes of empire alongside vivid travel writing. The volume remains a major record of Kipling's early wanderings and of the craft that made him famous.
33099-the-truth-about-tristrem-varick-a-:
Saltus's novel Truth about Tristrem Varick, issued in Chicago, New York, and San Francisco in 1888, begins by warning that Varick's central tragedy has not been rightly understood. Saltus dedicates the book to Eduard von Hartmann as an attempt in ornamental disenchantment, and his epigraph insists truth is not always in white satin.

The novel that follows strips romance from a fashionable tragedy, showing a world of wealth, desire, and ruin without fairy tales or pastorals. Saltus writes with a decadent's polish and a cynic's eye, and his Varick stands as a figure of late nineteenth-century American sophistication. It remains a sharp, short novel for readers who enjoy literary decadence and the unmasking of polite society.
33143-east-angels-a-novel:
Constance Fenimore Woolson's East Angels opens under a blue sky that a traveler came more than anything else to be under. It is a novel published by Harper and Brothers with copyrights in 1884, 1885, and 1886. Asked if she is fond of sky, the young speaker begins a story set in the South. There, northern visitors, southern families, and the light and air of Florida shape lives and loves. Woolson writes southern sketches and novels with a Northerner's eye.

East Angels follows its characters through courtship, illness, and the moral choices of a region still marked by war and change. Woolson's prose is careful and atmospheric, letting landscape carry feeling. The novel remains a thoughtful period work, valued for its Florida setting and for a woman writer's view of the postwar South. It is neither sentimental nor harsh, but attentive to people caught between old and new.
33187-by-right-of-conquest-a-novel:
Arthur Hornblow's By Right of Conquest, in its hundredth thousand printing, is a thrilling story of shipwreck on a deserted island, pairing a millionaire's daughter with a common stoker. A contemporary notice called it a sensational situation handled with delicacy and vigor. The pairing drives the novel: wealth and rank stripped away by wreck, leaving two strangers to depend on each other for survival.

Hornblow, also known for John Marsh's Millions, The Third Degree, The End of the Game, and The Profligate, writes popular romance with a keen sense for dramatic situations. The island setting lets class, courage, and love be tested without society's rules. The novel remains a lively period adventure, built for readers who enjoyed a strong situation played out to its emotional end.
33206-plashers-mead-a-novel:
Compton Mackenzie's novel follows Guy and Pauline through two full years at Plashers Mead, told season by season from autumn to summer and back again. Copyrighted in 1915, its chapters mark each month, from September's slow train to winter, spring, and summer days in the English countryside. The tale lingers on walks, talks, and the small rhythms of a shared life, rather than on high drama.

Mackenzie writes with a poet's eye for place, letting the house and its mead carry much of the feeling. Guy and Pauline's story unfolds gently, shaped by the year itself. For readers who like a novel of mood and setting, where character grows through seasons, Plashers Mead offers a calm, rich portrait of young love in rural England.
33234-shadows-of-flames-a-novel:
Amélie Rives's novel centers on Sophy, a young woman whose bright surface hides a restless inner life. The story opens with Sophy before her mirror, noting the marks of feeling under her eyes, and then follows her through love, pride, and the pull of past choices. Rives traces how small acts and sharp words cast long shadows over Sophy's days, and how joy and sorrow live close together in one life.

Set among well-to-do people, the novel lingers on talk, glances, and the quiet turns of a heart under strain. Its title points to its main theme: that human passions, like flames, throw dark shapes even as they give light. Rives writes with a keen eye for social life, and the book moves at a slow, rich pace toward a close that weighs what Sophy has gained and lost.
33251-hempfield-a-novel:
David Grayson's novel Hempfield, published in 1915, opens with the discovery of a printing office, a scene that sets its small-town tale in motion. Grayson, author of Adventures in Contentment and The Friendly Road, writes of country life with warmth and humor, following folk who run presses, keep shops, and weigh big questions in small rooms. The novel is illustrated by Thomas Fogarty, whose pictures add to its homely charm.

The story's appeal lies in its gentle portrait of a community, where work, friendship, and faith shape daily life. Its pace is calm, its talk natural, and its lessons worn lightly. For readers who love Grayson's earlier books, Hempfield offers another visit to a world where contentment is found not in wealth but in good neighbors and honest work.
33279-the-riddle-of-the-spinning-wheel:
Mary E. Hanshew and Thomas W. Hanshew's mystery, copyrighted in 1922, opens with a girl from Scotland and Cleek to the rescue, then moves to a castle of dreams and morning scenes that deepen the plot. The Hanshews, authors of the Cleek tales and other riddles, write of a spinning wheel whose secret turns a quiet tale into a chase. Published by arrangement with Doubleday, Page, the book belongs to a popular detective series.

Cleek, the man of forty faces, brings his usual wit and disguise to a puzzle that blends romance with crime. The novel's pace is brisk, its clues laid with care, and its close rewards close reading. For fans of early detective fiction, The Riddle of the Spinning Wheel offers a lively, well-spun mystery.
33294-on-the-heights-a-novel:
Berthold Auerbach's novel On the Heights, translated by Simon Adler Stern, opens with early mass in a chapel, a scene that sets its high, earnest tone. Published in New York in 1907, with an earlier copyright in 1875, the novel follows lives lived on literal and moral heights, where duty, love, and faith are tested. Auerbach, known for The Villa on the Rhine, writes with a German novelist's breadth.

The book's appeal lies in its serious, humane portrait of people striving to live well amid temptation and sorrow. Its chapters move slowly, rich in talk and landscape. For readers who enjoy classic European fiction, On the Heights offers a thoughtful, old-fashioned novel of character, where the heights are both place and ideal.
33312-faith-and-unfaith-a-novel:
This novel, by the author of Phyllis, Molly Bawn, and Airy Fairy Lillian, takes faith and unfaith as its theme, with a line from Tennyson as its epigraph. The story opens with a line from Pope on dust and pride, then follows lovers whose trust is tested by doubt, pride, and the pull of the world.

The book belongs to the Victorian romance tradition, where feeling and honor drive the plot and a single choice can change a life. Its prose is rich and sentimental, suited to readers who enjoy a tale of hearts tried by faith. For fans of the author's other romances, Faith and Unfaith offers a familiar blend of passion, pride, and a hard-won happy end.
33400-the-book-of-susan-a-novel:
Lee Wilson Dodd's Book of Susan, copyrighted in 1920, is a novel whose heroine is praised in verse. She tracks wilds and breasts crags, choosing no path, yet her kirtle tears not and her sandals are silver. The book went through six printings between April and July 1920, a sign of how quickly readers took to Susan. Dodd writes of a woman whose spirit carries her past rough ground unharmed.

The novel's charm lies in Susan herself, a figure of grace under trial, and in Dodd's lyrical, thoughtful prose. Its story moves between inner life and outward adventure, with a poet's eye for image. For readers who enjoy a novel of character with a romantic cast, The Book of Susan offers a warm, distinctive portrait.
33475-the-broken-gate-a-novel:
Emerson Hough's Broken Gate, copyrighted in 1917, is a novel of American life, illustrated by M. Leone Bracker. Hough, author of The Man Next Door and The Mississippi Bubble, writes of a gate, literal and moral, whose breaking sets a story in motion. The book is dedicated to Arthur T. Vance, a faithful friend, and its tone is that of a popular novelist at his peak.

The novel blends romance, drama, and social observation, as its characters face choices that test honor and love. Its pace is steady, its scenes vivid, and its setting rich in American detail. For readers who enjoy early twentieth-century popular fiction, The Broken Gate offers a well-told tale of a community and a conscience.
33490-the-gambler-a-novel:
Katherine Cecil Thurston's Gambler, published in Toronto in 1905, is a novel of chance, love, and ruin. It has illustrations by John Cameron. Thurston, author of The Circle and The Masquerader, writes of a gambler whose fortunes turn on cards and character. One scene shows a man lowering candles and drawing back, a quiet image of suspense. The book is dedicated to her mother's memory.

The novel's appeal lies in its tense, romantic portrait of a world where one throw can change a life. Its pace is steady, its mood both glamorous and grave. For readers who enjoy Edwardian novels of society and risk, The Gambler offers a well-told tale of a man who stakes all, and a woman who watches the stakes.
33500-ayala-s-angel:
Anthony Trollope's 1881 novel follows two sisters left penniless by the death of their father, Egbert Dormer. Lucy, twenty-one, is thought plain and simple, while her nineteen-year-old sister Ayala is seen as poetic, charming, and romantic. The sisters go to live with different relatives, and their contrasting fortunes in love and society drive the story.

Suitors gather around both young women, including Tom Tringle, Isadore Hamel, Frank Houston, and Jonathan Stubbs, and Trollope weighs money, marriage, and character with his usual patient irony. The novel moves between London, Scotland, Rome, and country houses across three volumes. It is a late Trollope comedy of courtship, family pressure, and the search for an honest match.
33557-the-moonlit-way-a-novel:
Robert W. Chambers writes a 1919 romance of love, blackmail, and watching eyes, opening with a prologue called Claire-de-Lune. A shadow dance, sunrise, sunset, and dusk lead into Dragon Court and the world of Dulcie, whose day, evening, and night the novel follows in turn. A last mail, a midnight conversation, problems, and a watcher tighten the plot as a conference, a babbler, and a chance encounter raise the stakes.

Later chapters move through Grogan's, a white blackbird, Foreland Farms, a lion in the path, a silent house, and starlight, with Irish phrases and songs coloring the close. Chambers balances society romance with mystery, and the moonlit way of the title becomes a figure for a path toward love taken in darkness. Readers of his popular novels will recognize the blend of glamour and suspense.
33565-the-bachelors-a-novel:
William Dana Orcutt opens his 1915 novel in a golf club, where members gossip about an unlikely friendship. Huntington, an older man of dignity and quiet philosophy, and Cosden, a younger man of driving energy, play round after round together, each tempering the other's faults. Their companions cannot quite explain the bond, and the two men enjoy hearing themselves discussed.

From that clubroom start, the novel follows the bachelors through social life, courtship, and the question of whether men who have lived freely should marry. Orcutt studies temperament, reputation, and the tug between independence and attachment. The book is a light social novel, observant about club manners and the ways friends reshape one another.
33715-the-cottage-of-delight-a-novel:
Will N. Harben writes a Southern novel of labor, love, and ambition in this 1919 book. It opens before dawn with John Trott, a young mill hand under twenty, waking at five to the hoarse, mellow whistle of great cotton mills beyond low hills half a mile away. In lamplight he dresses in a lime-and-mortar-splotched shirt and overalls, cheap cotton socks holed at heel and toe, a belt tied with twine, and oddly new shoes.

Trott, tall, slender, sinewy, blue-eyed, and brusk in manner, works his way through a world of mills, families, and small-town hopes toward the cottage of delight itself. Harben, known for Ann Boyd, Abner Daniel, and The Triumph, writes with sympathy for working people and with attention to Southern speech and custom. The novel suits readers of early twentieth-century American regional fiction.
33747-an-engagement-of-convenience-a-nov:
Louis Zangwill writes a novel of love, observation, and convenience in this 1908 London book. Miss Robinson first saw Wyndham, a handsome artist with a knightly air and a winning smile, on the day he appeared as a neighbor and set up his studio. She fell in love with him at once, though years passed before she made his acquaintance. From her magic window in a big corner house, she watched his goings and comings, his picturesque Italian models, and great canvases borne in and out.

She also sensed his brilliant social world in smart broughams and victorias carrying stylish people. From that long, silent watching, Zangwill builds a story of engagement, convenience, and feeling, with an epigraph from George Meredith that in tragic life no villain need be. Readers of Edwardian fiction will enjoy its sympathetic portrait of a woman loving from a distance.
33773-a-yankee-from-the-west-a-novel:
Opie Read writes a novel of northern Illinois in this 1898 book, in its fourteenth edition. The opening rejects the traveler's flat picture of Illinois as a tiresome kitchen garden. It insists that the north of the state, the scene of the story, holds a spread and roll of romantic country. These include green billows of Wisconsin breaking into Illinois, lakes like jewels thrown broadcast, quiet rivers among rushes, great oaks, heavy forests, flowered valleys, and grape-vined fences.

Read's hero, a Yankee from the West, moves through that landscape of hillsides, lanes of accidental poetry, wild crab-apple, and green walnut scent. The novel belongs to Read's Arkansas and regional fiction, including Judge Elbridge and The Waters of Caney Fork. Readers who enjoy turn-of-the-century American local color will find a warm, landscape-rich story of character and place.
33779-majesty-a-novel:
Louis Couperus, newly translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos with a preface by Stephen McKenna, writes a novel of royalty in Majesty, published in New York in 1921. The preface notes that if the book is a roman à clef, its child of fate, Prince Othomar, hesitating, melancholy, and despairing, recalls the last Russian tsar. McKenna cautions, however, that the book does not stand or fall on such likenesses.

Couperus succeeds, the preface argues, as a sympathetic and imaginative artist. He creates first the collective life of a caste trained to formalize life and suppress emotion, then human characters who stand out vital against shadowy romance kings and queens. The novel follows Othomar through court, family, and fate, and suits readers of serious European fiction about power and inward life.
33886-the-wish-a-novel:
Hermann Sudermann's novel came out in English in 1895, translated by Lily Henkel with a life sketch by Elizabeth Lee. Sudermann was then counted among the fresh German writers of the late nineteenth century, beside men like Gerhard Hauptmann. The novel centers on a wish and the price it exacts from the people who make it.

Its scenes move through family life, love, and social pressure in a Germany near the end of a century. Sudermann watches how a single desire can bend a life out of shape. The book still reads as a study of longing, guilt, and the gap between what people want and what they can bear.
33958-a-sister-s-love-a-novel:
W. Heimburg wrote this German novel, translated by Margaret P. Waterman and published in Chicago by M. A. Donohue. The story opens in a storm off the North Sea, beating against the gray walls of a manor on the Luneburg heath. The house has belonged for centuries to the Von Hegewitz family, and its gables, tower, and pond set a somber scene.

Within that house, sisters and kin face love, pride, and family duty under clouded skies. Heimburg writes with the full feeling of a popular romance of her day. The novel endures as a moody tale of a noble house and the women who hold it together.
33989-love-works-wonders-a-novel:
Bertha M. Clay wrote this novel, published in New York in 1878 after an 1877 copyright entry by Street and Smith. Clay, author of Thrown on the World, dedicates the book through her publishers to readers of the New York Weekly, who had stood by the paper for nearly twenty years. An epigraph from Moore on love in rosy bondage opens the volume.
