The story that follows turns on love's power to undo plans and remake lives, in the sentimental manner of its age. Clay writes for a wide popular audience, with feeling and directness. The novel offers a period sample of the weekly-paper romance.
3476-henry-viii-and-his-court-a-historic:
Louise Muhlbach sets this historical novel in England in 1543, when Henry the Eighth marries for the sixth time. The bride is Catharine Parr, the young widow of Baron Latimer, and the opening chapter is called Choosing a Confessor. Bells ring across the kingdom as Henry declares himself the happiest man alive, while Catharine walks to the altar with bishops at either side.

Muhlbach follows the dangers of life beside a powerful, aging king. Courtiers plot, queens fall, and a new wife must guard every word. The novel blends real history with invented scenes, in the popular style of its time. It suits readers who enjoy Tudor romance, court intrigue, and a heroine who must survive by wit and patience.
3537-frederick-the-great-and-his-family-:
Louise Muhlbach writes a historical novel about Frederick the Great and his family, translated by Mrs Chapman Coleman and her daughters. The first book opens with the king, Prince Henry, Louise von Kleist, a masked ball, a secret captain, and the legacy of Colonel von Trenck of the Pandours. Later chapters follow an unwilling bridegroom, traveling musicians, and adventures in Amsterdam.

Muhlbach blends court gossip, military life, and romance around the Prussian king. Her Frederick is a sharp, restless figure, surrounded by family quarrels and loyal soldiers. Readers should treat the book as popular romance built on history, not as a scholarly life, and enjoy it for its pace and period color.
3666-andreas-hofer-an-historical-novel:
Louise Muhlbach writes a historical novel about Andreas Hofer, the Tyrolean innkeeper who led his people's rising against Bavarian and French rule in 1809. Hofer, a hero of the Alps, rallied mountain sharpshooters against Napoleon's allies, won battles in the valleys, and held Tyrol for a season before betrayal and defeat.

Muhlbach follows Hofer from his inn to the battlefield and at last to captivity and execution at Mantua in 1810. She blends real history with invented scenes, in the popular style of her time. The novel suits readers who enjoy romantic history of mountain freedom fighters and a hero who chose death rather than surrender.
3671-christie-johnstone-a-novel:
Charles Reade writes a novel about Christie Johnstone, a Scottish fisherwoman of Newhaven, and Lord Ipsden, a young lord who started life with nothing to win and lived only for amusement. Reade notes that the story was written three years before publication, so one or two topics are treated as they seemed then rather than now. He dedicates all that is good in the work to his mother.

The novel follows Ipsden as he learns real life among fisherfolk, and Christie as she judges a lord by his deeds rather than his rank. Reade writes with sympathy for working people and with humor about high society. The book suits readers who enjoy Victorian social novels and a heroine whose plain sense reforms a idle gentleman.
3693-louisa-of-prussia-and-her-times-a-h:
Louise Muhlbach writes a historical novel about Louisa, Queen of Prussia, during the Napoleonic wars. The book opens in Vienna, where the population is paralyzed with terror and a heavy gloom weighs on all minds, as couriers arrive from camp with dreadful tidings. Early chapters follow Minister von Thugut, an interview, two ministers, a house in the Gumpendorfer suburb, Joseph Haydn, General Bonaparte, and the Treaty of Campo Formio.

Later sections follow the young queen herself, admired for beauty, courage, and patriotism as Prussia faces French power. Muhlbach blends court life with war news, in her popular romantic style. The novel suits readers who enjoy historical romance centered on a beloved queen in a time of defeat.
3793-joseph-ii-and-his-court-an-historic:
Muhlbach, the popular historical novelist, dramatizes the court of Joseph the Second, the reforming emperor who tried to remake his lands by decree. The novel moves through palaces, anterooms, and secret conferences, where ministers hide behind screens to hear royal talk and copy it for foreign empresses. Joseph's plans for tolerance, reform, and enlightened rule clash with priests, nobles, and the slow habits of empire.

A vivid scene shows Frederick of Prussia laughing with his minister Hertzberg over a conference taken down word for word, ready to send to Empress Catharine. The book mixes real courts with invented talk, in the manner of the nineteenth century historical romance. Readers who like palace intrigue with a reformer's ideal at its center will find a long and colorful tale.
3801-napoleon-and-blu-cher-an-historical:
Louise Muhlbach pairs Napoleon with his Prussian foe Blucher in this historical novel of the empire's fall. The story moves through palaces and camps in winter, where a king's carriage waits at the gate while patrols change guard in the snow and drivers laugh unheard. Prussian officers, courtiers, and common soldiers all watch the same storm from different sides of the square.

The novel belongs to Muhlbach's long series of court romances, which dress real campaigns in invented dialogue and domestic scenes. Napoleon the gambler and Blucher the blunt old soldier make a vivid contrast. Readers who like Napoleonic fiction with court color will find a long tale of pride, defeat, and stubborn resistance.
40571-the-angel:
Guy Thorne wrote this tale, printed at New York in 1908. He had made his name with past tales of faith and dread. The first part bears the head And God Spake. Two men stand in front of a shop of a bird man in the East End of London. The shop is not far from the docks, and does a great trade with men of the sea. Small birds of green and gold shriek in their cages.

A box of glass in the glass of the shop holds lizards with eyes like live red gems. A foul small ape, chained to a hook, clangs in wild rage. In a cage at the door hangs a huge parrot, and the two men stop to look at it.
41483-the-yazoo-mystery-a-novel:
The Yazoo Mystery is a novel by Irving Craddock. It came out in New York from the Britton Publishing Company, with a copyright date of 1919. The book is offered to those who love adventure, as its dedication page states. A note states that small slips in marks have been set right, while varied spellings have been kept.

The first chapter opens at a port. The harbor-master comes brisk and yet in doubt into the room of the ship's first officer. What about the five men for the Domus? he bellows. The manager of a hiring office says all are ready to sign. He points to two men, a Spaniard, and a limp figure half asleep in the corner of the room. One hand of the sleeper grips a costly thing, as the first page breaks off.
430-the-grain-of-dust-a-novel:
David Graham Phillips opens this 1911 novel in the offices of a famed New York law firm, where a plain young typist seeks work. She seems, at first glance, a mere grain of dust in the city's vast ferment. Yet her steady tact, neat work, and quiet will soon draw the notice of rich lawyers and their sons.

Phillips follows her rise through offices, salons, and love affairs that test her pride. Men offer rank and wealth; she weighs what each gift costs. The novel reads as a sharp study of a working girl who keeps her self-respect while the city tries to buy it.
4394-a-romance-of-two-worlds-a-novel:
Marie Corelli wrote this novel of two worlds, opening with a prologue on an age of universal inquiry and universal skepticism. Its contents move from an artist's studio and a mysterious potion through three visions, a dance and a promise, and Cellini's story. Later chapters bring Zara and Prince Ivan, a symphony in the air, and an electric shock.

The heroine's strange departure leads to a miniature creation, secrets of sun and moon, and an electric creed. Corelli mixes romance with the science talk of her day, especially electricity as a spiritual force. The novel is characteristic Corelli: bold, mystical, and earnest about a world beyond the seen one.
4721-darkness-and-daylight-a-novel:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes, author of Lena Rivers and Tempest and Sunshine, wrote Darkness and Daylight as a novel. Its contents open at Collingwood, where Edith Hastings goes, and where Grace Atherton appears. Richard and Edith, visitors at Collingwood and Brier Hill, and Arthur and Edith follow, with Richard and Arthur, womanhood, and Edith at home.

Later chapters move to Grassy Spring, lessons, Friday, and a mystery there. Nina, Arthur's story, Nina and Miggie, Dr. Griswold, and a decision lead to the Deering woods, where darkness deepens. Parting, a nineteenth birthday, destiny, Edith and the world, and the land of flowers follow, with Sunnybank, sisters, and Arthur and Nina. Last days, parting with the dead and living, home, Nina's letter, a fiery test, and a sacrifice close before a bridal and six years later. Readers get a long, sentimental Victorian romance of love, trial, and light after darkness.
4732-prolegomena-to-the-history-of-israe:
Julius Wellhausen, professor of oriental languages at Marburg, wrote Prolegomena to the History of Israel, with a reprint of his article Israel from the Encyclopaedia Britannica. J. Sutherland Black and Allan Menzies translated it from German under Wellhausen's supervision, with a preface by W. Robertson Smith. The work first appeared in 1878 as History of Israel, volume one, and it made a great impression across Europe.

Its main thesis holds that Mosaic history is not the starting point for ancient Israel's history, but for the history of Judaism. Many leading Hebrew teachers in Germany, once aloof from the Grafian hypothesis, were won by its argument. That hypothesis dates Levitical law and connected Pentateuch parts after Judah's fall, rather than to Moses' day. Chapters cover worship, sacrifice, feasts, clergy, chronicles, judges, Samuel, kings, and the Hexateuch. Readers get a landmark of biblical criticism, dense but clear.
4733-when-egypt-went-broke-a-novel:
Holman Day opens When Egypt Went Broke with Tasper Britt starting to collect, at grey dawn. Some fishermen stay up late to jack angleworms with a bull's-eye light, since big worms roam soil under darkness. Others rise early to dig while dew holds smaller worms near the surface. The shrewd operator makes the job easy, and Britt, called Twelve-per-cent Britt, trims his slumber at both ends, owl and early bird both, in pursuit of people's pence.

Britt is the money boss for Egypt, and those who will not give him his per cent nickname call him Phay-ray-oh behind his back. To his face, his debt slaves speak obsequiously, since nearly every Egyptian with collateral owes him money. Britt believes that he is popular. Readers get a Maine novel of debt, power, and a town that goes broke, with humour and sharp local character.
4915-the-heart-of-rachael:
A bright April Saturday at the Long Island Country Club opens this novel, with two hundred golfers scattered over the links in plaid stockings, scarlet coats, and white skirts. The day marks the year's turning point, when winter gives way to summer's bathing, tennis, and moonlight motor trips.

Rachael, the heroine of the title, moves through this fashionable world of clubs and country houses, where romance and reputation are negotiated on lawns and dance floors. Authorship is left unnamed in the record. Readers get a society novel of the early twentieth century, attentive to manners, money, and the choices open to a young woman.
4929-the-fashionable-adventures-of-joshu:
Joshua Craig, a young man of small-town values, rents the cheapest flat in Washington's grand Wyandotte hotel, and this novel follows his fashionable adventures in the capital. Ninety dollars a month looms large in his eyes, though the hotel calls itself the most exclusive in the city, and its deluxe quarter sets the stage for his rise.

Craig arrays himself for society, courts influence, and learns the price of ambition among senators' wives and social climbers. No author appears in the catalog record. Readers get a Washington novel about a striver measuring himself against wealth, with satire sharp enough to cut through the hotel's polished manners.
4952-life-of-john-coleridge-patteson-mis:
Charlotte Mary Yonge's life of John Coleridge Patteson follows a missionary bishop of Melanesia from childhood onward. The biography begins at home and school between 1827 and 1838, arguing that a man's character depends so much on parents and upbringing that no life can skip them.

Yonge dwells on the father whose career shaped the son, and on parental training that led without forcing. From that quiet start, Patteson grows toward the Pacific islands where he would serve and die. Readers get a Victorian biography of faith and duty, written by a friend of the family with warmth and moral seriousness.
4955-leah-mordecai-a-novel:
Leah Mordecai opens on a rainy dismissal day at Madam Truxton's fashionable school, where pupils watch the showers and wait for rescue from the storm. Under the entrance arch, four maidens chat apart from the rest, and Helen Le Grande trusts her father or brother to fetch her through the rain.

Leah herself stands at the story's center, a young woman navigating school friendships, family expectation, and first love in a world of careful manners. The author goes unnamed in the catalog record. Readers get a schoolgirl novel of the older tradition, where character shows in small choices made while waiting out the weather.
5051-the-morals-of-marcus-ordeyne-a-nove:
William J. Locke's Morals of Marcus Ordeyne opens in Verona, where the narrator sits down to write the history of his extravagant adventure from diary notes lying open before him. He begins with a happy afternoon in May, six months earlier, and with a London note marking the seventh anniversary of his release from captivity.

For seven blessed years he has been free from the degrading influences of Jones Minor and the First Book of Euclid, and his adventure follows from that liberation. Locke mixes schoolboy memory with continental romance. Readers get an Edwardian novel about a man remaking his morals abroad, witty about English schooling and Italian sunlight alike.
5109-ragnarok-the-age-of-fire-and-gravel:
Ignatius Donnelly's Ragnarok argues that a comet striking the earth explains the gravel and drift deposits found across the northern world. Donnelly first examines the drift itself, its heat and its scale, then claims a comet caused it. He finally reads world myths as memories of the disaster: Norse Ragnarok, legends of fire and darkness, the Book of Job, and Genesis.

The book is a sequel to his Atlantis, and it shows Victorian speculation at its boldest, joining geology to mythology. Modern science does not accept its comet theory. Readers interested in the history of ideas will find a vivid example of how one writer tried to make myth and earth history tell a single story.
5153-rung-ho-a-novel:
Talbot Mundy's novel is set in Howrah City in India, a place that bows, as its opening verse says, to king, prince, and the god Siva. The city pays taxes in pain. Its heroine, Rosemary McClean, a girl of twenty, wanders unprotected through streets where an old sweeper woman follows her like a toothless dog, and danger gathers around her.

Mundy, known for Indian adventure, builds a story of empire, intrigue. Local power shapes the tale, with soldiers, priests, and rulers in the background. The novel offers readers a vivid, if dated, portrait of British India, told with the pace and colour of popular adventure fiction.
54687-the-ladies-paradise-a-realistic-no:
Émile Zola wrote this tale of a great shop in Paris, put in English dress in full from the French in 1886. It is the next book to one named Piping Hot. The first part opens at the Saint-Lazare stop of the trains. Denise has come in on a train from Cherbourg, with her two brothers in her care. They have sat the night on the hard bench of the third class of the train.

She leads the small Pépé by the hand, and Jean trails at her back. All three are worn by the trip, and feel lost and in fear in the vast town. They ask their way at each nook to the street where their uncle Baudu lives. But at a square on the way the girl stops short, in awe. There stands the great shop, the Ladies' Paradise, lit and huge.
5622-at-last-a-novel:
Marion Harland wrote At Last, a novel published in New York in 1870, opening with Mrs. Rachel Sutton, a born matchmaker who cultivated the gift by diligent practice. As a tendrilled vine suggests a trellis, and a stray glove recalls its fellow, every disengaged spinster of marriageable age appeals to her helpful sympathy. Unappropriated bachelors crossing her orbit draw her whole soul's compassion like blind and dizzy comets.

The novel follows matchmaking, courtship, and family life in Harland's domestic style, with dewless roses as its first chapter's emblem. Readers get a warm Victorian domestic romance, full of weddings plotted and hearts managed.
5705-the-queen-of-sheba-and-my-cousin-th:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich pairs two stories in this volume: The Queen of Sheba and My Cousin the Colonel. Its contents open with Mary, a family jar, and Mary taking a new departure. They then follow an odd adventure that befalls young Lynde in the hill country. A Cinderella's slipper figures among the later turns. The Boston and New York edition of 1907 presents Aldrich's polished, gently comic prose.

Readers get New England manners, family feeling, and romance treated with wit rather than melodrama. Aldrich favors character and dialogue over grand incident, letting small misunderstandings grow into real feeling. The book suits readers who enjoy late nineteenth-century American short fiction, and it offers a pleasant, civilized counterpoint to louder adventure tales of the same era.
5753-st-george-and-st-michael:
St George and St Michael, in its complete form, tells a long romance of love and civil war in seventeenth-century England. Dorothy and Richard stand at its center, with Richard's father, a witch, fools, preparations, and an adventure opening the story. Love and war soon intertwine, as Dorothy seeks refuge, Raglan Castle looms, two marquises contend, and a magician's vault hints at hidden power.

Across its full length, the novel follows divided loyalties through households, castles, and campaigns, letting personal feeling test political allegiance. Readers get a leisurely historical romance, rich in period manners and moral reflection, rather than a fast battle tale. It suits those who enjoy long Victorian romances where the fate of a marriage matters as much as the fate of a kingdom.
5805-the-league-of-the-scarlet-pimpernel:
Baroness Orczy continues the Scarlet Pimpernel saga in The League of the Scarlet Pimpernel, with Sir Percy explaining his league's work in the opening chapter. Contents follow a question of passports, two good patriots, the old scarecrow, a fine bit of work, and how Jean and others play their parts. The league rescues victims of the French Revolution under the noses of its agents.

Readers get swashbuckling adventure with disguise, daring, and romance, as Percy and his men outwit revolutionaries. Orczy writes with brisk, theatrical energy, letting secret identities and narrow escapes carry the plot. Fans of historical adventure will enjoy a direct sequel to the famous original, and new readers will find a self-contained tale of courage in dangerous times.
5807-sylvia-s-marriage-a-novel:
Upton Sinclair follows Sylvia through wifehood, motherhood, and rebellion in Sylvia's Marriage, a novel in three books. Book one presents Sylvia as wife, book two as mother, and book three as rebel, tracing how marriage, family, and social expectation shape a woman's life. Press notices quoted in the volume stress the importance of its theme, and the ravages of an unnamed evil that Sinclair means to expose.

Readers get Sinclair's reforming fiction at full stretch, as a society marriage becomes a study of disease, double standards, and women's rights. The novel argues passionately, using Sylvia's story to indict customs that harm wives and mothers. It suits readers of Sinclair, feminist history, and social-problem novels, and it remains a frank document of its era's debates.
5950-the-fortunes-of-nigel:
Walter Scott opens with a frank note on his choice of hero. He wants a man without high birth, romantic flair, or the usual gifts of romance heroes, and instead rests the tale on worth of character, goodness of heart, and rectitude of principle. The name Nigel is borrowed with a nod to a famous Scottish giver.

Scott points south-of-England readers toward George Heriot, whose charity left grand marks on the capital of Scotland. The introduction frames the novel as a test of whether plain virtue can carry a story. Readers meet a hero meant to earn regard by conduct, not by rank.
5962-oh-money-money-a-novel:
Eleanor H. Porter builds a comedy around a fortune and the people it unsettles. The chapter list opens with the exit of Mr. Stanley G. Fulton and the entrance of Mr. John Smith, then moves through poor Maggie, a held-up Santa Claus, and letters about money. Questions of dates, albums, and old ties keep surfacing.

Porter asks what becomes of money once its owner has done spending it, and who should gain when it changes hands. The tone stays light even as cousins, lawyers, and hopeful kin press their claims. At its heart the novel treats wealth as a test of character, not just a prize.
5964-love-s-pilgrimage-a-novel:
Upton Sinclair frames a love story as a slow capture. It opens in a woodland glen, where a young woman sits by a birch tree above a pool while her companion reads poems aloud on the mossy ground. Joyful images pass before them, yet the book titles warn of a snare tightening.

The parts are named for entanglement, captivity, and a break for freedom, with books called The Victim, The Bait Is Seized, The Torture-House, and The Price of Ransom. Sinclair treats love as a bond that can bind, chafe, and at last be fled. The novel follows that arc from tender ease to open struggle.
60-the-scarlet-pimpernel:
Paris in September 1792 runs red with the guillotine, yet some aristocrats vanish to safety. Baroness Orczy's Scarlet Pimpernel follows the secret league behind those escapes. Its leader signs his notes with a small red flower.

Marguerite Blakeney, a French actress wed to a foppish English lord, holds the key to his identity. Agent Chauvelin hunts the Pimpernel across Dover, Calais, and Paris ballrooms. Disguise, wit, and daring rescues drive the plot. The novel founded the masked-hero adventure. Sequels and stage versions followed, and the flower badge became shorthand for secret rescue.
6008-the-midnight-passenger-a-novel:
Richard Henry Savage opens on a Saturday in April 1897, as Randall Clayton steps from an elevator in a sedate Fourteenth Street building and sniffs the morning breeze. Shoppers already pour from Simpson, Crawford and Simpson's on Sixth Avenue, and the city hums with trade.

The books that follow run under the arch, through an inside ring, dreaming by the sea, a strange tug's voyage, and a message from Amoy. A girl bride rebels, a lonely pursuer follows, and secrets are shared aboard the yacht Rambler. Savage spins a tale of money, pursuit, and midnight passages.
6058-bricks-without-straw-a-novel:
Albion W. Tourgee frames Bricks Without Straw with an Egyptian jest: Pharaoh orders the Israelites to make bricks without straw, gathering stubble instead, and Neoncapos the king's jester laughs at the order. In wrath, Pharaoh gives him an owl and sets him outside the palace gate, forbidden to return or speak.

Tourgee dedicates the novel to his wife, praising her unflinching courage, unfaltering faith, unfailing cheer, and steadfast love. The title turns an ancient tale of forced labor into a figure for Reconstruction, where freed people are asked to build without materials. The novel argues that justice needs more than orders.
627-essays-of-travel:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers travel essays in this 1905 volume, opening with The Amateur Emigrant. Steerage scenes, sick men, and stowaways fill a Clyde-to-New York crossing, followed by Cockermouth, autumn effects, winter walks, forest notes, and Alpine diversions. A dedication to his cousin recalls a friendship older than their lives.

Stevenson writes with keen, observant prose, catching fellow travelers in a few strokes. The essays mix hardship with humor, and health with mountains. The volume serves as a fine travel companion, where a young Scot learns the world by boat, foot, and rail.
66676-the-king-of-the-mamozekel:
Charles G. D. Roberts wrote this tale of the wild beasts, printed at Boston in 1902. Charles Livingston Bull drew the cuts for the book. It stands in a set of the author's tales of beasts, with such books as The Watchers of the Trails and The Kindred of the Wild. A list of his works at the front of the book shows the range of his fame at that day.

The list is long: Red Fox, The Haunters of the Silences, The Heart of the Ancient Wood, and more. Prices stand by each name, from a coin and a half down to half a coin for the small books. This tale of a king beast stands at the small price in that list. The name of its beast is not a word of the tongue of trade or of the schools.
6884-sleeping-fires-a-novel:
Gertrude Atherton sets this novel in San Francisco of the 1860s, when Rincon Hill and South Park held the city's fine houses. Streets were muddy in winter and dusty in summer, sidewalks were wooden and uneven, and large plain homes stood behind deep gardens, willow trees, and roses. Some houses had come round the Horn, and Castilian roses on Rincon Hill still recalled the Spain that had shaped California.

Against that backdrop the novel follows the people of the residence streets, aloof from the busy heart north of Market Street. Atherton paints a city half built and half dreaming, where old romance lingers in walled gardens even as modern life presses in, and where private fires sleep beneath a calm social surface.
6900-rudin-a-novel:
Ivan Turgenev's Rudin comes here in Constance Garnett's translation from the Russian, with an introduction by S Stepniak. The introduction recalls how Turgenev won readers first in France, then in Germany and America, and at last in England. At his funeral Ernest Renan hailed him as a master in whom a whole world lived and spoke, a voice not of Russia alone but of the whole Slavonic world.

That fame grew slowly, unlike the sudden wave that lifted Tolstoi to world renown. Rudin itself stands among the novels that built that standing, a study of a gifted talker whose fine words outrun his deeds. Garnett's English gives English readers a clear path into Turgenev's art and his Russia.
7031-the-sheik-a-novel:
E M Hull's Sheik opens with Lady Conway refusing to watch the dancing, in sharp disapproval of Diana Mayo's planned desert tour. Diana means to travel alone into the desert with no chaperon or attendant of her own sex, only native camel drivers and servants. Lady Conway calls it recklessness and impropriety that may slur Diana's name and her country's prestige abroad.

English folk abroad, she insists, cannot be too careful, since continental neighbors seize any chance to cast stones. Another voice answers that the plan is unconventional and perhaps unwise, but not so bad as all that. The novel that follows carries Diana into the desert, where the sheik of the title awaits and romance overtakes judgment.
7063-a-terrible-secret-a-novel:
May Agnes Fleming dedicates A Terrible Secret to Christian Reid, author of Valerie Aylmer, as a token of admiration and esteem, from Brooklyn in September 1874. The contents open with bride and bridegroom elect, wife and heir, and how Lady Catheron came home. A Desdemona line on honesty, twilight, moonlight, nursery, and darkness follow, with news from the Chesholm Courier and bells ringing out mourning shows.

The first ending of the tragedy closes part one, and part two opens with Miss Darrell, a night in the snow, and Trixy's party. Under gaslight, old copies of the Courier, and moonlight nights lead through two boats, Alas for Trix, and St Partridge Day. Fleming writes a sensation novel of marriage, suspicion, and a secret kept too long.
7077-we-can-t-have-everything-a-novel:
Rupert Hughes opens We Can't Have Everything with Kedzie Thropp. She has never seen Fifth Avenue, a yacht, a butler, a glass of champagne, an ocean, or a person of social prominence. She wants to see them all. The novel notes that for each five minutes of day and night, one girl comes to New York to make her life, or so statisticians claim. An illustration shows war the sunderer reaching the characters with his great divorce.

The book runs in four parts: Miss Kedzie Thropp comes to town, Missus Tommie Gilfoyle has her picture taken, Missus Jim Dyckman is not satisfied, and the marchioness has qualms. Hughes, author of What Will People Say, writes a novel of New York society, marriage, and wanting more than life allows.
7230-not-george-washington-an-autobiogra:
P. G. Wodehouse and Herbert Westbrook call this 1907 book an autobiographical novel, and its contents show why the joke needs several voices. Miss Margaret Goodwin narrates first. Then James Orlebar Cloyster takes over for the invasion of Bohemia, the orb, Julian Eversleigh, and a run of ghosts, before Sidney Price adds his own gathering of ghosts.

The title's denial becomes a running gag, as a would-be writer's career unrolls through deceptions, columns, and New Year's Eve. Wodehouse's light touch keeps the many narrators distinct while the plot slips between farce and confession. Readers get a comic life story told by turns, with each teller adding a fresh twist.
7374-an-american-politician-a-novel:
F. Marion Crawford sets this novel in Boston society, a world where everyone knows everyone else's age, family, and standing. Mrs. Sam Wyndham, about forty and still handsome, moves through that world with dignity and ease, a woman fully equal to the part she has to play. Around her circle, reputation is watched as closely as money, and a misstep is remembered for years.

Into that close society comes the world of American politics, with its ambitions, alliances, and compromises. Crawford, who knew both American and European society well, uses the Boston scene to test what public life costs private character. The novel is a study of manners and power: how a person keeps standing in a city that never forgets, while playing a game whose rules keep shifting.
7414-poor-white-a-novel:
Sherwood Anderson, author of Winesburg, Ohio, tells the story of Hugh McVey, born in a miserable river town on the Mississippi in Missouri. The place, called Mudcat Landing in derision, sits on worthless yellow soil. Hugh's father, a tannery hand, loses his wife and raises the boy alone in a fishing shack by the river. No one quite knows how the boy lived through those years.

From that poor start, Hugh grows into an inventor whose machines help transform an Ohio town, and the novel follows what industry does to a community and a marriage. Anderson writes about the cost of progress: the old handcraft world gives way to factories, and people grow lonely in the new plenty. Poor White is a companion to Winesburg, darker and larger in scope.
7502-annie-kilburn-a-novel:
W. D. Howells's novel opens after the death of Judge Kilburn, when his daughter Annie comes back to America. She and her father had spent eleven winters in Rome. They always meant to return but stayed on year after year, as people do who have nothing definite to call them home. Toward the last, Annie had tacitly given up getting her father away, though both kept saying they would sail as soon as the spring weather settled.

Home again, Annie must find what her life is for. An old lady, away from America twenty years, is astonished to hear her talk of going back. She insists that the apartment where Annie lived longer than most inhabitants live in American towns is home itself. Howells uses Annie's return to ask what duty a woman of conscience owes her neighbors. It is a quiet novel of homecoming and moral awakening.
759-james-pethel:
Max Beerbohm wrote this short tale about James Pethel, a man the narrator learns of only when he reads of his sudden death in the morning paper. The shock, Beerbohm notes, is not quite grief: Pethel was a mere acquaintance, lately seen, and his death pricks the sense of mortality more than it wounds the heart.

From that small start Beerbohm spins a wry meditation on how we know people, how little we truly know them, and how death turns an acquaintance into a subject for thought. The prose is polished and dry, with jokes that sting gently. The tale shows Beerbohm at his most characteristic, finding a whole essay in a newspaper paragraph.
7837-the-nest-builder-a-novel:
Beatrice Forbes-Robertson Hale's The Nest-Builder opens outbound from Liverpool, as the Lusitania bucks down the Irish Sea in a September gale. In second class, propellers race out of water, gongs call diners, and ragtime pounds amid food smells, an effect Stefan Byrd finds sordid and demoniac.

Parts titled Mate-Song, Mated, The Nestling, Wings, and The Builder trace a marriage and a home built through art, travel, and strain. Through shipboard scenes and later homes, Hale asks what love needs to nest and grow, and what pride, work, and tenderness can build together.
79581-hell-s-angel:
Raoul F. Whitfield wrote this tale of the airmen of America in the Philippine Isles. Its lead man is Dantone Marcosson. Hot blood ran in his veins, the tale says at the start. He was the second son of a match of France and Italy, born in Morocco and raised in Africa. His mother lives in his mind as a lean, wiry shape who burst into rages too dread to see.

His big brother fled one night to the fields of gems, once their sire had used a hide whip with a hard hand. Then swift doom came to the house. The boy saw the red on the white of his mother's breast, and for years the green hilt of a knife swam in his night dreams. Three hours past the act the native force came, and the boy saw his sire no more.
7968-lying-prophets-a-novel:
Eden Phillpotts set this novel in Newlyn, the Cornish fishing village of grey stone, slate roofs, and narrow streets that opens the book. Its title comes from a village judgment quoted in the epigraph: two men are called lying prophets. One who finds God only in nature's beauty and one whose God laughs beside hell's mouth. Between those two visions stands a young woman, and the novel follows how each creed shapes her life.

Phillpotts divides the story into books on art and its rival claims, letting painters, preachers, and fisherfolk argue their cases in scene after scene. The Cornish coast is rendered with the same care as the debate. The result is a thoughtful, locally rooted novel about faith, art, and the danger of mistaking a partial truth for the whole.
7989-the-great-god-success-a-novel:
John Graham, the pen name of David Graham Phillips, wrote this novel of newspaper New York, following a Yale graduate into the world of Park Row journalism. Its chapters move from the candidate's arrival through city editorship, Bohemian life, yellow journalism, and the struggle between ambition and conscience. Headings such as I Must Be Rich and The Promised Land mark the hero's climb toward wealth and the price it exacts.

Phillips knew the newspaper trade from inside, and his portrait of editors, owners, and society is sharp and unsparing. The novel asks whether success itself becomes a god demanding sacrifice. As a picture of Gilded Age New York and its press, it remains energetic and pointed, and a useful companion to his better-known muckraking fiction.
8009-the-bible-king-james-version-book-9:
First Samuel bridges the age of judges and the age of kings. It opens with Hannah's prayer for a child, and Samuel grows up in the tabernacle to become Israel's last judge. When the people demand a king, Saul is anointed, wins battles, then loses God's favour through disobedience. The young shepherd David enters, slays Goliath, wins Jonathan's friendship, and survives Saul's jealous hunt through the wilderness.

The book's power lies in its characters: the faithful Hannah, the torn Saul, the loyal Jonathan, and David, gifted and flawed. Its stories of calling, kingship, and friendship have shaped Western literature for centuries. In the King James Version, the narrative's pace and pathos make First Samuel one of the most readable histories in Scripture.
8010-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
David's reign, in triumph and in ruin, fills the second book of Samuel. The king unites Israel, brings the ark to Jerusalem, and wins his wars, then falls through his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah. The prophet Nathan confronts him, and the rest of the book follows the cost: the death of a child. The rebellion of his son Absalom, and a kingdom shaken by grief and civil war.

Second Samuel is the Bible's great study of power and repentance, told with a storyteller's pace. David remains both hero and sinner, and the narrative never flattens him into either. In the King James Version, its scenes, from Nathan's parable to Absalom's death, rank among the most memorable in Scripture, and they shaped centuries of preaching and literature.
8026-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Ezekiel, a priest among the captives by the river Chebar, saw the heavens opened in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity. His book begins with a whirlwind from the north, a great cloud, and fire, and a vision of living creatures and wheels. From there it moves through oracles against Jerusalem, strange acted parables, and finally, after the city's fall, promises of restoration: dry bones rising, a new temple, and a river of life.

Ezekiel is the most visionary of the major prophets, and his images have haunted art and literature ever since. His message turns on responsibility: each person answers for his own ways. In the King James Version, the valley of dry bones and the new temple remain among the most powerful passages in the Old Testament.
8027-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Daniel tells of Jews in exile at Babylon who keep faith under foreign kings. Its stories are famous: Daniel in the lions' den, his friends in the fiery furnace, the handwriting on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, and Daniel interpreting Nebuchadnezzar's dreams. The second half turns to visions of beasts, kingdoms rising and falling, and a final deliverance, written in apocalyptic images that later readers have pondered for centuries.

The book's message is that earthly empires pass, while faithfulness endures. Its tales of courage under pressure have encouraged persecuted communities ever since. In the King James Version, the stories read with a storyteller's clarity, while the visions keep their mystery. Daniel remains essential for understanding both biblical narrative and the roots of apocalyptic writing.
8135-the-cathedral-a-novel:
Hugh Walpole's novel The Cathedral, dedicated to Jessie and Joseph Conrad, is set in a cathedral town where the great church dominates life. Its books move from a prelude on the Brandons and Ronders, through one of Joan's days, seatown mist and cathedral dust. And Ronder's day, into a whispering gallery, a May-day prologue, and quarrels that shake the close. The cathedral itself, its music, ritual, and stone, stands at the story's centre.

Walpole writes about ambition, faith, and family pride, with the cathedral as both backdrop and judge. The novel's atmosphere, mist, bells, and chant, gives it a brooding power. For readers of English cathedral fiction, from Trollope onward, it is a major example, and one of Walpole's most ambitious works.
8236-the-world-english-bible-web-1-samue:
First Samuel, in the World English Bible, opens at Ramathaim Zophim with Elkanah, his wives Hannah and Peninnah, and yearly worship at Shiloh, where Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas serve as priests. Hannah, childless, receives a double portion from her husband, and her prayer will lead to Samuel's birth. The book, lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, follows Samuel, Saul, and David through the founding of Israel's monarchy.

The modern English keeps the narrative's human detail: rival wives, a mother's grief, a boy called in the night, a king's rise and fall. Readers who know the King James version will find the same stories in plainer prose. First Samuel in this version is an inviting entry to the histories, told with warmth and pace.
8237-the-world-english-bible-web-2-samue:
Second Samuel, in the World English Bible, opens after Saul's death, when David, returned from slaughtering the Amalekites, has spent two days in Ziklag. On the third day a man comes from Saul's camp, clothes torn and earth on his head. Falling before David to report that Israel fled, many fell, and Saul and Jonathan are dead. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows David's reign, his sin with Bathsheba, and Absalom's rebellion.

The modern version keeps David's triumphs and tragedies in plain, moving prose, so Nathan's rebuke and Absalom's death hit hard. Second Samuel here reads as a study of power and repentance, accessible to readers who found the older version's language a barrier. It remains one of Scripture's great narratives.
8253-the-world-english-bible-web-ezekiel:
Ezekiel was a priest carried into exile in Babylon, and his book records the visions he saw by a river there. He describes strange living creatures and wheels, a valley of dry bones that rises to life, and a new temple measured in exact detail. Between the visions come fierce judgments on Jerusalem, on Israel's shepherds, and on neighboring nations.

The prophet often acted out his message: lying on one side for months, shaving his head, or eating bread baked over dung. Behind the strangeness lies a clear hope, that God would gather the scattered people and give them new hearts. Ezekiel has fed art and preaching for centuries, from the valley of bones to the river flowing from the temple.
8254-the-world-english-bible-web-daniel:
Daniel, in the World English Bible, opens in the third year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, when Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieged Jerusalem and carried off vessels of God's house to Shinar. The king orders Ashpenaz to bring Israelite youths of royal and noble seed, without blemish, well-favoured, skilful in wisdom and science, to serve in his court. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows Daniel and his friends through furnace, lions' den, and visions.

The modern version keeps the court tales crisp and the apocalyptic visions vivid, so the book's message stands out: empires pass, faithfulness endures. For readers new to Daniel, this rendering eases the way into both story and prophecy. Daniel here remains essential for understanding exile, courage, and the roots of apocalyptic hope.
8403-young-people-s-pride-a-novel:
Stephen Vincent Benêt published this novel in 1922, before the poems that made him famous, and it takes young pride as its subject. The book follows young people testing themselves against older expectations, in love, work, and friendship, with the bright, confident voice Benêt kept all his life. Henry Raleigh's illustrations picture the world they move through.

Benêt, later a Pulitzer winner for John Brown's Body, wrote here as a young man himself, and the novel reads as a young writer's book about youth. Readers who know his poetry will find the same energy in prose: quick dialogue, warm feeling, and a belief that young people, for all their pride, learn by living. It is an early work worth reading for its promise.
8545-amiel-s-journal-the-journal-intime-:
Henri-Frédéric Amiel's Journal Intime, translated with introduction and notes by Mrs. Humphrey Ward, appears here in a second edition, with many new passages from the last French edition inserted. Amiel, a Swiss professor at Geneva, kept a private journal for decades, recording thought, feeling, and self-scrutiny with painful honesty.

Ward's translation made Amiel famous in English as the journal writer par excellence, a man who thought more than he acted, and knew it. Readers get a classic of introspection, where a life is examined day by day. The journal suits anyone who keeps a diary, or who wonders what a life of thought costs.
8711-the-living-link-a-novel:
James De Mille, author of The Dodge Club and Cord and Creese. Sets The Living Link in motion on a pleasant May evening in 1840, on the portico of Plympton Terrace, a fashionable boarding school near Derwentwater. Young ladies walk arm in arm, effusive as girls will be, but a hush hangs over them, born of some unusual cause. They talk in low, earnest tones about one engrossing matter, and the chapter's title, A Terrible Secret, names what holds them.

From that schoolgirl opening, De Mille builds a sensation novel of secrets, identities, and links between past and present, in the style Victorian readers loved. The living link of the title binds characters across time and class, and its revelation drives the plot. Fans of De Mille's earlier adventures will find the same pace and mystery here, with a more domestic, school-and-society setting.
9089-handel:
Edward J. Dent wrote this short life of George Frideric Handel, the German-born composer who made London his home. Dent follows Handel from boyhood lessons under Zachow at Halle, through Hamburg and Italy, to London, where Rinaldo and later the Water Music won him fame. The chapters trace each phase of a long, busy career.

Opera wars, rival singers, the Royal Academy of Music, bankruptcy, and a final turn to English oratorio all pass in review. Dent keeps the story clear and the music in view, noting how Handel bent with taste and trouble. The book is a fine short guide to a composer whose choruses still fill halls.
9102-run-to-earth-a-novel:
The author of Lady Audley's Secret wrote this sensation novel of hidden wills, dreams, and dark deeds. Its chapters, with titles such as Warned in a Dream, Done in the Darkness, and Disinherited, promise shocks at every turn. A heroine in peril, a maniac's power, and a disputed testament drive the plot through picnics, towers, and midnight visits.

The novel belongs to the Victorian taste for secrets, bigamy, and sudden reveals, told with brisk pace and high feeling. Readers who like melodrama will find it in full flood here. It also shows how the sensation tale kept readers buying month after month in the 1860s and after.
9189-henry-dunbar-a-novel:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon wrote this sensation novel around the house of Dunbar, Dunbar, and Balderby. After office hours, a meeting at a railway station, and a stroke of death, the past must be sunk. Clement Austin's diary, an inquest, and an arrest follow, with Margaret's journey and three who suspect.

Laura Dunbar's hopes, a broken picture, and a steeplechase carry the tale to its close. Braddon dedicates it to actor John Baldwin Buckstone, praised for his genius on stage. The novel is full-blooded Victorian melodrama, with secrets, law, and love in high gear.
9407-the-little-colonel:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote this Kentucky children's book in 1895, inscribed to one of Kentucky's dearest little daughters. The Little Colonel stands one morning in one of the prettiest places in all Kentucky, on tiptoe, her eager face pressed to iron bars. She is much like her grandfather, the old Colonel, in temper and pride.

Pictures show her with a parrot on her broom, clattering up and down the hall, and singing at the top of her voice. Mrs. Sherman and Amanthis join the tale. Johnston's heroine charmed generations. The book remains a classic of American children's fiction, sunny and spirited.
9507-the-coryston-family-a-novel:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote The Coryston Family in 1913, a novel of politics, rank, and a mother's will. The tale opens in the House of Commons, as a minister speaks on a new Land Bill and the Opposition leader rises. Lady Coryston, strong and lined of face, rules her house with a firm hand. Her children, Marcia among them, test her rule with love, art, and new ideas.

Chapters follow speeches, drawing rooms, and family strife, as land, class, and duty collide. Ward writes with grave care for motive and manners. A reader gets a late Edwardian novel of power and family, rich in debate and in the cost of a proud mother's love.
9816-lo-michael:
Grace Livingston Hill wrote Lo, Michael!, an inspirational novel whose title quotes Daniel: one of the chief princes came to help. The tale opens on Madison Avenue, where a newsboy named Mikky dashes up stone steps toward a smiling baby in a crowd. A revolver cracks from the opposite curb as boy and baby fall together. Confusion follows in the great stone house's shadow.

Hill, beloved for wholesome romance, builds her story on rescue, faith, and a child's brave act. Mikky's golden hair and papers mark him as a street lad with heart. A reader gets a warm, old-style tale of help arriving in danger, told with Hill's earnest, hopeful voice.
9906-in-the-sargasso-sea-a-novel:
Thomas A. Janvier's 1898 novel is told by a man who pays for passage to Loango and boards the brig Golden Hind. Captain Luke makes him an offer, a gale wrecks the Hurst Castle, and the narrator finds himself on the edge of the Sargasso Sea, the great weed-choked calm of the Atlantic.

Stranded among drifting weed, he ties up a broken head, tries to attract attention, suffers fever and visions, and hears a strange cry in the night. Janvier builds suspense from solitude and the sea itself. Readers get a gripping castaway tale, stranger than a desert island because the prison is made of water and weed.
a-canadian-heroine-volume-1-a-novel: Mrs. Coghill begins her Canadian novel in this first volume, A Canadian Heroine. Its epigraphs praise the farms, mountains, and shores of the St. Lawrence country. The story follows a heroine whose trials and choices unfold against that Canadian landscape. This first volume opens the tale that the later volumes carry forward.
a-canadian-heroine-volume-2-a-novel: Continuing Mrs. Coghill's Canadian novel, this second volume follows the heroine onward. The story moves on through the farms, mountains, and St. Lawrence country praised in its epigraphs. New trials and relationships test her resolve as the plot deepens. This middle volume carries the tale from its opening toward its close.
a-canadian-heroine-volume-3-a-novel: The final volume of Mrs. Coghill's Canadian novel brings the heroine's story to its close. Her trials among the farms, mountains, and St. Lawrence country reach their resolution. The volume gathers the threads of love, duty, and endurance from the earlier books. It ends a Canadian story told across three volumes.
a-comedy-of-masks-a-novel: Ernest Christopher Dowson sets this novel among London artists and the world of the docks. Its opening scenes visit an Academy picture on varnishing day and a dry dock called Rainham's Dock. The story follows painters, sailors, and lovers whose masks hide real feeling. Dowson writes of art, love, and disillusion in the London of wooden ships and studios.
a-crooked-path-a-novel: Mrs. Alexander tells a crooked path of a novel set in London society. Its first chapter, Gathering Clouds, opens in early June as traffic streams toward Constitution Hill. Katherine, the heroine, is drawn into visits to a children's refuge and other institutions. Alexander follows her through weeks of social life, duty, and romance.
a-life-for-a-love-a-novel:
A Life for a Love is an 1891 novel by L T Meade. It opens in July in a rectory garden, where roses shower their petals over the grass of a large, somewhat untidy plot. Two girls are at the center of the scene, with children's laughter drifting in from a hay-field nearby and an empty tennis court waiting.

That calm, old-fashioned garden opening sets up the love story promised by the title, in which a life is staked on a love. Meade wrote prolifically for girls and for the domestic fiction market, and this novel belongs to her romantic line. It preserves her warm, scene-setting style and the rectory world in which much of her fiction moves.
a-little-rebel: The Duchess tells a little rebel story opening with a perplexed professor at breakfast. Two letters lie before him, one in his hand and one on the tablecloth. The memory of past favors, bright as a rainbow, frames his dismay. The Duchess writes a romance of rebellion and feeling in her popular manner.
a-little-rebel-a-novel: A novel by the Duchess, author of Her Last Throw and April's Lady, tells a little rebel. Its first chapter, perplexed in the extreme, finds a professor before an untasted breakfast. Two letters trouble him, and past favors shine like a rainbow in memory. This Canadian edition preserves the Duchess's romance of a rebel heroine.
a-romance-of-two-worlds-a-novel:
Marie Corelli's A Romance of Two Worlds is a novel of spiritual seeking dressed as a fashionable story. Her narrator, a young artist worn down by doubt, opens with a prologue on modern scepticism. Thinkers of the age deny God, the soul, and any life after death. The narrator's own strange experiences answer them.

A mysterious potion and three visions begin the change. The artist meets Cellini, a healer who teaches an electric creed linking faith with unseen forces. Chapters visit the Hotel Mars, its owner, Zara, and Prince Ivan. Secrets of the sun and moon and a miniature creation widen the tale's cosmic reach. Death by lightning and a struggle for mastery end the arc. Corelli blends society romance with occult doctrine, arguing that the unseen world is real.
a-short-history-of-a-long-travel-from-ba: Stephen Crisp recounts a long spiritual travel from Babylon to Bethel, beginning in his youth in his father's house. He heard talk of the house of God, where entrants enjoyed happiness in this world and the next. He longed to enter it, though neither he nor his talkers knew the way. Books by visitors to that house, read over and over, strengthened his belief and set his feet on the road.
a-strange-world-volume-1-of-3-a-novel:
Volume one of A Strange World, an 1875 novel by Mary Elizabeth Braddon, opens the three-volume story. Braddon, who wrote as M E Braddon, was one of the best-known Victorian novelists of her day. Like many novels of the period, A Strange World was issued in the three-volume form that lending libraries demanded and readers expected.

This opening volume begins the tale that the following two volumes continue and complete. It sets out the world of the title and the characters whose fortunes the later volumes decide. The volume is presented from the original edition, keeping the form in which Victorian readers first began the story and waited for its continuation.
a-strange-world-volume-3-of-3-a-novel:
Volume three of A Strange World, an 1875 novel by Mary Elizabeth Braddon, brings the three-volume story to its close. Braddon, who wrote as M E Braddon, was one of the best-known Victorian novelists of her day. Like many novels of the period, A Strange World was issued in the three-volume form that lending libraries demanded and readers expected.

This closing volume carries the tale begun in the first two volumes to its resolution. Readers who have followed the full set reach the ending here, with the threads of the earlier volumes drawn together. The volume is presented from the original edition, keeping the form in which Victorian readers first finished the story.
a-terrible-secret-a-novel:
May Agnes Fleming built her name on fast, emotional story-paper fiction, and A Terrible Secret is her kind of melodrama at full tilt. Her dedication page is dated Brooklyn, September 1874. The novel opens at Catheron Royals in Cheshire, where nineteen-year-old Inez Catheron is promised to her cousin Sir Victor, master of the great house and its wide estates.

Told in three parts, the plot runs through brides, heirs, newspaper reports, and a tragedy that seems to end more than once. Lady Helena, Trix, and Charley each take the blow differently as the hidden fact works its way toward daylight. In the final part the secret is told outright, and the book closes on forgiveness, parting, and a second bridal.
a-trip-to-venus-a-novel: John Munro sends his travellers to Venus in this 1897 novel, opening with a strange item glimpsed in the Times on a morning train for London. The chapters ask how we can get to other planets and discover a new force. They build an electric orrery, leave the earth, and cross space to the crater land of Venus. A flower of the soul, Alumion, a flying ape, and a sunward course carry the voyage home again, under epigraphs from Dante and Tennyson.
ailsa-paige-a-novel: Robert William Chambers tells the story of Ailsa Paige, a young woman whose life is reshaped by the American Civil War. The novel follows her through divided loyalties, romance, and the hardships of wartime, with period detail and a romantic plot. Chambers, a popular novelist of his day, gives the war a personal face through one heroine's trials and choices.
all-along-the-river-a-novel: All along the River is an 1893 novel by Mary Elizabeth Braddon, who wrote as M E Braddon. Braddon was one of the most popular novelists of the Victorian age, famous for sensation fiction built on secrets, crime, and passion. This book is a late work, written three decades after the novels that made her name. It stands in her large body of later fiction, the work of a veteran storyteller still writing for the library readers who had followed her since the eighteen sixties.
amiel-s-journal-the-journal-intime-of-he: Henri Frédéric Amiel keeps a journal intime that records, day by day, the thoughts of a Swiss thinker torn between ambition and inward life. Edited with a preface by Mary Augusta Ward, the journal moves through reading, nature, faith, and self-scrutiny. Its honesty about doubt and solitude made it a classic of introspective writing.
an-american-politician-a-novel:
F. Marion Crawford dated the dedication of An American Politician at Constantinople in October 1884, but the novel itself sits in Boston drawing rooms. It opens on Mrs. Sam Wyndham of Beacon Street, a hostess of old family and strong position, receiving callers on terms she sets herself rather than by Boston's Monday-afternoon custom.

Around her, Crawford builds a story of ambition in the republic: money, newspapers, party men, and a rising politician whose career tests what the drawing room will excuse. Boston manners are drawn with an insider's patience, down to who may say what to whom. The book belongs on the shelf of Gilded Age political novels that asked whether American public life rewarded character or management.
andreas-hofer-an-historical-novel:
Luise Mühlbach builds her historical novel around Andreas Hofer, the Tyrolean innkeeper who led his mountain people against Napoleon and Bavaria. The contents open in 1809 with the Emperor Francis, couriers and ambassadors, and a performance of The Creation, before Hofer himself appears. Flags are consecrated and farewells said as the valleys rise.

Forty-four chapters follow the story to its end. They cover the capture of Innsbruck and the battles on the Iselberg. They show Hofer ruling as the Emperor's lieutenant. They end with the treaty of peace that abandons Tyrol, and the final catastrophe of betrayal and execution. Mühlbach mixes court scenes in Vienna with camp and kitchen scenes in the Tyrol. Her Hofer is a patriot saint of the German historical novel.
annie-kilburn-a-novel:
William Dean Howells opens Annie Kilburn with a death in Rome: Judge Kilburn dies after eleven winters abroad. And his daughter Annie, thirty-one, gives up the apartment and sails home to America. She had nursed her father through helpless age, and the opening chapters measure how completely her life had been given to him, as nurse, companion, and child at once.

Back in her New England home town, Annie must build a life of her own among old acquaintances. Church questions, and her attempts at useful charity toward working people. The novel is Howells's realism at its most domestic: no villains, only habits, money, class feeling, and conscience pulling quiet people in different directions. Its drama is whether good intentions can survive a real town.
at-last-a-novel:
At Last, a novel by Marion Harland published at New York in 1870, opens in the county world of Mrs Rachel Sutton, a born matchmaker. Harland describes her gift with open comedy. Every unmarried woman of the right age appeals to her sympathy. Every bachelor crossing her path is sized up as a possible lover for someone waiting. Young people adore her, and careful mothers never quite call her dangerous.

Chapter I, titled Dewless Roses, sets that hobby loose among her neighbors. Chapter II promises an exchange of confidences, and the matchmaker's web tightens from there. Harland, a well known writer on home life, uses the comic frame to study courtship as a social system. Who may speak? Who must wait? Reputations bend under kindly meant meddling. The plot runs on engagements hoped for, mistaken, and finally sorted.
bella-donna-a-novel:
Robert Hichens published this novel of Egypt in 1908, here in a fifth edition from A. L. Burt. Hichens, author of The Call of the Blood, opens in London with Doctor Meyer Isaacson, whose rise to fashion was as sudden as a bullet's arrival. Society talks of nothing but his cures. Into his orbit comes the beautiful, tarnished Mrs. Cheyne, the bella donna of the title, who marries Nigel Armine and carries him to Egypt.

Nile scenes turn sinister by small signs. Nigel comes in from Sennoures to find his wife asking, too casually, about the shell tassels Egyptians wear: cowries, a charm against the evil eye and bad spirits, he tells her. A hand let go, teeth shown in the dark, a flitting shadow — Hichens builds his tale of slow poisoning and desert temptation out of such touches.
bessie-s-fortune-a-novel:
Mary J. Holmes published this novel with Dillingham of New York in 1888, dedicating it to her nephew Walter Twichell in memory of a happy year in Europe. The Jerrolds of Boston open the tale: Grey Jerrold, Lucy, Thanksgiving at Grey's Park, and the dinner at which Bessie is introduced. Miss Betsey McPherson and a horror at the farm-house set the machinery of secret and fortune in motion.

Bessie's suitor Neil declares himself at her workbasket. Taking the sock and darning-needle from her hands, he confesses he cannot keep it longer: he loves her and wants her for his wife. She looks up once, then lets her eyes fall, crying that he cannot be in earnest. Holmes writes her standard plot — a poor relation, a buried wrong, a fortune waiting — in the fluent domestic manner that filled American parlours for forty years.
birthright-a-novel:
T. S. Stribling published this novel in 1922, illustrated by F. Luis Mora and dedicated to his mother. Peter Siner, a Black graduate of Harvard, rides home to Tennessee in the first chapter. At Cairo, Illinois, the Pullman conductor asks him to take his bags forward into the Jim Crow car. The request surprises him like a blow; his education has not prepared him for Hooker's Bend.

Village life closes round him. The illustrations promise the Knights and Ladies of Tabor in white aprons with swords and spears, and old Rose raving in the Siner cabin quarter. Rose hopes God will send two she-bears to eat the white children who mocked her. Peter marvels at her unending flow of concentrated venom. He listens while splashing water from a tin pitcher. Stribling, a white Southerner, won praise for facing his region's caste lines head-on.
bluebell-a-novel:
Mrs G C Huddleston wrote Bluebell, a novel printed in 1875 from a copy held by the Toronto Mechanics' Institute. Huddleston centers the tale on Bluebell, a girl of seventeen when the story opens, her brother Bertie, and Gentle Annie. Garrison life and winter sport fill the Canadian scenes.

Chapters move from sleigh club nights and toboggan runs to a perilous sail and northern lights. Bertie's debts and his love for Cecil run beside the main courtship plot. The scene then shifts to England, where Bluebell makes her debut and meets Lord Bromley at Bromley Towers. A trip to the Baltic, a sad find, and deaths part the cast before the close. The tale mixes Canadian snow with English country-house life.
bred-in-the-bone-or-like-father-like-son:
James Payn published Bred in the Bone in New York in 1872, under his byline as author of A Beggar on Horseback. Payn opens in Breakneckshire with Carew of Crompton, a squire and mighty hunter who never turned aside for any man. His black horse Trebizond shares his fame.

Like father, like son, the subtitle warns, as the Carew line runs through love and money. Richard Yorke falls under a dark charge when bank-notes in Trevethick's strong-box prove false. A daughter's hand, a miner named Solomon, and Welsh scenes at Gethin fill the later action. Payn mixes sport, courtship, and crime in the three-volume manner. The close returns each year to a churchyard on a hill, and a wife's green memory.
bressant-a-novel:
Julian Hawthorne published Bressant, his first novel, in 1873. Hawthorne sets the tale at Professor Valeyon's walled garden house, where the professor loses a handkerchief on a hot June day. Two sisters, Sophie and Cornelia, make a covenant that binds the plot.

Bressant, a cold, brilliant young man, picks a tea-rose and enters the sisters' world. A daguerreotype, a keepsake, and nursing through sickness turn his heart by slow degrees. His own school tale, told mid-book, of a friend who lied over an exam, shows the rot and the cure in him. Partings, a lost-and-found close, and a parsonage door at noon end the tale. Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel, writes a study of pride thawed by love.
bricks-without-straw-a-novel:
Bricks Without Straw, a novel by Albion W Tourgee, takes its title from Exodus, where Pharaoh demands bricks without supplying straw. Tourgee had been a judge of the Superior Court of North Carolina. He opens with a fable. He pretends to translate it from an ancient Egyptian papyrus. A king's jester laughed at the order and was punished with an owl. He may speak to no one until the bird answers him. The allegory of an impossible command governs everything after.

The novel itself turns to Reconstruction in North Carolina, where Tourgee had served on the bench and fought the Ku Klux Klan in court. Freedmen, northern settlers, and defeated slaveholders contest land, labor, schools, and votes, while night riders answer ballots with terror. Tourgee writes as a participant with a brief: the South's new citizens asked to build freedom with bricks, and the nation that withheld the straw.
britannica-1911-abel:
Abel receives a Bible entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abel, second son of Adam, was slain by his elder brother Cain, as Genesis tells it. God had respect to Abel's offering and not to Cain's, the entry notes, and Hebrews adds that faith made the sacrifice more excellent.

Name study fills the rest: Hebrew for breath, a doubtful link to Assyrian ablu, son, and a likelier sense of herdsman. Pastoral Abel stands against farmer Cain in the reading. Winckler and Meyer feed a guess that Abel began as a South Judaean hero or demigod. Augustine's Abelitae, a North African sect, get the closing line. First John lays the murder to Cain's evil works against his brother's righteous ones.
britannica-1911-abu-simbel:
Abu Simbel, also called Ipsambul, is a group of temples of Rameses II in Nubia, cut into cliffs on the left bank of the Nile. Burckhardt found the main temple in 1812, and Belzoni cleared its entrance in 1817. Four seated colossi of the king, each about sixty-five feet high, guard the front, with smaller figures of his queen and children beside them.

Inside, coloured sculpture shows offerings, wars in Syria, Libya, and Ethiopia, and the battle of Kadesh against the Hittites. Sunlight was planned to reach the innermost sanctuary at dawn. Greek, Carian, and Phoenician soldiers later scratched their names on the colossi, evidence prized for the early history of the alphabet.
britannica-1911-acominatus-michael:
Michael Acominatus (about 1140-1220) was a Byzantine writer and churchman. He was born at Chonae, the ancient Colossae. He studied young at Constantinople. About 1175 he became archbishop of Athens. When Franks captured Constantinople in 1204, he retired to Ceos. He died on that island. His works include homilies, speeches, and poems. His letters also survive in number.

Writings show a city's decline. His memorial to the emperor Alexis protests abuses in Byzantine rule. A poem laments how far Athens had fallen. Monodies mourn his brother Nicetas and Archbishop Eustathius. The entry also treats Nicetas at length. Nicetas wrote a history in twenty-one books. It covers the years 1180 to 1206. His account of the capture of Constantinople is prized.
britannica-1911-acosta-uriel:
Uriel Acosta (died 1647) was a Portuguese Jew of noble family. He was born at Oporto late in the sixteenth century. His father had converted to Christianity. Uriel was raised in the Roman Catholic faith. Long, painful doubt led him to abandon it. He chose Judaism instead. At Amsterdam the synagogue received him. His name changed from Gabriel to Uriel there.

Peace eluded him in both faiths. Conflict with synagogue authorities brought excommunication. Fifteen years of exclusion ended in recantation. A second excommunication followed soon after. Seven more years passed before humiliating penance readmitted him. His autobiography declares against both religions. He admits only the law of nature as authority. Acosta took his own life in 1647.
britannica-1911-adams-samuel:
Samuel Adams (1722-1803) was an American statesman. He was born at Boston in September 1722. John Adams was his second cousin. His father was a wealthy Boston citizen-politician. The Caucus Club counted the elder Adams a member. Harvard graduated young Samuel in 1740. His master's thesis asked about resisting magistrates. Lawful resistance, if the commonwealth required it, was his theme. Business repeatedly failed under his management. Politics absorbed the attention his malt-house needed.

Town meeting made him formidable instead. Boston's tax collector proved unsuccessful in office. Yet Adams became the Man of the Town Meeting. He drafted Boston's Stamp Act instructions in 1764. The Boston Massacre excitement served his purposes skilfully. He managed the Boston Tea Party's proceedings. Opinion in his community bent to his direction.
britannica-1911-adanson-michel:
Michel Adanson (1727-1806) was a French naturalist of Scottish descent. He was born at Aix in Provence in April 1727. Paris cabinets employed him after college there. Reaumur and Bernard de Jussieu were his patrons. The Jardin des Plantes also gave him work. In 1748 he sailed for Senegal. That colony was a terra incognita to naturalists. Its climate's unhealthiness kept explorers away.

Five African years filled his collections. Adanson described immense numbers of animals and plants. He gathered every object of commerce too. Maps, weather observations, and language grammars followed. His Histoire naturelle du Senegal appeared in 1757. Its shell essay proposed a universal method of classification. His Familles naturelles des plantes followed in 1763. Organs, not single characters, grounded his natural system.
britannica-1911-ahithophel:
Ahithophel, a counsellor of King David, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His Hebrew name is read as brother of foolishness. He was a man of Judah whose son served in David's bodyguard, and he may have been Bathsheba's grandfather. David trusted his advice deeply, since his counsel was valued as if someone had inquired of the word of God.

That trust made his defection to Absalom's revolt a severe blow, and David prayed that his counsel be turned to foolishness. Ahithophel advised Absalom to seize his father's concubines as a claim to the throne, then to pursue David at once. The entry notes tangles in the surviving accounts, including Hushai's rival counsel of delay, meant to gather all Israel from Dan to Beersheba before striking.
britannica-1911-ainmuller-maximilian-emm:
Ainmuller, Maximilian Emmanuel, a German artist and glass-painter of 1807 to 1870, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Munich in February 1807, he took advice from Gartner, director of the royal porcelain works, and studied glass-painting as both a craft and an art. In 1828 he was made director of Munich's newly founded royal painted-glass manufactory.

There he perfected a method grown from the Renaissance enamel process. The design was painted directly onto the glass, and each colour was fired at a carefully adjusted heat as it was laid on. His earliest windows stand in Regensburg Cathedral, and nearly all Glasgow Cathedral's windows are his work. St Paul's, Peterhouse at Cambridge, and Cologne Cathedral also hold his glass. He painted interiors in oils too, and his views of Windsor's Chapel Royal and Westminster Abbey were much admired.
britannica-1911-allport-samuel:
Samuel Allport (1816–1897) was an English petrologist, a geologist who studies rocks, born in Birmingham on 23 January 1816 and educated in that city. Business occupied most of his working life, but his leisure went to geological studies. A short residence at Bahia in South America produced observations on local geology that the Geological Society published in 1860.

Allport's chief work lay in microscopic petrology, drawn onward by the investigations of H. C. Sorby. He became a pioneer of that branch, cutting his own rock sections with remarkable skill. Between 1869 and 1879 he described the basalts of South Staffordshire, Warwickshire diorites, Arran pitchstones, and other igneous rocks. He served as librarian of Mason College from 1880, received the Lyell medal in 1887, and died at Cheltenham that decade's end, in July 1897.
britannica-1911-anguier-francois-and-mic:
François Anguier (c. 1604–1669) and Michel Anguier (1612–1686) were French sculptor brothers. Both were natives of Eu in Normandy. They served their apprenticeship under Simon Guillain. François made a monument to Cardinal de Bérulle in Paris. Only the bust of that work survives. He also made the Montmorency mausoleum at Moulins. That tomb honoured Henri II, the last duke.

Michel's works carry the greater fame. He carved sculptures for the Porte St Denis arch. That arch, begun in 1674, honours Louis XIV's conquests. His marble Nativity at Val de Grâce was reckoned his masterpiece. He directed that church's sculpture from 1662 to 1667. He also decorated Anne of Austria's Louvre apartments. The financier Fouquet employed him at Vaux as well.
britannica-1911-asher-ben-yehiel:
ʾAsher ben Yehiel, known as Rosh, was a Jewish rabbi and codifier. He was born in the Rhine district about 1250. He died at Toledo in 1327. Persecutions endangered German Jews in his century. He fled to Spain to escape them. Toledo made him its rabbi there. Exile impoverished him significantly. His case changed medieval rabbis' status importantly.

Rabbis previously earned livings by secular professions. Medicine was a common such profession. They received no salary for rabbinic work. Salary began with figures like Asher. Meir of Rothenburg had been his teacher. Talmud was his sole interest thereafter. He was austere, profound, and narrow. Philosophy study met his determined opposition. His Compendium systematised the Talmud between 1307 and 1314. It largely superseded Al-phasi's earlier work. Later codes built directly on his Turim.
britannica-1911-ayscough-samuel:
Ayscough, Samuel (1745-1804), was an English librarian and index-maker born at Nottingham, where his father, a printer and stationer, ruined himself by speculation. Samuel moved to London and found work cataloguing at the British Museum, rising to assistant librarian about 1785 and later taking holy orders.

His private ventures built his name. First came a two-volume catalogue of the museum's undescribed manuscripts in 1782. Then came indexes to the Monthly Review and the Gentleman's Magazine. In 1790 he made the first index-concordance to Shakespeare. At the museum he shared in the 1787 catalogue and listed 16,000 ancient rolls and charters. A Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, he has been called the Prince of Indexers. He died at the museum in 1804.
britannica-1911-bahadur-khel:
Bahadur Khel is an Indian salt mine in the Kohat district of the North-West Frontier Province, set in hills south of the village of the same name between Kohat and Bannu. For four miles by a quarter mile, an exposed mass of rock-salt breaks the surface, with great salt hillocks on either side.

Quarries run a mile long, and men hew the salt out in large blocks with picks and wedges. The government once kept a large preventive staff to guard the salt revenue, withdrawn in 1898. Kohat salt pays lower duty than other Indian salt. Its sale is therefore limited to lands north of the Indus and to the frontier tribes. The rate was fixed in 1903. It stood well above the rest of India's rate.
britannica-1911-bailey-gamaliel:
Bailey, Gamaliel (1807-1859), was an American journalist born at Mount Holly, New Jersey. He graduated in medicine at Philadelphia in 1827. He edited a religious journal at Baltimore. In 1831 he moved to Cincinnati. There he practised medicine and lectured on physiology at Lane Theological Seminary.

The Lane debates of 1834 between pro-slavery and anti-slavery students made Bailey an ardent abolitionist. He joined Birney on the Philanthropist, then edited it alone through mob attacks that wrecked his printing office three times. In 1847 he took over the National Era at Washington, also mobbed, with his staff besieged three days in 1848. That paper first published Uncle Tom's Cabin in 1851-1852. Bailey died at sea on a trip to Europe in 1859.
britannica-1911-bailey-samuel:
Bailey, Samuel (1791-1870), was a British philosopher and author born at Sheffield. He first went to America to build trade links for Sheffield merchants. Then he retired young with a solid fortune. He kept only the chairmanship of the Sheffield Banking Company. Twice he stood for parliament as a philosophic radical and lost.

His life is mostly his books. Essays on the Formation and Publication of Opinions, from 1821, won most notice. Works on truth, political representation, and money followed. His work on value argued against Ricardo's school. His Review of Berkeley's Theory of Vision, from 1842, drew replies from John Stuart Mill and from Ferrier. His Theory of Reasoning examined inference. It also examined the syllogism, the formal pattern of argument. Clear style and original treatment mark all his writing, the entry says. He left over £80,000 to Sheffield.
britannica-1911-baillie-lady-grizel:
Baillie, Lady Grizel (1665-1746), was a Scottish song-writer born at Redbraes Castle in Berwickshire, eldest daughter of Sir Patrick Hume of Polwarth. At twelve she carried letters for her father to the imprisoned patriot Robert Baillie of Jerviswood, a friendship that put her family under suspicion.
