When royal troops seized Redbraes, her father hid in a churchyard and Grizel kept him fed; after Baillie's execution in 1684 the family fled to Holland, returning at the Revolution. In 1692 she married George Baillie, the patriot's son. Her songs, some printed in Ramsay's Tea-Table Miscellany, survive in a manuscript her daughter kept, the most famous being And werena my heart light I wad dee, first printed in 1725.
britannica-1911-baius-michael:
Baius, Michael (1513-1589), was a Belgian theologian. He was born at Melun in Hainault. Louvain University educated him well. He won a string of academic posts there. Charles V made him professor in 1552. His field was scriptural interpretation.

Baius went to the council of Trent in 1563. He arrived too late for real weight there. At Louvain he led the anti-scholastic reaction. That movement fought under Augustine's banner. His Augustinian leanings clashed with Rome. Grace and free will were the battlegrounds. In 1567 Pius V condemned seventy-nine of his claims. Baius submitted to the bull. Gregory XIII renewed the censure in 1579. Baius still kept his chair. He became chancellor of Louvain in 1575. Harnack called his work a curious mixture. Catholic orthodoxy and Protestant leanings met in it.
britannica-1911-ballantyne-robert-michae:
Robert Michael Ballantyne (1825–1894) was a Scottish writer of adventure stories for the young, born at Edinburgh on 24 April 1825. At sixteen he went to Canada and spent six years with the Hudson's Bay Company. Home in 1847, he printed his first book the next year, on life in the wilds of North America.

From 1856 Ballantyne wrote full time, starting the run of tales that made his name. The 1911 Britannica entry lists The Young Fur-Traders, The Coral Island, The World of Ice, The Dog Crusoe, and The Lighthouse among more than a hundred books. His rule was to write from first-hand knowledge of the scenes he described, and his tone was held healthy throughout.
britannica-1911-balmaceda-jose-manuel:
José Manuel Balmaceda (1838–1891) was president of Chile, born at Santiago in 1838 to wealthy parents. His early years went to business and farming ventures. In 1865 he represented Chile at the South American congress at Lima, and after his return he won fame as a speaker in the national assembly.

Balmaceda later held the foreign and interior portfolios, pushing through civil marriage and other laws the clergy hated. Elected president in 1886, he fell out badly with the assembly. On 1 January 1891 he refused to call it together and ordered taxes collected on his own word. The 1911 Britannica entry ends with the civil war that followed, his fall, and his suicide that September.
britannica-1911-bamford-samuel:
Samuel Bamford (1788–1872) was an English labour politician, born at Middleton in Lancashire on 28 February 1788. A weaver himself, he opposed violent movements and tried to restrain rough resistance to trade oppression. Yet he spoke at the Peterloo meeting at Manchester in 1819, a peaceful gathering for parliamentary reform and repeal of the Corn Law.

When that meeting ended in massacre, Bamford was arrested, convicted, and jailed for twelve months. The 1911 Britannica entry notes his popular poems, many in Lancashire dialect, voicing sympathy with his own class. His Passages in the Life of a Radical, printed in 1840–1844, is called an authoritative history of working-class life after Waterloo. He died at Harpurhey in 1872.
britannica-1911-barlow-joel:
Joel Barlow (1754–1812) was an American poet and politician, born at Redding, Connecticut, on 24 March 1754. He graduated at Yale in 1778, studied on for two years, and served as chaplain in a Massachusetts brigade until the revolutionary war ended. At Hartford he joined the circle of young writers known as the Hartford Wits.

Barlow founded the weekly American Mercury in 1784, was admitted to the bar in 1786, and shared in the satirical Anarchiad papers. His long poem The Vision of Columbus, printed in 1787, won him a wide reputation. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his 1788 move to France as agent of the Scioto Land Company, whose fraud, unknown to him, ruined its French settlers at Gallipolis, Ohio.
britannica-1911-baron-michel:
Michel Baron (1653–1729) was a French actor, born in Paris, son of a leading actor and a talented actress, both dead in his childhood. His family name was Boyron. At twelve he joined the company of child players called the Petits Comédiens Dauphins, and he was its brightest star. Molière, delighted with his talent, took him into his own company with the king's leave.

A quarrel with Molière's wife drove Baron out, but he rejoined in 1670 and stayed until Molière's death. At the Hôtel de Bourgogne he then reigned as undisputed master of the French stage until his retirement in 1691, creating leading roles in Racine's tragedies and writing comedies of his own. He returned to the stage in 1720 and worked on until his death in December 1729.
britannica-1911-barrel:
Barrel is a word of uncertain origin shared by the Romance languages. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it first as a cask, a round vessel built from staves held together by hoops. The same word also names a measure of capacity, dry or liquid, whose size changed with the goods being measured. Cross-references send readers to the article on weights and measures for those differing amounts.

Beyond casks, the entry lists the many round objects that borrow the name. A barrel can be the drum that winds a crane or capstan chain. It can also be the pinned cylinder inside a barrel-organ or musical box. Other uses name the hollow shaft where a pump piston moves, or the tube of a gun. Even a horse has a barrel, the part of its body between the shoulders and the quarters. A final note points to barrel-vaulting in building.
britannica-1911-barrington-samuel:
Samuel Barrington (1729–1800), a British admiral and fourth son of the first Viscount Barrington, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He joined the navy young and had reached post-captain by 1747. Service ran almost without pause through the peace after 1748 and into the Seven Years' War. He served with Hawke and Rodney, fought a strong French privateer, and sailed to destroy the fortifications of Louisburg.

Later commands took Barrington further. In 1768 he took the frigate Venus as governor to the duke of Cumberland, who served under him through several ranks. As rear-admiral in 1778 he helped take Santa Lucia in the West Indies and beat off a French attempt to retake it, then fought at Grenada and St Kitts. His last active service was the relief of Gibraltar in 1782.
britannica-1911-battel:
Battel, or battels, is an Oxford University word explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its origin is left unsure: it may link to battle, a northern English word meaning to feed, or to batten, to grow fat. At Oxford it names the food that members of a college order for themselves, apart from the usual commons, the set meals served to all. From that first sense the word spread to the bill a man ran up for his board.

Accounts and rank close the entry. Battels came to mean the accounts for board and food from the kitchen and buttery. Then it meant the whole of a man's college accounts. A batteler, in the entry's day a man who lived in college, was at first a rank of student between commoners and servitors. Such men got only the food they ordered for themselves, paid for in their battels.
britannica-1911-baudier-michel:
Michel Baudier (about 1589–1645), a French historian born in Languedoc, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In the reign of Louis XIII he held the post of historiographer, or official historian, to the court of France. His first works served French history at home. They were a history of the war in Flanders, 1559 to 1609, and lives in defence of Cardinal d'Amboise and the abbé Suger.

The Turks drew his strongest interest abroad. Baudier wrote a general inventory of Turkish history. He wrote a history of the Turkish religion with a life of Mahomet, and a history of the seraglio, the sultan's palace, turned into English in 1635. From a Jesuit fresh back from China he took material for a history of the court of the king of China, also later Englished.
britannica-1911-baumgarten-michael:
Michael Baumgarten (1812–1889), a German Protestant theologian born in Schleswig-Holstein, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at Kiel and in 1850 became professor of theology at Rostock. A liberal scholar, he won wide notice in 1854 with Die Nachtgesichte Sacharjas. That work took Old Testament texts and, in a prophet's tone, spoke on all questions. In 1856 he boldly defended free practice over the legal sanctity of Sunday.

Clash and loss followed. His bids to loosen the hold of church law brought him into conflict with the church authorities of Mecklenburg, and in 1858 they stripped him of his professorship. He then travelled through Germany demanding justice, told his life in print, and lectured on the life of Jesus. He helped found the German Protestants' Union in 1865, though he left it in 1877. He sat in the Reichstag three times for the progressive party.
britannica-1911-bellman-karl-mikael:
Karl Mikael Bellman (1740–1795) was a Swedish poet born at Stockholm, son of a civil servant. As a small child, in the delirium of a bad illness, he showed a strange gift for making up verse and tunes. He became a bank clerk at nineteen, then a customs clerk, but his habits were unsteady and want often dogged him.

Bellman’s great work, built up from 1765 to 1780, is the pair of song collections Fredmans Epistlar and Fredmans Sånger. Fredman and his friends were real figures from Stockholm’s taverns, which Bellman knew at first hand. His poems smell of life, not of the lamp, and his singing, mimicry and fine voice made him a favourite of King Gustavus III.
britannica-1911-bendl-karel:
Karel Bendl (1838–1897) was a Bohemian composer born at Prague. He studied at the organ school there, and by 1858 had written a run of small choral works. His Poletuje holubice won a prize in 1861 and became a favourite with local choral societies at once.

Bendl conducted opera briefly at Brussels, visited Amsterdam and Paris, then led Prague’s Hlahoe choral society from 1865 to 1879. His first opera, Lejla, succeeded in 1868, and more followed, among them the comic Stary Zenich and the prize opera Dite Tabera. His ballad Svanda dudak grew very popular, and many of his songs and choruses are counted national possessions of Bohemia.
britannica-1911-beni-israel:
Beni-Israel, “Sons of Israel,” are a colony of Jews settled on the Malabar coast in the Kolaba district of the Bombay presidency. They centre chiefly in the native state of Janjira. With the Jews of Cochin they stand for a very old Jewish coming to India.

That sets them apart from Jews who reached India in modern times for trade. Some authorities place the Beni-Israel’s settling in Kolaba in the fifteenth century. Their own traditions, though, claim a far longer tie with India, and the entry sends readers to the article on the Jews for the fuller story. The note is a short placing of an old community whose roots its members trace deep into the past.
britannica-1911-bernkastel:
Bernkastel is a German town in the Prussian Rhine province, set on the Mosel river. It stands in a deep, romantic valley. A branch line links it at Wengerohr to the main Trier to Coblenz railway. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its population as 2,300. Ruins of the castle Landshut stand above the town. The town first belonged to the chapter of Trier.

Wine is the chief industry here, not manufacture. The entry singles out Berncastler Doctor wine as enjoying great repute. Other manufactures are called unimportant. The town took its name from a cathedral provost, Adalbero of Luxemburg. His name survives in the older form, Adalberonis castellum. That Latin form means Adalbero's castle.
britannica-1911-biel-gabriel:
Gabriel Biel (about 1425–1495) was a scholastic philosopher, born at Spires in Germany. He became the first professor of theology at the new university of Tübingen, founded in 1477. He served twice as rector of that university. Late in life he entered a religious fraternity. His work set out the system of his master, William of Occam. His Epitome and Collectorium on the Sentences gave nominalist doctrine a clear, consistent form.

The 1911 Britannica entry calls that book the best specimen of scholasticism's final phase. Its stress on faith over reason touched Luther and Melanchthon, the entry claims. Biel picked up the odd title Papista Antipapista, papist anti-papist, from scattered remarks. The label Ultimus Scholasticorum, last of the schoolmen, is wrongly given to him, the article warns. Scholastic thought lived on long after him, above all in Spain.
britannica-1911-birch-samuel:
Samuel Birch (1813–1885) was an English Egyptologist and antiquary, born in London. His father was rector of St Mary Woolnoth in the city. From early age he leaned to out-of-the-way studies, including Chinese. After a short spell in the Record Office he joined the British Museum's antiquities staff in 1836. He owed that post to his knowledge of Chinese. He soon turned his research to Egyptian as well.

When the department split, Birch took charge of the Egyptian and Assyrian branch. For years almost the whole arrangement of that branch fell on him alone. Still he produced a hieroglyphic grammar and dictionary of high value. His translations include The Book of the Dead and the Harris papyrus. The 1911 Britannica entry also credits his standard history of pottery. He probed the Cypriote syllabary and kept his Chinese studies alive. He died in December 1885.
britannica-1911-bomberg-daniel:
Daniel Bomberg was a Christian printer of Hebrew books whose work in Venice changed Hebrew printing. His chief years there ran from 1516 to 1549, the year of his death. The entry is short and honours two great undertakings above all.

First came the first printed rabbinical Bible, in 1516–1517, giving the Hebrew text with rabbinical commentaries around it. Then came the first complete edition of the Talmud, issued from 1520 to 1523. Those two works set the pattern for Hebrew books for centuries, and the entry credits Bomberg with opening a new era in Hebrew typography.
britannica-1911-boone-daniel:
Daniel Boone (1734–1820) was an American pioneer and backwoodsman who opened Kentucky to settlement. Born near present Reading, Pennsylvania, of English descent, he moved with his father about 1751 to the Yadkin valley in North Carolina, then frontier country. He farmed, hunted, and trapped, and in 1755 served as wagoner and blacksmith on Braddock's failed expedition.

He first saw Kentucky in 1767 and roamed it from 1769 to 1771, gathering skins and fighting roving Indian bands. In 1775 he led the settlers who founded Boonesborough. Captured by Shawnees in February 1778, he was adopted by the tribe, taken to Detroit, and escaped in time to warn Boonesborough of attack, covering 160 miles in four days. The siege that followed opens the entry's later story.
britannica-1911-bouchotte-jean-baptiste-:
Jean Baptiste Noël Bouchotte (1754–1840) was a French cavalry officer who became minister of war in the Revolution's hardest year. Born at Metz, he was a captain of cavalry when the Revolution broke. His zeal won him a colonel's rank and the command at Cambrai, which he bravely defended.

When Dumouriez handed the war minister Beurnonville to the Austrians in April 1793, the Convention called Bouchotte to the ministry. He served until 31 March 1794. The Committee of Public Safety left him little room, yet he helped organise the republican armies and picked officers with sharp judgment, among them Kléber, Masséna, Moreau, and Bonaparte. In the reaction after Thermidor he was accused, tried, and acquitted, his honesty not in doubt, and he lived quietly until 1840.
britannica-1911-bredow-gottfried-gabriel:
Gottfried Gabriel Bredow (1773–1814) was a German historian born at Berlin on 14 December 1773. He held posts as professor at Helmstadt, then at Frankfort-on-Oder, and later at Breslau, where he died on 5 September 1814. His career was short, yet he left a shelf of handbooks and chronicles on ancient and modern history.

Chief among them stand a handbook of ancient history, geography and chronology from 1799, later Englished in 1827, and a chronicle of the 19th century from 1801. Tables of world history and a sketch of the most notable world events from 1796 to 1810 also appear. After his death J. G. Kunisch edited his remaining writings at Breslau in 1823 and added a life of the author.
britannica-1911-bruce-michael:
Michael Bruce (1746–1767) was a Scottish poet born at Kinnesswood in Kinross-shire on 27 March 1746, son of Alexander Bruce, a weaver of exceptional ability. He learned to read before he was four, with Sir David Lyndsay's works among his favourite books. Schooling came broken by work: he often herded cattle on the Lomond Hills in summer, and that early companionship with nature greatly influenced his poetic genius.

A delicate child, he grew up contemplative, devotional and humorous, the pet of family and friends, and his parents gave him schooling beyond their station, Latin and Greek included. At fifteen a small legacy and neighbours' help sent him to Edinburgh University for the winter sessions of 1762 to 1765. In 1765 he taught in summer at Gairney Bridge for about 11 pounds a year in fees plus free board, then became a divinity student at Kinross with the Burgher sect. The path the short life follows.
britannica-1911-brunsbuttel:
Brunsbuttel is a seaport town of Germany in the Prussian province of Schleswig-Holstein, on the north bank of the Elbe, 60 miles north-west of Hamburg. It held 2500 people in 1905. Canal, not coast trade alone, defines the place: Brunsbuttel is the western terminus of the Kaiser Wilhelm Canal, closed there by double locks.

Works listed are an inner harbour 1640 feet long and 656 feet wide, a coaling station, and a small harbour for the tugs and other vessels belonging to the canal company. Those few facts, Elbe bank, distance from Hamburg, canal terminus with its locks and harbours, make the whole of the brief port notice, a gazetteer entry built entirely around the canal's mouth.
britannica-1911-brute-simon-william-gabr:
Simon William Gabriel Bruté (1779–1839) was a French-born priest. He became the first Roman Catholic bishop of Vincennes, Indiana. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his life. He was born at Rennes on 20 March 1779. He trained first for medicine. Then he entered the Sulpician Seminary of Paris in 1803. He was ordained in 1808 and refused a post as chaplain to Napoleon.

Bruté settled in Baltimore in 1810. He taught at Mount St Mary's College at Emmitsburg. From 1815 he was president of St Mary's College, Baltimore. In 1834 the see of Vincennes was created, and he became its first bishop. He built his cathedral and several schools there. He also taught and preached in his own diocese. He died at Vincennes on 26 June 1839. Local Indians called him “chief of the Black robes.”
britannica-1911-cappel:
The Cappel family gave France jurists and theologians. They flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries. This 1911 Britannica entry traces the line. In 1491 Guillaume Cappel was rector of the university of Paris. He protested against a papal tithe claim. His nephew Jacques Cappel founded the family's fame. Jacques was advocate-general at the parlement of Paris. In 1537 he pleaded against the emperor Charles V in court.

Jacques left nine children, and the entry follows several. Three sons turned Protestant in the religious wars. Jacques the younger wrote treatises on jurisprudence. Louis Cappel of Moriambert was a most ardent Protestant. In 1570 he presented a confession of faith to Charles IX. He disputed with a Jesuit at Sedan in print and person. Ange Cappel served as secretary to Henry IV. Guillaume, who stayed Catholic, translated Machiavelli. The entry ends with the next generation at Sedan. Jacques the pastor taught Hebrew there.
britannica-1911-caravel:
A caravel was a ship of the age of discovery. The name was used in many countries at different times. This 1911 Britannica entry traces its forms. In Turkey it named a ship of war. In France it named a small herring-fishing boat. In the 15th and 16th centuries the word meant something grander. Portuguese and Spanish sailors used caravels for long voyages.

Those caravels were roundish ships with high stern castles. A double tower stood at the stern of each. A single tower stood in the bows. They were rigged in the galley fashion of the day. Two of Columbus' three ships were caravels. The entry closes with the English form of the word. Carvel survives in the term “carvel-built” for boats. In such boats the planking lies flush, edge to edge. That contrasts with clinker-built work, where the edges overlap.
britannica-1911-carmel:
Carmel is a mountain promontory on the coast of Palestine. It interrupts the seacoast south of the Bay of Acre. This 1911 Britannica article describes the ridge. It runs about 20 miles in a south-easterly direction. It finally joins the mountains of Samaria. The ridge is oolitic limestone, broken by ravines. Caves honeycomb its rock in many places. Its highest point, at Esfia, is 1760 feet.

Carmel lay in the territory of the tribe of Asher. No great political event is tied to its name. In the Old Testament it appears as symbol and as sanctuary. Its name means “garden-land” in Hebrew. Isaiah and Amos both praise its fruitfulness. Micah describes it as wooded in his day. That cover made it a noted hiding-place for fugitives. Today it is mostly wild brushwood of evergreens. Rock-hewn wine and olive presses recall its richer farming past.
britannica-1911-carrera-jose-miguel:
José Miguel Carrera (1785–1821) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the leading figure in Chile's early fight for independence. Born at Santiago, he was sent to Spain for a military career and served in the Spanish army during the Napoleonic war. He returned to Chile in July 1811, and his energy and experience let him seize the head of the nationalist government through a series of coups.

Carrera worked at first to build a stable administration, promote education, and organise the Chilean forces. His arrogance, though, split the patriot camp, and his rivalry with Bernardo O'Higgins led to the defeat at Rancagua in 1814. He had no part in the liberation expedition of 1817 and later raised rebellion in Argentina after his brothers were executed at Mendoza. Captured at last, he was shot at Mendoza on 4 September 1821.
britannica-1911-casabianca-raphael:
Raphael, Comte de Casabianca (1738–1825), is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French general from a noble Corsican family. In 1769 he took the side of France against Genoa, then mistress of Corsica. Serving the revolutionary government from 1793, he became lieutenant general in Corsica in place of Paoli, who was outlawed for dealings with England. His defence of Calvi against the English won him the rank of general of division.

Casabianca served in Italy from 1794 to 1798, entered the senate after the 18th of Brumaire, and was made count of the empire in 1806. He joined Louis XVIII in 1814, rejoined Napoleon in the Hundred Days, and reached the chamber of peers in 1819. The entry adds his nephew Louis, captain of the Orient at the battle of the Nile. Badly wounded, Louis fought the burning ship to the end and died with his ten year old son, who refused to leave him.
britannica-1911-castagno-andrea-del:
Andrea del Castagno (1390–1457) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian painter of the Florentine school, probably born at Castagno in the Mugello district. He copied Masaccio and the naturalists of his time in boldness of pose. The entry finds him weaker in grace and in colouring. For about four centuries his name carried a charge of murder.

The charge said that he had treacherously killed his colleague Domenico Veneziano to keep the new secret of oil painting for himself. The entry states plainly that the story is an untruth, since Domenico died four years after Andrea. His nickname, “of the Hanged Men,” came from a 1435 commission to paint the fallen Peruzzi and Albizzi leaders in Florence. Among his surviving works the entry names the equestrian figure of Nicola di Tolentino in Florence cathedral.
britannica-1911-cavaliere-emilio-del:
Emilio del Cavaliere is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a sixteenth century Italian composer born in Rome about 1550. He held a post at the court of Ferdinand I of Tuscany from 1588 to 1597. In Florence he moved among Peri, Rinuccini, and Caccini, the Bardi circle. In 1597 he returned to Rome and joined the Congregation of the Oratory of St Philip Neri.

In 1600 Rome saw his contribution to the musical reform his Florentine friends had begun. The work was La Rappresentazione di Anima e di Corpo, a sacred drama. It is regarded as the first example of what is now called oratorio. He may have died before its performance, though some authorities give 1602 for his death. The entry rates his style as easier than that of Peri and Caccini, but less deep. He was the first to apply the new monodic style to sacred music.
britannica-1911-chattel:
Chattel is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a term of English law, equal in meaning to personal property. Such property passes on the owner's death to his executor or administrator. It is then shared among the next of kin under the Statutes of Distributions, unless a will says otherwise. Chattels real are interests in land below freehold, such as estates for years. Chattels personal belong directly to the person of the owner.

The entry then turns to the chattel mortgage in United States law. It is a transfer of personal property as security for a debt. If the borrower fails to meet the terms, the title passes to the lender. At common law such a mortgage could be made without writing. Most states now require it to be written and recorded to bind third parties.
britannica-1911-cherchel:
Cherchel is a seaport of Algeria, in the department of Algiers, set 55 miles west of the capital. The town serves a farming and vine growing district, but its small port is hard to enter and trade stays modest. Its best known building is the Great Mosque of the Hundred Columns, used as a military hospital. The mosque holds 89 columns of diorite with varied capitals taken from older buildings.

The entry traces the site from Carthaginian Jol to Caesarea, capital of Juba II and the Mauretanian kingdom. Vandals, Byzantines and Arabs held the town in turn, and Khair-ed-Din took it in 1520. An earthquake ruined it in 1738, and French troops occupied it in 1840. Ruins, old cisterns and a museum with fine statues, among them figures of Aesculapius and Bacchus, fill the closing account.
britannica-1911-clonmel:
Clonmel is a municipal borough and the county town of County Tipperary, Ireland, 112 miles south-west from Dublin, holding 10,167 people in 1901. It is built on both sides of the Suir and also occupies Moore and Long Islands, joined to the mainland by three bridges. Parish church, two Roman Catholic churches, a Franciscan friary, two convents and an endowed school of 1685 are its principal buildings. The beauty of the river and environs, under the Galtee and Knockmealdown mountains, deserves mention.

Breweries, flour mills and tanneries work in the town, with a considerable export trade in grain, cattle, butter and provisions. Clonmel stands at the head of navigation for barges on the Suir. Charles Bianconi centred here from 1815 his system of light cars for travellers, extending over much of Leinster, Munster and Connaught. A woollen manufacture founded in 1667 had flourished until the close of the 18th century.
britannica-1911-cobet-carel-gabriel:
Cobet, Carel Gabriel (1813–1889) was a Dutch classical scholar, born at Paris on 28 November 1813 and educated at the Hague Gymnasium and Leiden university. In 1836 he won a gold medal for an essay characterising all the persons in Xenophon's Memorabilia, Symposium and Oeconomicus. His critical work on the remains of Plato the comic poet in 1840 revealed a remarkable critical faculty. A travelling pension let him study almost every Greek manuscript in the Italian libraries over five years.

In 1846 he married and took an extraordinary professorship at Leiden, his inaugural address being called the most perfect piece of Latin prose written in the 19th century. The rest of his life passed uneventfully at Leiden in teaching and editing. From 1856 he was joint editor of Mnemosyne, which he soon raised to a leading position among classical journals. Many critical notes and emendations from that journal were afterwards collected in book form.
britannica-1911-colman-samuel:
Samuel Colman (born 1832) was an American landscape painter born at Portland, Maine, on 4 March 1832. He learned his craft in New York as a pupil of Ashur B. Durand. From 1860 to 1862 he studied in Spain, Italy, France and England. He spent the years 1871 to 1876 in Europe once more. Water-colour work brought him his finest praise.

In 1860 he joined with James D. Smilie to found the American Water Color Society. He served as its first president in 1866 and 1867. In 1862 he was elected to the National Academy of Design. Two named works close the entry. The Ships of the Western Plains hangs in the Union League Club in New York. The Spanish Peaks, Colorado, hangs in the Metropolitan Museum in that same city.
britannica-1911-colt-samuel:
Samuel Colt (1814–1862) was an American inventor born at Hartford, Connecticut, on 19 July 1814. His father made silks and woollens there. At ten the boy left school for the factory. At fourteen, from a boarding school at Amherst, he ran away to sea for India. On that voyage, in 1829, he carved a wooden model of his future revolver.

Back home he learned chemistry in his father's works. Under the name Dr Coult he toured the United States and Canada with lectures on that science. Two years of profit let him return to his gun work. In 1835 he brought a six-barrelled rotating breech to completion. He took patents in London and Paris, then the American right at home. That year he founded the Patent Arms Company at Paterson, New Jersey. Troops used his revolvers with success by 1837.
britannica-1911-cooper-samuel:
Samuel Cooper (1609–1672) was an English miniature painter, called in the entry the greatest painter of miniatures who ever lived. He is believed to have been born in London. His uncle, John Hoskins, also a miniaturist, raised and taught him. He lived in Henrietta Street, Covent Garden, and haunted the coffee-house there. Pepys writes of him more than once.

Pepys calls him a fine musician who played the lute well. He spoke French with ease as well. Other writers paint him as short and stout, with a ruddy face. In 1668 Pepys set him to paint Mrs Pepys and paid thirty pounds for the work. He also painted John Aubrey's portrait, later given to the Ashmolean Museum. Evelyn saw him at work on the king's face in 1662. The entry closes with doubt over his last illness and recovery.
britannica-1911-cousins-samuel:
Samuel Cousins (1801–1887) was an English mezzotint engraver born at Exeter on 9 May 1801. He stands above all as the interpreter of Sir Thomas Lawrence, his contemporary. In his apprenticeship to S. W. Reynolds he engraved many of the best of the small mezzotints of Sir Joshua Reynolds's works. His master issued those prints under his own name.

Lawrence gave his gift its best field. Lady Acland and her Sons, Pope Pius VII and Master Lambton show his range. Brilliance and force in a high key mark his work. Those traits matched Lawrence's own traits stroke for stroke. Steel came into engraving about 1823 and changed the trade. Soft copper plates wore out too fast to match line engraving for large editions. Cousins had to work on steel from then on, like his peers. He kept the painter-like quality of mezzotint alive and in favour.
britannica-1911-cox-samuel:
Samuel Cox (1826–1893) was an English nonconformist divine born in London on 19 April 1826. For some years he worked as an apprentice in the London docks. He then entered the Baptist College at Stepney to train for the ministry. In 1851 he became pastor of a Baptist church at Southsea. He moved to Ryde in 1855 and to Nottingham in 1863.

He led the Baptist Association as its president in 1873. Saint Andrews gave him a doctorate of divinity in 1882. His gifts as a Bible expositor stood out among his peers. In 1875 he founded a monthly journal, The Expositor, and edited it until 1884. His books on theology run to a long list. Salvator Mundi came in 1877 and a commentary on Job in 1880. The Larger Hope followed in 1883. The entry keeps to posts, degree, journal and those three named books.
britannica-1911-coxcie-michael:
Michael Coxcie (1499–1592) was a Flemish painter born at Malines. He studied under Bernard van Orley, who most likely urged his trip to Italy. At Rome in 1532 he painted a chapel for Cardinal Enckenvoort in Santa Maria dell'Anima. Vasari knew him and wrote that he fairly gained the manner of an Italian. Design for engravers formed his chief work all the same.

The fable of Psyche, in thirty-two sheets by Agostino Veneziano and the Master of the Die, shows his skill in that line. Back in the Netherlands he spread that practice far and wide. His works hid for years under a woven monogram of his initials. In 1539 he came home to Malines and joined its painters' guild. For its chapel he painted the wings of an altarpiece now at Prague. At van Orley's death his standing rose to the first rank.
britannica-1911-coypel:
Coypel is the name of a French family of painters. Noel Coypel (1628–1707), called Coypel le Poussin for his debt to Poussin, was the son of an artist who met small success. Charles Errard set him to paint works for the Louvre. Royal commissions then brought him wide fame. In 1672 he became director of the French Academy at Rome.

After four years he came back to France and rose to direct the Academy of Painting. His Martyrdom of Saint James in Notre Dame may be his finest work. Antoine learned under his father and spent four years with him at Rome. At eighteen he entered the Academy of Painting. He became its professor and rector in 1707 and its director in 1714. In 1716 he was named king's painter and gained a patent of nobility a year later.
britannica-1911-damask-steel:
Damask steel, or Damascus steel, is a steel with a watered or streaked look, seen in the blades of fine Eastern swords. One way to gain that look is to twist together strips of iron and steel of unlike quality. The strips are then welded into one solid mass. A like but weaker result comes from etching a metal surface with acid. Grease shields chosen parts of the surface, so the watered pattern shows where the acid bites.

The art has been practised in Eastern lands from a remote period. The most famous blades came from Isfahan, Khorasan, and Shiraz in Persia. True damask work and acid imitation stand as its two methods. The entry gives no account of how the steel was hardened or ground. Pattern, method, and origin are all it offers the reader.
britannica-1911-daniel-samuel:
Samuel Daniel (1562–1619) was an English poet and historian, son of a music-master, born near Taunton in Somersetshire. He spent about three years at Magdalen Hall, Oxford, from 1579, then gave himself to free study of poetry and philosophy. The countess of Pembroke encouraged him and, by his account, taught him verse. He served as tutor to her son, and his first book, a translation of Paulus Jovius, appeared in 1585.

Daniel's sonnet cycle To Delia and The Complaint of Rosamond came out in 1592 and were often reprinted. The tragedy Cleopatra followed in 1594, and The First Four Books of the Civil Wars in 1595. His Poetical Essays of 1599 hold his finest, most mature manner, the entry judges. The closing estimate calls his style full, easy, and stately, lacking fire but rich in scholarly grace. His works were edited by Grosart in the years 1885 to 1896.
britannica-1911-emmanuel:
Emmanuel, or Immanuel, is a Hebrew symbolical name meaning “God (is) with us.” The entry sets the name in its first setting. In 734 to 733 B.C. Ahaz, king of Judah, feared the Syro-Ephraimitish alliance ranged against him and leaned toward seeking Assyrian help. Isaiah sought to calm that fear. The prophet said the danger would pass, and gave a sign: a young woman bearing a son within the year might call him Immanuel.

 The entry notes other readings of the passage and its mother. In the post-exilic period the first sense was forgotten, and a new one grew with later teaching about the end times. That reading appears in Matthew i. 23, where the name is applied to Jesus as the Messiah. The word occurs in only three passages of Scripture, the entry adds, though it is common in hymns as a title of Christ.
britannica-1911-emmons-nathanael:
Emmons, Nathanael (1745–1840), was an American theologian born at East Haddam, Connecticut, on 20 April 1745. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Nathanael Emmons article within it. In April 1773 he became pastor of the Second church at Franklin, Massachusetts, and stayed until failing health ended his active ministry in May 1827.

As a theologian Emmons was, for half a century, among the most widely felt clergymen in New England. He built an original system of divinity on the plan of Samuel Hopkins, and was seen as the chief voice of the “new school.” His system held that holiness and sin are free, willed acts, and that the least sin deserves eternal punishment, yet sinners, though wholly depraved, ought to repent. He died at Franklin on 23 September 1840.
britannica-1911-enamel:
Enamel, once “amel,” from a Latin word smaltum first found in a 9th-century life of Leo IV, is strictly the hard glassy compound fused onto the surface of metal objects. It serves for show or for use. The compound is a form of glass made of silica, minium, and potash, coloured by metallic oxides melted with it in the crucible. The term widened to mean the metal object so coated.

The long entry traces the craft through the ancient world. Egyptians and Assyrians did their greatest enamelling on pottery and brick, as on the enamelled walls of the palace of Rameses III at Tell el-Yehudia. Greek and Roman work followed in personal ornaments. Greek sculptors of the 4th and 5th centuries B.C. even set enamel eyes in bronze heads, and Pheidias enamelled the gold drapery of his colossal Zeus at Olympia with figures and flowers.
britannica-1911-encina-juan-del:
Encina, Juan del (1469 to about 1533), is often called the founder of the Spanish drama. He was born in 1469 near Salamanca, probably at Encinas. After leaving the university of Salamanca he joined the household of the second duke of Alva. In 1492 he entertained his patron with the Triunfo de la fama, a dramatic piece marking the fall of Granada.

In 1496 Encina published his Cancionero, a gathering of dramatic and lyrical poems, headed by a prose treatise on the state of the poetic art in Spain. He later visited Rome, won the notice of Alexander VI by his skill in music, and was made choirmaster. His fourteen dramatic pieces mark the shift from the church stage to the secular stage. The entry judges their own interest slight but their place in history large, and praises his lyrics for deep sincerity and devout grace.
britannica-1911-ettmuller-michael:
Michael Ettmüller (1644–1683) was a German physician born at Leipzig on 26 May 1644. He studied at Leipzig and Wittenberg, then travelled in Italy, France and England. Leipzig recalled him in 1668. He joined its medical faculty in 1676 and took the chair of botany. The university also made him extraordinary professor of surgery and anatomy. He died at Leipzig on 9 March 1683.

He won a great name as a lecturer and wrote many tracts on medical and chemical subjects. His son Michael Ernst published the collected works in 1708. The son himself held Leipzig chairs in turn: medicine in 1702, anatomy and surgery in 1706, physiology in 1719 and pathology in 1724. The entry is a short life of a well-regarded Leipzig medical teacher. It closes with the son's career rather than the father's writings.
britannica-1911-faure-gabriel:
Gabriel Faure (1845- ), French composer, was born at Pamiers on 13 May 1845. He studied at Niedermeyer's school of sacred music, first under Dietsch and then under Saint-Saens. He became maitre de chapelle at the church of the Madeleine in 1877 and its organist in 1896. The entry lists his works across many forms, and judges his place among modern French composers as one he holds alone.

His output includes a symphony in D minor, two piano quartets, an orchestral suite, a violin sonata and concerto, a pavane, and a requiem. He wrote incidental music for plays, a cantata, The Birth of Venus, performed at Leeds in 1898, much piano music and many songs. The entry praises his love of the unexpected, his wandering, maze-like harmonies, and the fascination and originality of his music, which it calls essentially aristocratic in character.
britannica-1911-favre-jules-claude-gabri:
Jules Claude Gabriel Favre (1809-1880), French statesman, was born at Lyons on 21 March 1809 and began his career as an advocate. From the revolution of 1830 he declared himself a republican, using political trials to voice his views. After 1848 he sat in the Constituent Assembly among the moderate republicans. He opposed Louis Napoleon, tried to organize armed resistance to the coup of December 1851, then withdrew to the law.

Favre returned as deputy for Paris in 1858, one of the Five who led republican opposition to the Empire. He denounced the Mexican expedition and the occupation of Rome, entered the French Academy in 1867, and opposed war with Prussia in 1870. In the Government of National Defence he served as vice-president and foreign minister, facing the hard task of negotiating peace with victorious Germany. His speeches were later published in eight volumes.
britannica-1911-featley-daniel:
Daniel Featley (1582-1645), also called Fairclough, was an English divine born at Charlton in Oxfordshire on 15 March 1582. A scholar of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and fellow in 1602, he went to France as chaplain to the English ambassador. He later served Archbishop George Abbot as domestic chaplain and held the rectories of Lambeth, Allhallows Bread Street and Acton. The hosted file opens with the closing pages of the Feather article before his entry begins.

Featley's busy career took in a scholastic duel with James I in 1625 and a reported conference with Jesuits in 1624. His books include a devotional manual of 1626 and seventy sermons opening hard texts of scripture. Made provost of Chelsea College in 1630, he sat in the Westminster Assembly of 1643 as its last remaining Episcopal member. Expelled and imprisoned for revealing its proceedings, he died at Chelsea on 17 April 1645.
britannica-1911-flannel:
Flannel is a woollen cloth of varied weight and fineness, usually made from loosely spun yarn. Its name is of uncertain origin, but in the sixteenth century flannel was a well-known product of Wales, and a Welsh source has been suggested. The French form flanelle came late in the seventeenth century. Baize, a coarse flannel with a long nap, reached England about the middle of the sixteenth century with refugees from France and the Netherlands. The hosted file opens with the closing pages of the Flanders article.

Making flannel changed over time, and cheap grades mixed in silk or cotton. Rochdale, the historic seat of the trade, employed over 2,000 people in it. Welsh flannel kept a high name, and blankets formed a special branch made at Bury and Dewsbury. The entry gives export figures for 1904 to 1906 and notes how flannelette, the cotton rival, checked the trade's growth.
britannica-1911-foote-samuel:
Samuel Foote (1720-1777), English dramatist and actor, was baptized at Truro on 27 January 1720. He loved his native Cornwall and put its praises into the mouth of Timothy, the country booby of his play The Knights. Toward his family he showed loyal affection. In his prosperity he supported his mother Eleanor Goodere freely. After her death he defended her character with heat against charges cast by the duchess of Kingston, whose spite the entry blames for the scandal.

About the time Foote came of age he inherited his first fortune in a grim way. His uncle was murdered by his own brother, and the estate came down through that crime. Foote was educated at the collegiate school at Worcester and at Oxford. The long entry follows the wit, mimic and theatre manager whose plays and impersonations made him one of the famous figures of the London stage.
britannica-1911-foster-sir-michael:
Sir Michael Foster (1836-1907), English physiologist, was born at Huntingdon on 8 March 1836. After graduating in medicine at London University in 1859, he practised in his native town. In 1867 he returned to London as teacher of practical physiology at University College, becoming professor two years later. In 1870 Trinity College, Cambridge, made him its praelector in physiology. Thirteen years later he took the university's newly created chair of physiology, holding it until 1903, and built much of the Cambridge biological school.

Foster excelled as a teacher and organizer, the entry stresses. As a secretary of the Royal Society from 1881 to 1903 he shaped the study of biology across Britain. He was made K.C.B. in 1899 and sat in parliament for London University from 1900 to 1906. His Textbook of Physiology of 1876 became a standard work. He died suddenly in London on 29 January 1907. The notice stands in a shared Foster file.
britannica-1911-franklin-william-buel:
William Buel Franklin (1823-1903), a Federal general in the American Civil War, was born at York, Pennsylvania, on 27 February 1823. He graduated at the head of his West Point class in 1843, joined the Engineer Corps, and won a brevet for his conduct at Buena Vista in the Mexican War. Later engineering work brought him a captaincy in 1857.

In the Civil War he led a brigade at Bull Run, then a division and the VI Corps before Richmond, at South Mountain, and at Antietam. At Fredericksburg he led the Left Grand Division, and General Burnside charged him with neglect there. His last field service was with the XIX Corps on the Red River expedition, where he was badly wounded in 1864. Retired in 1866, he became a vice-president of the Colt firearms company and died at Hartford in 1903.
britannica-1911-fremiet-emmanuel:
Emmanuel Frémiet (1824- ), French sculptor, was born in Paris, nephew and pupil of Rude. He gave himself chiefly to animal sculpture and to equestrian statues in armour. His start was in scientific drawing of bones, and hard times once put him in the grim post of painter to the Morgue. A Gazelle study reached the Salon in 1843.

His Wounded Bear and Wounded Dog of 1850 were bought at once by the Luxembourg Museum. From 1855 to 1859 he made military statuettes for Napoleon III. His equestrian Napoleon I came in 1868, and his first Joan of Arc for the Place des Pyramides in 1874, replaced by a finer version in 1889. The Gorilla and Woman won a medal of honour in 1887. He joined the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 1892 and followed Barye as professor of animal drawing at the Paris museum of natural history.
britannica-1911-gabriel:
Gabriel, in the Bible, is the heavenly messenger sent to Daniel to explain the vision of the ram and the he-goat and to declare the prediction of the Seventy Weeks. He announced the birth of John the Baptist to Zacharias and the birth of the Messiah to the Virgin Mary. Since he stands in the divine presence, Jewish and Christian writers call him an archangel. In the Book of Enoch he is one of the four archangels, set over all the powers, sharing in intercession.

Later Jewish writings credit Gabriel with showing Joseph his way, helping to bury Moses, and destroying the host of Sennacherib. He is also named as the spirit presiding over fire, thunder and the ripening of fruits. In the Koran he holds prominence as the medium of divine revelation, and Muslim interpreters identify him with the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of Truth.
britannica-1911-greco-el:
El Greco, the name commonly given to Dominico Theotocopuli (died 1614), was a Cretan painter, architect and sculptor. The 1911 Britannica entry says he was born in Crete between 1545 and 1550, and signed his Cretan origin in Greek letters on his greatest pictures. He studied first in Venice.

At Rome in 1570 he is described, in the miniaturist Giulio Clovio's letter, as a pupil of Titian. Yet the entry insists he was never an exponent of Titian's spirit, and his early pictures were ascribed to many hands but never to his master's. Two versions of the Healing of the Blind Man and four of Christ driving the money-changers from the Temple head the early list. He came to Spain in 1577. The long article follows the Spanish career that made his strange, elongated style famous.
britannica-1911-greene-nathanael:
Nathanael Greene (1742-1786) was an American general, son of a Quaker farmer and smith, born at Potowomut, Rhode Island, on 7 August 1742. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that his father's sect discouraged literary accomplishments. Greene still taught himself widely, with special study of mathematics, history and law.

He ran a forge at Coventry from 1770, urged the town's first public school, and sat in the Rhode Island legislature. His militia zeal cost him his place among the Friends, the entry says. In 1775 he led the Rhode Island contingent to Cambridge and was made brigadier by Congress. Washington gave him Boston after its evacuation. The long article follows his rise to the southern command, where his generalship saved the revolutionary cause in the Carolinas.
britannica-1911-ground-squirrel:
Ground-squirrel is a name for a group of mostly North American striped, ground-living squirrel-like rodents, more generally known as chipmunks. They sit close to the squirrels but differ in having cheek-pouches for storing food. Light stripes bordered by dark bands mark the sides or back, the ears are small and untufted, and the tail is relatively short.

With one Siberian exception, Tamias asiaticus, the group is confined to North America, where many species and races belong to the genus Tamias. Their numbers shift oddly, abundant in a district one year and absent the next. They eat nuts, beechmast, corn, roots and grubs, hoard large winter stores in their pouches, and lie dormant in holes through the cold season, though when hunted they will climb trees.
britannica-1911-groundsel:
Groundsel (Senecio vulgaris) is an annual plant of the Compositae order. Its branched, succulent stem grows 6 to 15 inches high. Its leaves are deeply lobed and coarsely toothed. Small cylindrical heads hold yellow tubular florets. The ribbed fruit carries a soft, feathery tuft of hairs. The plant is native to Europe. It has spread into all temperate climates.

Groundsel flowers throughout the year. Its light fruits spread it fast, making it a troublesome weed. It still serves as food for cage-birds. Ragwort, Senecio Jacobaea, is a showier relative in pastures. The huge genus Senecio spans temperate and cold climates worldwide. Some tropical African species grow into trees. The account also covers the North American groundsel tree. It closes with two rival derivations of the English name.
britannica-1911-hallel:
Hallel is a term in synagogue liturgy. It derives from a Hebrew word meaning to praise. It names, first, Psalms 113 to 118. Those are often called the Egyptian Hallel. They were recited at the paschal meal on Passover night. The term also names Psalm 136, the Great Hallel. C. A. Briggs traced Hallelujah through many psalm endings. Four groups of Hallel psalms are distinguished.

The official Hallel's extent changed over time. In Gamaliel's day its Passover use was still new. The school of Shammai advised only Psalm 113. The school of Hillel favoured Psalms 113 and 114. Four more psalms joined during the 2nd century AD. From the 3rd century the Hallel spread to other feasts. It entered the liturgy of eighteen festal days. The Great Hallel served general thanksgiving instead. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hallel entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-heinicke-samuel:
Samuel Heinicke (1727–1790) founded systematic deaf education in Germany. He was born at Nautschütz on 10 April 1727. He entered the electoral bodyguard at Dresden. Teaching afterward supported him. About 1754 his first deaf and dumb pupil was brought to him. That pupil's success fixed his life's work. The Seven Years' War interrupted his plans badly. He was taken prisoner at Pirna, then escaped from Dresden.

At Hamburg in 1768 he taught a deaf boy to talk. He followed Amman's Surdus loquens but improved its methods. The elector of Saxony recalled him home. In 1778 he opened Germany's first deaf and dumb institution at Leipzig. He directed that school until his death in 1790. He wrote a variety of books on deaf instruction. The entry is a short, admiring notice of a teaching pioneer.
britannica-1911-heinsius-daniel:
Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655) was a scholar of the Dutch Renaissance. He was born at Ghent on 9 June 1580. Spanish war troubles drove his family through Zeeland and England. Franeker university polished his Greek in 1594. Leiden then held him for the remaining sixty years of his life. Scaliger was his teacher there. Douza and Merula moved in his circle as equals.

In 1602 he became professor of Latin at Leiden. The Greek chair followed in 1605. He succeeded Merula as university librarian in 1607. Offers from abroad never tempted him away. His life thereafter is a list of productions. He edited Hesiod, Theocritus, Horace, Aristotle and Seneca. His Latin poems filled three volumes by 1605. His Dutch poems influenced Opitz and the German alexandrine. He died at the Hague on 25 February 1655.
britannica-1911-holdheim-samuel:
Samuel Holdheim (1806–1860) was a Jewish rabbi and a leader of reform in the German Synagogue, born in Posen in 1806. He became rabbi at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1836 and moved to Mecklenburg-Schwerin in 1840. He won prominence for pressing two causes at once: religious freedom, then much trammeled by Prussian law, and reform within the Jewish community itself.

At the rabbinical conferences of Brunswick (1844), Frankfort (1845) and Breslau (1846), Holdheim backed changes to ritual, above all on Sabbath observance, marriage laws and liturgical custom. In 1846 he became rabbi of the new Berlin congregation, where he shaped the course of Jewish reform. Graetz judged him harshly, and his stance drew real opposition. He died in Berlin in 1860.
britannica-1911-holinshed-raphael:
Raphael Holinshed (d. c. 1580) was an English chronicler, probably of a Cheshire family. About 1560 he came to London and worked as a translator for the printer Reginald Wolfe. Wolfe was preparing a universal history, and Holinshed laboured on it for years. After Wolfe's death in 1573 the plan was cut down, and the work appeared in 1578 as the Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, in two illustrated volumes.

Holinshed did much of the work, helped by William Harrison and others; the Scottish part is mainly a translation of Hector Boece. A second edition of 1587, enlarged but unillustrated, offended Elizabeth and her advisers, and the privy council ordered pages cut out at once. The Chronicles hold a mass of information and show great industry in their compilers. Their chief interest now is that Shakespeare and other Elizabethan dramatists drew largely on them.
britannica-1911-homel:
Homel, or Gomel, is a town of Russia, in the government of Mogilev, 132 m. by rail S.S.E. of the town of Mogilev, on the Sozh, a tributary of the Dnieper. Its population was 45,081 in 1900, nearly half of them Jews. It is a major railway junction, on the lines from Vilna to Odessa and from Orel to Poland, and steamers link it with Kiev and Mogilev.

Before Prince Paskevich's castle stands an equestrian statue of the Polish general Joseph Poniatowski. In the cathedral lies the tomb of the chancellor Rumantsev, by Canova. The town trades briskly in hops, corn and timber, and has paper-pulp mills and oil factories. Founded in the 12th century, it passed between Poles and Russians before annexation to Russia in 1772. In 1648 it suffered at the hands of Bogdan Chmielnicki's Cossacks.
britannica-1911-hone-nathaniel:
Nathaniel Hone (1718–1784) was a British painter, son of a Dublin merchant. With no regular training he gained much skill as a portrait painter while young. He left Dublin for England, worked in provincial towns, and settled in London, where he soon built a solid name. His oil paintings were popular, but his chief success came in miniatures and enamels, done with masterly power.

Hone joined the Incorporated Society of Artists and became a foundation member of the Royal Academy. His relations there were stormy: the Academy once rejected two of his pictures, one read as a satire on Reynolds and one on Angelica Kauffman. Most of his exhibition pieces were portraits, and the quality of his work varied greatly. His miniatures and enamels still earn him a place among the ablest artists of the British school.
britannica-1911-hostel: A hostel is the old name for an inn. At Oxford and Cambridge the word also named the lodgings where students of the university lived in early times, under rules set to some extent by the authorities. Some English public schools keep a hostel system still: their boarding houses are organized as separate lodgings, each under its own master. The entry is a short note on the word and its uses.
britannica-1911-jebel: Jebel, with the plural jibal, is an Arabic word for a mountain or a range of mountains. It is also spelled Gebel, with a hard g, and in French it appears as djebel. The word turns up often in place names. A related form, Jebeli, means a mountaineer. The hard g sound in the Gebel form comes from the speech of Egypt, as the article notes in its brief entry.
britannica-1911-kayser-friedrich-heinric:
Friedrich Heinrich Emanuel Kayser (1845– ) was a German geologist and student of fossils, born at Königsberg on the 26th of March 1845. He was trained at Berlin, where he took his doctor's degree in 1870. In 1882 he became professor of geology at the university of Marburg.

He studied fossils of many ages and from all parts of the world. His chief ground was the Palaeozoic formations, among them those of South Africa and the polar regions. The Devonian fossils of Germany, Bohemia, and other parts of Europe drew his closest work. His books include a two volume textbook of geology, a study of geological formations issued in 1891, and a work on the fauna of the Siegen greywacke. The first volume of his general geology was turned into English by P. Lake in 1893 as a Textbook of Comparative Geology.
britannica-1911-keel:
The keel is the bottom timber, or set of plates, of a ship or boat. It runs lengthwise from bow to stern and carries the framework of the hull. The origin of the word is clouded by the mixing of two words, the Old Norwegian kjole and a Dutch and German kiel. The first held the English sense of keel, and the other meant a ship or boat.

On the Tyne, a keel is a flat bottomed boat used to carry coals out to the colliers. A second word keel, meaning to cool, lives in Shakespeare, where greasy Joan keels the pot. That word comes from the Old English célan, to cool: stopping a pot from boiling over by cold water or stirring.
britannica-1911-keene-charles-samuel:
Charles Samuel Keene (1823–1891) was an English artist in black and white, the son of Samuel Browne Keene, a solicitor. He was born at Hornsey on the 10th of August 1823 and schooled at Ipswich Grammar School until he was sixteen. He showed a gift for art early. Two years after his father's death he was bound to a London solicitor, but the work jarred on him, and he was moved to the office of an architect.

His spare time went to drawing in water colour. His mother found a buyer for these small works, which brought him to the notice of the Whympers, the wood engravers. He was bound to them as apprentice for five years. His earliest known design is the frontispiece, signed Chas. Keene, to The Adventures of Dick Boldhero, issued in 1842. When his term ended he took a studio of his own.
britannica-1911-kelly-michael:
Michael Kelly (1762–1826) was a British actor, singer, and composer, son of a Dublin wine merchant and dancing master. He had a musical training at home and in Italy. For four years from 1783 he was engaged to sing at the Court Theatre at Vienna, where he became a friend of Mozart.

In 1786 he sang in the first performance of the Nozze di Figaro. He appeared at Drury Lane in London in 1787 and met with great success. From then on he was the chief English tenor at that theatre. In 1793 he became acting manager of the King's Theatre, and he was much in demand at concerts. He wrote many songs, among them The Woodpecker, and the music for many stage pieces now forgotten. In 1826 he issued his lively Reminiscences, written with the help of Theodore Hook. He ran a music shop and a wine shop beside his stage work, with ruinous results.
britannica-1911-la-margherita-clemente-s:
Clemente Solaro, count della Margherita (1792–1869), was a Piedmontese statesman, born at Mondovi. He studied law at Siena and Turin. While Piedmont lay under French rule he refused to take his degree. After the Sardinian kingdom was restored he graduated and entered the diplomatic service in 1816. He won the trust of King Charles Albert, who in 1835 made him minister of foreign affairs.

La Margherita was a fervent Roman Catholic, friendly to Austria and to the Jesuits, and firm for autocracy. He fought every move towards political change and was bitterly hated by the liberals. When the cry for a constitution rose, the king had to let him go, though he had served with skill. His Memorandum storico-politico of 1851 sets out his creed and his policy of 1835 to 1847. In 1853 he was elected a deputy, and as leader of the Clerical Right he opposed Cavour's policy to the end.
britannica-1911-label:
A label is a slip, ticket or card fastened to an object such as a parcel or bottle, bearing a name or description for identification. The word is French, now represented by lambeau, and its origin is obscure; it may connect with a Teutonic word seen in the English "lap," a flap or fold. At first it meant a band or ribbon, and so was applied to a bishop's mitre fillets. In heraldry a label is a mark of cadency.

In architecture the label is the outer projecting moulding over doors, windows and arches, also called a dripstone, weather moulding or hood mould. In Norman work it barely projected, if at all. In Early English work it could be undercut, a quarter round with chamfer, or a roll moulding. Labels often run on sideways as string-courses, and are less common in Continental than in English building.
britannica-1911-lady-chapel:
A Lady-chapel, dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, is attached to churches of large size. It was usually built east of the high altar, projecting from the main building, as at Winchester, Salisbury, Exeter, Wells, St Albans, Chichester, Peterborough and Norwich. The earliest Lady-chapel stood in the Saxon cathedral of Canterbury; Lanfranc's rebuilding moved it to the west end. At Ely the Lady-chapel is a separate building on the north transept, and at Rochester it lies west of the south transept.

Probably the largest was Henry III's chapel of 1220 at Westminster Abbey. It was 30 ft. wide and ran to the end of the ground now held by Henry VII's chapel. Some parish Lady-chapels were built over the chancel, and Croyland Abbey had two. In French cathedrals they form part of the chevet; Belgium took them up only in the 14th century.
britannica-1911-laing-samuel:
Samuel Laing (1810–1897), British author and railway administrator, was born at Edinburgh on the 12th of December 1810, nephew of Malcolm Laing. He entered St John's College, Cambridge, in 1827, graduated as second wrangler, and was called to the bar in 1837. He was private secretary to Labouchere at the Board of Trade. Then, as secretary to the railway department from 1842 to 1847, he became an authority on railways; the "parliamentary" rate of a penny a mile was his suggestion. In 1848 he took the chair of the London, Brighton & South Coast Railway and greatly raised its prosperity.

He sat for Wick from 1852, became financial secretary to the Treasury in 1859 and finance minister in India. He later represented Orkney and Shetland from 1873 to 1885 and chaired the Brighton line from 1867 to 1894. His books, Modern Science and Modern Thought (1885), Problems of the Future (1889) and Human Origins (1892), were read. He died at Sydenham on the 6th of August 1897.
britannica-1911-lambert-daniel:
Daniel Lambert (1770–1809), an Englishman famous for his great size, was born near Leicester on the 13th of March 1770. He was the son of the keeper of the jail, a post he himself took in 1791. About then his size and weight grew enormously, though he had led an active, athletic life: in 1793 he weighed thirty-two stone (448 lb). In 1806 he resigned his office, went up to London and exhibited himself for profit.

He died on the 21st of July 1809, measuring 5 ft. 11 in. and weighing 52¾ stone (739 lb). His waistcoat, now in the King's Lynn Museum, measures 102 in. round the waist, and his coffin took 112 ft. of elm and was built on wheels. His name became a synonym for immensity, used by Meredith of London and by Herbert Spencer of learning, and his figure was painted on many tavern signs.
britannica-1911-oesel:
Oesel is a Russian island in the Baltic, lying across the mouth of the Gulf of Riga. With Worms, Mohn, and Runö, it forms a district of the government of Livonia. The island lies 106 miles north-north-west of the city of Riga. It runs 45 miles in length and covers 1,010 square miles. Its coasts are bold and steep, and to the north and west they form sheer cliffs of limestone. The Oesel ponies, like those of Shetland, are small but prized for their fire and their power to last.

The people of Oesel numbered 60,000 in 1900, and most are Protestant in faith. Apart from the German nobility, the clergy, and some townsfolk, they are Estonian by race. The chief town is Arensburg, on the south coast, with 4,600 souls.
broken-to-the-plow-a-novel:
Charles Caldwell Dobie wrote a novel that opens on a tired office man in San Francisco life, Fred Starratt by name. Payday math fills the first pages. His wife Helen has set a dinner for guests he has never met. Oyster cocktails and cigars must be bought. Cash must come from old Wetherbee, the hard cashier at Ford, Wetherbee and Co.

Starratt dreads the four o'clock ask, when Wetherbee counts his cash and snaps at breaks in the rite. Five dollars would do, yet twenty-five feels safer against the month's claims. A racy tale might sweeten the man, but none comes to mind. Harper and Brothers put out the book at New York and London. Dobie had earlier written The Blood Red Dawn. A note gives the book to his brother, who made his writing path possible.
by-advice-of-counsel:
Arthur Train wrote tales of the law firm Tutt and Tutt, put out in March 1921. Seven tales line the contents page. The Shyster opens the set, with a word-book sense of the term set at its head: one who does trade in a tricky way, with no pride of craft.

Terry McGurk heaves a brick through a butcher's pane to start that tale — by chance, on no plan, as the tale opens. The Kid and the Camel, Contempt of Court, and the title tale fill the heart. That Sort of Woman, You're Another, and Beyond a Reasonable Doubt close the list. A front plate shows Mr. Tutt stepping from past the jury box to a client's side. Court craft, soft hearts, and sharp wits form the stock of the set.
c-f-meyer-der-schu-von-der-kanzel:
A general's tall tales, a pastor's shot from the pulpit, and a Swiss village in uproar fill C. F. Meyer's Der Schuss von der Kanzel, given here in German. The Shot from the Pulpit is his most humorous novella, a comedy of errors built with a watchmaker's care. Serious Meyer lets his hair down, and the result delights.

A boastful soldier's yarns tangle with village vanity until a sermon, a rifle, and a christening collide in farce. Every misunderstanding is planted early and pays off on time. Light and witty, the tale shows how gracefully Meyer could handle comedy when he chose. Beneath the laughter sits his usual precision about honor and reputation. The novella remains the friendliest of his works for new readers of German.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achitopel:
Achitopel, an able and honoured counsellor of David, joined Absalom's rebellion, a desertion that deeply affected the king. Hearing that the man whose word he had trusted as an oracle of God now advised the enemy, David prayed God to infatuate Achitopel's counsel. Some see reflections of David on this faithless friend in Psalms 54 and 40. On Achitopel's advice Absalom seized his father's harem, cutting off all hope of reconciliation.

Achitopel then urged sending 12,000 men from Jerusalem in pursuit of the king, offering to lead them himself. Chusai, David's secret friend, defeated his purpose. Proudly, he withdrew to Gilo, settled his house, and strangled himself. The entry adds that he was likely grandfather of Bethsabee, and suggests a secret grudge over David's treatment of her and Urias may explain his turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-vin:
Alexandre Vincent Jandel was General of the Dominican order, born at Gerbévillers in Lorraine in July 1810 and dead at Rome in December 1872. Remarkable from youth for intelligence and resolution, qualities he owed to his mother, who had sheltered priests during the Revolution. He took a brilliant course at Nancy and entered the diocesan seminary there. Ordained a priest in September 1834, he became professor of Scripture and soon met Lacordaire, whose example turned him toward restoring the Dominicans in France.

In 1839 Jandel went to Rome, consulted Gregory XVI, and received the Dominican habit in May 1841. Two years later he and Lacordaire began rebuilding the order in France, Lacordaire as orator and Jandel as a calm, grave, practical ruler of men. Many holy people in France sought his guidance, but Pius IX called him to Rome. He was made vicar-general of the order in 1850 and general for six years in 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfred-rethel:
Alfred Rethel, born at Aachen in 1816, died at Düsseldorf in 1859. He joined Romantic and Italian idealism and Dürer's realism, and might have been Germany's greatest painter but for crippling ill health. Recommended to Schadow by Bastiné, his first oil, shown at Düsseldorf in 1832, depicted St. Boniface, as did two more canvases recalling Lessing's power. Sempach and Winkelried sketches show Cornelius's influence; Veit developed his colour and dramatic spirit in 1836. Otto I's reconciliation with Henry and the Monk at Henry IV's Coffin are important works.

His ripest works: Hannibal's March in six Alpine pictures, and restrained Charlemagne frescoes at Aachen's Rathaus. Kehren finished the series less well; the Death Dance treats 1848's revolutionary horror. Nemesis pursuing a Murderer crystallized the darker mood clouding his later life, and he admired Titian's colour against the Nazarenes' pale art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amraphel:
King of Sennaar, or Babylonia, Amraphel was one of four Mesopotamian kings who invaded Canaan, in the fourteenth chapter of Genesis. They beat the five kings of the Plains and carried off Lot with his family and rich spoil. Abraham, with 318 men, fell on them by night in the vale of Siddim near the Dead Sea, routed them, and brought the prisoners home.

On the way back Abraham met Melchisedech, high priest of El-Elion at Jerusalem. He blessed the victory with bread and wine and took a tenth of the spoil. Most Assyriologists identify Amraphel with Hammurabi, sixth king of the first Babylonian dynasty, who reigned about 2250 before Christ. His famous Code of Laws turned up at Susa in 1901 and 1902, and the article argues that the monuments of his age fit the political picture Genesis assumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-danie:
A Huron missionary, Anthony Daniel was born at Dieppe in 1601 and slain at Teanaostae in 1648. After philosophy and law studies, he joined the Jesuits in 1621. In 1633 he went to Canada, first posted at Cape Breton, where his brother had built a fort in 1629. For two years he ran a Quebec school for Indian boys, otherwise serving the Ihonatiria mission from 1634 until his death.

In summer 1648 the Iroquois attacked suddenly while most braves were away. Father Daniel did all he could for his people, baptizing the catechumens. He tried no escape, but calmly walked out to meet the attackers. Amazed, they halted, then let fly a shower of arrows at him. Bancroft's wilderness-grave account is wrong: his body was thrown into the burning chapel and consumed with it. Daniel was New France's second Jesuit martyr and its first Huron missionary. His superior Ragueneau called him remarkable, humble, and obedient.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-cesar:
Antoine-César Becquerel, a French physicist born in 1788, left the army for the study of electricity. After service in Spain and a spell at the Polytechnic School, he turned to laboratory work full time. He challenged Volta's contact theory, arguing that chemical action, not mere contact, drives the current in a battery cell.

He built a steady two-liquid cell that foreshadowed the Daniell cell, and a fine gauge for measuring electrical resistance. His work on heat-driven electricity produced an electric thermometer for soil, air, and animal bodies. Honoured with the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1837, he published more than five hundred papers across a long career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-henri:
Antoine-Henri de Berault-Bercastel, a French writer of church history born in 1720, left the Jesuits after ordination to serve as a parish priest and canon of Noyon. His great work, a history of the church, appeared at Paris between 1778 and 1790 in twenty-four volumes. It carried the story from the founding of the church to 1721.

Written for educated Christians and busy priests rather than scholars, the history won wide circulation despite flaws in its later volumes. It was reprinted often, translated into Italian and German, and continued or condensed by later editors. The entry presents a useful, readable history that served ordinary readers long after its author's death about 1794.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apse-chapel:
An apse chapel is a chapel radiating outward from one bay of the apse, the rounded east end of a church. It is reached usually by a semicircular passage, or ambulatory, outside the apse walls or piers. Normally semicircular in plan, some are pentagonal or oblong with eastern apses. In England an ambulatory sometimes links north and south choir aisles, with eastern chapels projecting from it.

Westminster Abbey's eastern chevet, or apse end, ringed by five apsidal chapels, is the only intact example of this feature in England. The shared source of ambulatory and radiating chapels appears to have been St. Martin of Tours, where a choir of two bays and a five-bay apse stood within one ambulatory and five radiating chapels. Altars that had crowded the nave could now move into these new chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-barr:
Augustin Barruel was a French controversialist and publicist born at Villeneuve de Berg in 1741 who died at Paris in 1820. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1756, taught grammar at Toulouse, and was driven abroad by the storm against the Jesuits in France. He worked in colleges in Moravia and Bohemia until the order's suppression in 1773. Back in France, his first literary work appeared in 1774, and he soon joined the Annee Litteraire as a collaborator.

His first important book, the Helviennes, or Philosophical Provincial Letters, appeared in 1781 and sparked a long controversy. From 1788 to 1792 he edited the Journal Ecclesiastique, defending Pope Pius VI and writing pamphlets against the civil oath and the new civil constitution for clergy. Through a life of multiplied activity he stayed a wakeful defender of Christian truth and church rights. At his death he was working, unfinished, on a refutation of Kant's philosophy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-jean:
Augustin Jean Fresnel was a French physicist born near Bernay in Normandy in 1788 who died in 1827. Slow in letters as a boy, he showed talent for physical science and entered the Ecole Polytechnique at seventeen, where Legendre noticed him. He served as an engineer in Vendee, Drome, and Ille-et-Vilaine, lost his post when Napoleon returned from Elba, and joined the Lighthouse Commission in 1819. He became its secretary in 1824 and an examiner at the Polytechnique.

His field was optics, the science of light, and his memoirs put the wave theory of light on firm ground. He pressed Hooke's guess that light vibrations run crosswise to their path. He devised double mirrors and a biprism to study diffraction and interference, the bending and blending of light waves. His lens system changed lighthouse light across the world. A religious man, he won the Royal Society's Rumford Medal on his deathbed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-babel:
Babel is the Vulgate form only at Genesis 11:9, while Babylonia appears in Baruch and Babylon elsewhere. The name comes from Babylonian bab-ilu, gate of God, though Genesis suggests a Hebrew play on balal, to confound. The city bore many native names, such as Tintir, and the prophets called it daughter of the Chaldeans. It stood where the village of Hille stands. Herodotus rings it with a double wall fifty cubits thick and two hundred high, squared at 120 stadia.

Both Bible and cuneiform inscriptions give the city age. The ruins confirm the Genesis account of its material: baked brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. Its temples, palaces, and gardens included two shrines: E-sagila, Bel Merodach's temple east of the Euphrates, and E-zida, Nebo's temple west of it. Their ruins are those of Babil and Birs Nimrud, though views differ over Babil. Sources include Rawlinson, King, and Delattre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benjamin-elbe:
Benjamin Elbel, a Franciscan authority on moral theology, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Friedberg in Bavaria in 1690, he died at Söflingen in 1756 after rising to high posts in his order and teaching theology as lector. His field was the moral life: what conscience may do when theologians disagree.

His classic work on moral theology by the Ten Commandments and the sacraments, published at Venice in 1731, ran through several editions. A later editor brought it up to date in three volumes at Paderborn. Elbel defended probabilism, the view that a solidly probable opinion may be followed, in a style the entry calls simple and clear.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bertholet-fle:
