Bertholet Flémal, a painter of Liège, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Liège in 1614, son of a glass painter, he died there in 1675 after training under Trippez and Douffet. A visit to Rome in 1638 led to work for the Duke of Tuscany at Florence and decorative painting at Versailles in Paris.

His Adoration of the Magi for the Augustinian sacristy in Paris shows his grand manner. Returning to Liège in 1647, he painted many church pictures for his hometown, and a second Paris invitation came in 1670. The entry presents a Flemish decorator who carried Italian lessons home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beseleel: Beseleel, whose name means in the shadow of God, was son of Uri of the tribe of Judah and chief architect of the tabernacle, the portable shrine of Israel in the desert. Called by God for the work, he prepared holy oils, incense, and priestly vestments, and built the ark and the furniture of court and shrine. Divine gifts, shared with his assistant Ooliab, fitted him for the craft.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethel:
Bethel, a Hebrew name meaning house of God, was an ancient Canaanite town twelve miles north of Jerusalem, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its first name was Luz. Abraham sacrificed east of it twice, and Jacob gave it the name Bethel after his vision of a ladder reaching heaven.

Allotted to Benjamin at the conquest, it was taken by the Ephraimites and stayed important through the judges' age, when Israelites came there to consult God. Later kings made it a rival sanctuary with a golden calf, a sad turn the entry follows. Bethel thus moves from patriarchal shrine to a byword for false worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-thoma:
Thomas Abel, chaplain to Queen Catherine of Aragon, died at Tyburn in 1540 for defending the validity of her marriage to Henry VIII. An Oxford graduate, he taught the queen languages and music. He won the Bradwell benefice after a Spanish mission in her service. He then published Invicta Veritas in 1532 against the universities' ruling for divorce.

Imprisoned in Beauchamp Tower in 1532, he was freed for a year and jailed again in December 1533. He was charged with spreading the Maid of Kent's prophecies and urging Catherine to hold her title. Kept in close confinement, he begged Cromwell only to hear Mass and lodge on Tower Green. He was executed on 30 July 1540, two days after Cromwell himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-danie:
The Book of Daniel, in Hebrew Bibles, holds only its proto-canonical parts, while the Septuagint and Vulgate add deutero-canonical portions as an appendix. The Hebrew book divides into two halves: narratives told in the third person in chapters one to six, and visions told in the first person in chapters seven to twelve. Its heroes are Daniel and his fellow captives Ananias, Misael, and Azarias, who rise at Nebuchadnezzar's court without defiling themselves on royal food.

Daniel alone interprets the king's dream of a statue smashed by a small stone that grows into a mountain. He reads the statue's parts as kingdoms and the stone as the Messiah's everlasting kingdom. His companions survive the fiery furnace for refusing the king's statue. Later chapters add Nebuchadnezzar's letter, further dreams, and visions, while the deutero-canonical appendix brings Susanna, Bel, and the dragon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-s:
The Brothers of Saint Gabriel, properly the Brothers of Christian Instruction of Saint Gabriel, teach the young, the blind, the deaf and dumb, and orphans. Saint Louis Grignon de Montfort founded the congregation in 1705, but it spread little until it merged with a house founded in 1835 by Monsignor Deshayes of Rennes. It took its odd name from its first chapel, dedicated to Saint Gabriel at Boulogne.

Members take no vows, but after a three-year novitiate they promise obedience to the superior and devotion to the institute's works. Most support themselves from their own means. A superior elected for three years, with four counsellors, governs the body. By 1851 it held ninety-one houses, later 122 schools in France plus schools for the blind and deaf-mutes. Recent figures give 170 schools, eight deaf asylums, three blind asylums, and orphan homes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carmel:
Carmel in this entry is a city of Judah and its surrounding territory, named from a Hebrew word meaning garden or garden-land. It lay in Judah's hill country beside the lands of Maon, Ziph, and Jota. Its garden-like look against the wilderness to the south and east explains the name. Saul raised a victory trophy there after defeating Amalek, and Uzziah held farms and vineyards in its district.

The best-known episode belongs to Nabal of Maon, shearing sheep on Carmel's pastures, whose wife Abigail met the fugitive David and played the leading part in their encounter. Jerome in the fourth century calls the town a village with a Roman garrison. Crusader king Amalrich held it against Saladin. After long obscurity its ruins were recognized again in the nineteenth century about ten miles southeast of Hebron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cashel:
Cashel, a town in County Tipperary, Ireland, is a Catholic archbishopric crowned by the Rock of Cashel, a limestone height above the Golden Vein plain. Once called Fairy Hill, or Sid-Druim, it served as the fort of the Eoghnacht chiefs of Munster. Its name means a circular stone fort and may come from tribute stone, where tribes paid tribute. Corc built a fort there, and Cashel became Munster's capital, a celebrated court beside Tara and Armagh.

About 450 Patrick preached at the fort and converted King Aengus. His baptism, the Tripartite Life says, included the crozier spike piercing his foot, a wound the king endured. The province of Cashel joins the archdiocese and Emly to eight suffragan sees. They run from Cloyne, Cork, and Kerry to Waterford and Lismore and Kilfenora. In 1908 Cashel and Emly counted 46 parishes, 103 secular clergy, 84 churches, a Thurles seminary, and convents of nuns with 322 members.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caspar-riffel:
Caspar Riffel was a German historian born at Budesheim near Bingen in January 1807 who died at Mainz in December 1856. Klee taught him at Mainz and Bonn, and Möhler at Tübingen, was ordained in December 1830, and served as assistant priest at Bingen. In 1835 he took a Giessen parish and the moral theology chair there, moving to the church history professorship in 1837.

His church history's first volume, out in 1841, angered Protestants with an accurate but unflattering account of the Reformation. The Hessian government pensioned him off in November 1842. Catholic clergy denounced the Protestant air of the university. In Mainz, Bishop von Ketteler made Riffel church history professor in the new seminary in 1851. His writings include a church-state study, sermons for Sundays and feasts, and a history of the suppression of the Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cedar-son-of-:
Cedar, or Qedar, was the second son of Ishmael, and the name also denotes an Arabian tribe descended from him and the land it occupied. The tribe appears often in the Bible and in Assyrian inscriptions, where the people are called Qidrai and the country Qidri. Before Assyrian power crushed them, the Cedarenes ranked as a people of real importance, and the name Cedar came to stand for Arabia and the Arabians in general.

They were nomads living in black tents of goat's and camel's hair. Their encampments were ringed by rough enclosures. They owned many camels and other cattle, which they traded with Tyre. They were restless, warlike, and skilled with the bow. Assyrian records link them with kings of the Arabs, one of them, Hazael, being called a king in his own right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chancel:
The chancel is the part of the choir near a church's altar where deacons or subdeacons stand by the officiating priest. It takes its name from the cancelli, lattice work that originally railed it off. Today the term mostly covers parish churches and others with no aisles or chapels around the choir, though some add further chancels at side-aisle ends.

Latin cancellus named the low screen dividing presbyterium and choir from the nave. In time chancel came to mean the presbyterium itself. Few early chancels survive, but St. Clement's at Rome shows the normal arrangement. Sixth-century screens from the lower church were moved upstairs into the twelfth-century church above. The presbyterium screen stood at the apse's chord, with the altar on the same line. England used the term before the Reformation, and Anglicans still retain it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chapel:
Chapel comes from Latin capella, through French chapelle. St. Martin cut his military cloak, the cappa, in two and gave half to a beggar at Amiens' gate, wrapping the other half about his shoulders as a cape, the capella. The cape was kept as a relic and traveled with the Frankish kings on campaign. Its sheltering tent also took the name capella, and military chaplains, the capellani, celebrated Mass in it.

At rest in the palace, the relic named the oratory where it was kept. In time any oratory for Mass and Divine service took the name chapel. Marculfus in the seventh century first uses the word in this sense and gives the etymology, generally accepted since, though Durandus offered an alternative from capra, goat. The article then surveys kinds of chapels and the law governing them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-claud:
Charles-Claude Fauriel was a historian born at St-Etienne in 1772 and dead at Paris in 1844. Educated at the Oratorian College of Tournon and at Lyons, he joined the Pyrénées-Orientales army, then worked as private secretary in Fouché's cabinet under the Directory. Under the Empire he refused office to give all his time to study. He first embraced the ideas of the Philosophers and the Revolution, partly repudiating them later in life.

A tireless worker, he knew Greek and Latin, Italian and German, English, Sanskrit, and Arabic. He introduced Ossian and Shakespeare to the French public and spread knowledge of German literature in France. He pioneered Romance literature study, popularising a new field. He also gathered remnants of Basque and Celtic and translated Baggesen's Parthénéide and Manzoni's Conte di Carmagnola. Later he published a Provençal poem on the crusade against the Albigenses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-danie:
Charles Daniel was born at Beauvais in 1818 and died at Paris in 1893. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1841. He taught rhetoric to novices at Saint Acheul. In 1857 he founded, with Father Gagarin, the Etudes de théologie et d'histoire. The journal soon became monthly. He edited it until 1870. Widely and exactly learned, with unquestionable taste, he wrote articles for the Etudes on optimism, positivism, Leibniz, the Vatican Council, and French Protestantism.

He also wrote biographies of Père Beauregard, Mme. Swetchine, Lenormand, and Ducoudray, who died in the Paris Commune. His larger works include a study of classical studies in Christian society and a history of Blessed Margaret Mary and the Sacred Heart devotion, translated into Italian, Polish, and Chinese. He also wrote a life of Père Alexis Clerc, sailor and Jesuit, and a study of Jesuits as teachers of youth in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-emile:
Charles-Emile Freppel was born at Ober-Ehnheim in Alsace in 1827 and died at Paris in 1891. He became Bishop of Angers and deputy from Finistère. At seventeen he took his baccalaureate and entered the Strasburg seminary, where he received the subdiaconate in 1848 and was at once given the chair of history. Ordained priest in 1849, he joined the discussions of Bonnetty and Maret on traditionalism. A brilliant Sorbonne examination won him a doctorate, and after a competitive examination he became chaplain of Ste-Geneviève in Paris.

At Ste-Geneviève he preached sermons on the divinity of Jesus Christ, later published in book form, and gave Advent and Lenten exercises at several Paris churches. Pius IX then summoned him to Rome to help draft decrees for the Vatican Council and named him Bishop of Angers, consecrated there in April 1870.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-marte:
A long historical entry on Charles Martel, the Frankish ruler who held the Frankish kingdoms together in the early eighth century. Born about 688 as the natural son of Pepin of Herstal, he escaped prison after his father's death in 714. Power was then seized in the name of a child heir by his grandmother Plectrude. Charles rallied the Austrasian party, beat the Neustrians at Amblève and Vincy, and forced Plectrude to hand over his father's treasure.

From that base he spent decades at war and is best known for halting the Muslim advance into Gaul. To pay his followers he granted them the use of Church lands, a seizure later partly pardoned at the Council of Lestines in 743. Yet he also protected St. Boniface, the apostle of Germany, from 723, sharing in the credit for Boniface's work. He divided his lands between his sons Carloman and Pepin before dying in 741.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-ric:
Matthias Leimkuhler's entry treats Cornelius Richard Anton van Bommel, Bishop of Liège. Born at Leyden, Holland, on 5 April 1790, he died 7 April 1852. Educated at Willingshegge near Münster and at Borght, he entered Münster's seminary against opposition, ordained priest in 1816. Returning to Holland, he founded a college at Hageveld near Haarlem.

Catholics and Liberals joined against arbitrary Government policy, and van Bommel helped force the king to promulgate the Concordat with Leo XII. Under the Concordat he was nominated to Liège, consecrated 15 November 1829. He took no part in the 1830 revolution, but as Liège's bishop severed his Dutch connection. Within a few years he remedied evils from a vacancy of over twenty years, organizing the seminary, reviving Catholic schools, and advancing a Catholic university. Defender of the Holy See's primacy, opponent of Freemasonry, and advocate of religious education, he saw his views enforced in State schools in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel:
A scriptural entry presents Daniel, hero and traditional author of the book bearing his name. Daniel means God is my judge, fitting for a book where God's judgments fall repeatedly on Gentile powers. Of Judah's tribe and noble or royal descent, he was carried captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar about 605 BC, probably aged fourteen.

With Ananias, Misael, and Azarias, he was trained in Chaldean learning under Asphenez, master of the king's eunuchs, and renamed Baltassar. Jewish tradition inferred the youths were made eunuchs, but the entry warns this need not follow. The book's visions, its lions' den, its fiery furnace companions, and its prophecies are surveyed, and Daniel's feast as holy prophet falls on 21 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-don-isaac-abr:
Don Isaac Abrabanel was a Jewish statesman, apologist, and Bible scholar born at Lisbon in 1437. Trained from youth in Talmudic and rabbinic letters, he mastered secular learning as well. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his keen mind and business skill drew Alfonso the Fifth of Portugal, who made him treasurer until 1481. Favor to a Jew shocked opinion, and under John the Second he was charged with plotting with the Duke of Braganza.

Fleeing for his life to Castile in 1483, he soon served Ferdinand and Isabella until 1492. After Granada fell he shared his people's exile from Spain. His works, written in clear modern Hebrew, gather and explain all the messianic texts, above all in commentaries on Daniel. He died at Venice in 1508 and was buried at Padua.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duel:
A duel, in church and civil criminal law today, is a contest with deadly weapons fought by agreement between two persons over a private quarrel. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry stresses that weapons are essential, as is agreement, and the weapons must be able to inflict deadly wounds. Sameness of weapons is not essential, though custom demands it, nor are seconds or witnesses strictly required.

What matters is the private cause, such as wounded honor, which sets the modern duel apart from public combats ordered by authority, like the fight of David and Goliath. The entry weighs the guilt of dueling and the rules of proof, arguing that no authority may command a duel and put the innocent at the same risk as the guilty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmanuel:
Emmanuel, or Immanuel, means God with us, and this entry asks who the child of Isaiah's prophecy truly is. Isaiah 7:14 promises that a virgin shall conceive and bear a son called Emmanuel. The child is no mere figure of speech, the entry argues, nor the people of Israel in general, nor religious faith itself, for the text says he shall eat butter and honey. He is one individual, not a son of Isaiah, whose own son bears another name.

He is not a son of King Ahaz either, for Hezekiah lacks Emmanuel's chief marks. The child is the Messiah of Isaiah's other prophecies: Palestine is called the land of Emmanuel, and Isaiah 9 describes his mission so plainly that doubt ends. Matthew 1:23 expressly joins Emmanuel to Jesus the Messiah, as Christian tradition has always taught. The name is both a pledge of God's help and a picture of the Messiah's nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ezekiel:
Ezekiel, whose name means strong is God, was son of Buzi and one of the priests deported from Jerusalem with Joachim in 598 before Christ. With fellow exiles he settled at Tell-Abib by the Chobar in Babylonia, and seems to have spent his life there. Five years after Joachim's captivity, about his thirtieth year, he received his call as prophet in the vision that opens his book.

From a late date in his book, he prophesied for at least twenty-two years. His burden was God's faithfulness amid trial and in keeping promises. Part one foretells Juda's doom before Jerusalem fell, with siege, idolatry in the Temple, and God's majesty departing. Part two gathers prophecies against the Gentiles: Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, and Egypt. Part three promises restoration, with the second David gathering the sheep and dry bones living again.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-our-:
Our Lady of Good Counsel is venerated at Genazzano, a town near Rome. Tradition says her picture appeared there on 25 April 1467. Painted on thin plaster, it seemed to hang in the air unsupported. Pilgrims soon flocked to the shrine, and many miracles were recorded.

Several popes visited the shrine, and Innocent XI had the image crowned in 1682. Benedict XIII granted an Office and Mass for 25 April in 1727. Leo XIII raised the shrine church to a minor basilica in 1903. He also added the invocation Mater Boni Consilii to the Litany of Loreto.

Our Lady of Mount Carmel is the Carmelite patronal feast on 16 July. Carmelites instituted it between 1376 and 1386 for their order's victory over its enemies. Tradition says Mary gave the scapular to Simon Stock in 1251. The feast marks her special care for all those wearing her scapular.

Sixtus V first approved the feast in 1587 for all Carmelite churches. Clement X later granted it to Spain, Austria, Portugal, and their colonies in turn. Benedict XIII extended it to the whole Latin Church in 1726. The lessons tell the scapular legend and the Sabbatine promise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-and-sec:
First and Second Samuel form one history, from Samuel's birth to the close of David's reign. The two books were one work in Hebrew, titled Samuel, split in the Septuagint for scroll size. Samuel gives the books their name as the figure who shaped the kingdom and chose its first kings. The first book covers Samuel and Saul; the second covers David's reign.

The story runs in five parts: Samuel, Saul's rule, Saul and David, David's reign, and an appendix. It tells of Samuel's call, Saul's anointing and rejection, David and Goliath, and his outlaw years. David's reign, his sins, and the revolts against him fill the second book. The article traces the text through Hebrew, Greek, and Latin versions, noting Jerome's naming of the books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-antho:
Francis Anthony Drexel, born at Philadelphia on 20 June 1824 and dead there on 15 February 1885, was an American banker of strict integrity and broad liberality. His father Francis Martin Drexel, a Tyrolese portrait painter and musician turned financier, founded Drexel and Company in Philadelphia in 1837. It was linked with Morgan in New York and Drexel, Harjes in Paris. Francis Anthony began finance at thirteen and, on his father's death in 1863, became senior member of the firm and one of America's foremost financiers.

At critical moments the house generously supported the public credit, and its name became synonymous with honest dealing. Drexel's fortune never alienated him from religion or hardened him against charity. He stayed poor in spirit, treating wealth as a divine instrument for good. His second wife Emma Bouvier Drexel seconded him in piety and giving. His daughter Katherine later entered religion, carrying his charity into a new generation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Schlegel, poet and literary historian, stands with his brother as a founder of the German Romantic school. Born at Hanover in 1772 and meant for trade, he turned at sixteen to study, read law and then classics at Göttingen, and settled with his brother at Jena. His notorious romance Lucinde appeared at Berlin in 1799.

Schlegel lectured at Paris, edited the journal Europa, and with Dorothea Veit became a Catholic at Cologne in 1808. At Vienna he served the state chancellery, wrote fiery proclamations against Napoleon in 1809, and gave famous lectures on ancient and modern literature. His Concordia journal later pressed the idea of a Christian state, and his criticism, more than his poems, secured his fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-biel:
Gabriel Biel, called the last of the Scholastics, shaped the young University of Tübingen as its first professor of theology. Born at Speyer around 1425, he studied at Heidelberg and Erfurt, preached at Mainz, and led the Clerks of the Common Life at Butzbach. With Count Eberhard of Württemberg he founded Tübingen, taking its theology chair in 1484 at nearly sixty.

Biel's commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences calls Occam master, though its later books lean Scotist. Clear, exact, and loyal to the Church, he built a system free of heresy charges and friendly to humanists, who dubbed him monarch among theologians. His books fed Trent's debates. He upheld the pope's primacy, yet held that councils could press even a pope to resign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-danie:
Gabriel Daniel, a Jesuit historian born at Rouen in 1649, became historiographer of France under Louis XIV. He entered the Society in 1667, took final vows at Rennes in 1683, and won the Paris post by sheer talent. His writings crossed philosophy, theology, and history, and many were rendered into German, English, Spanish, Italian, and Latin.

Daniel answered Descartes with a Voyage to the World of Descartes and answered Pascal's Provincial Letters in turn. But his lasting fame rests on his seventeen-volume History of France, finished in 1713, the fullest and most exact of its day, with an eight-volume abridgment of his own making. His history of the French soldiery, drawn from original sources, added to his scholarly name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gall-morel:
Gall Morel, a Benedictine poet, scholar, and teacher, spent his life at the Abbey of Einsiedeln in Switzerland. Born Benedict Morel at Saint Fiden in 1803, he took the name Gall on entering the monastery, made final vows in 1820, and was ordained in 1826. He taught rhetoric and philosophy, then served as librarian from 1835 to his death, alongside posts as prefect, rector, archivist, and subprior.

As a poet he left ten volumes of lyric, teaching, and dramatic verse, by turns childlike, humorous, worldly, and sharply satirical. As a scholar he grew the abbey library by over 26,000 volumes in thirty-seven years, rescuing a tenth-century Horace now called the Codex Morellianus. His medieval Latin hymns, his Swiss archive calendars, and his art studies made him an authority beyond his abbey walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gamaliel:
Gamaliel, a Pharisee famed as a teacher of the Law, counseled restraint when the Sanhedrin weighed killing Peter and the apostles. Acts shows his advice prevailing, so great was his weight with his peers. Paul names him as his teacher, though Acts leaves the depth of that influence untold. The entry identifies him with the famed Jewish master of the same name.

In the Talmud this Gamaliel, grandson of Hillel, bears the title the Elder and first carries the name Rabban, our master. He sat on the highest Jewish court and framed many legal ordinances. Jewish accounts have him die a Pharisee, with honor, purity, and piety dying with him. Later Christian legend made him a secret believer, baptized by Peter and John, his body kept at Pisa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georg-witzel:
Georg Witzel, a theologian born in Hesse in 1501, crossed from Luther's camp back to Rome and spent his life seeking reunion. Schooled at Schmalkalden, Eisenach, Halle, Erfurt, and Wittenberg, he was ordained in 1520, then won by Luther in 1524, married, and took Lutheran parishes from Strauss and Luther himself. Study of Scripture and Fathers soon turned him back.

Witzel resigned in 1531, bore two years of poverty at Vacha, and published his defense of good works in 1532 and his Apologia for returning in 1533. Driven from place to place, he pressed reunion at a Leipzig disputation in 1539, offering the early Church as the model in his Methodus Concordiae. His efforts failed, but his ninety-four listed works fill a long shelf at Mainz, where he died in 1573.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-joseph:
George Joseph Camel, a botanist born in Moravia in 1661, catalogued the Philippines' plants for Europe. He joined the Jesuit order as a lay brother in 1682, though he may never have been a priest, and sailed as a missionary to the islands six years later. There he studied plants and natural history and sent his findings to London's Royal Society, which printed them in its Philosophical Transactions.

Linnaeus honored him by naming the camellia genus for him, the evergreen shrubs whose flowers include the Japan rose. Camel left two bulky volumes on the Philippines' medicinal plants, printed in part by the Royal Society and in Ray's History of Plants. A Louvain manuscript holds 360 of his plant drawings from Luzon. At Manila he ran a pharmacy where the poor received remedies free. He died there in 1706.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorio-nune:
Gregorio Nunez Coronel was a distinguished theologian, writer, and preacher born in Portugal about 1548, who died about 1620. He entered the Augustinian Order young, became famous for sacred eloquence, and was appointed by the Duke of Savoy as chaplain and preacher to his court. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a man who refused a bishopric at sixty.

Called to Rome, he took the degree of Doctor of Divinity and taught theology there for many years. He served as secretary to the Congregatio de Auxiliis, set up by Clement VIII to settle the Jesuit-Dominican dispute over grace and free will, continuing under Paul V. His principal works are Libri decem de vera Christi Ecclesia of 1594 and Libri sex de optimo reipublicae statu of 1597. De traditionibus apostolicis of 1597 completes the trio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hartmann-sche:
Nuremberg humanist Hartmann Schedel, born in 1440, was physician, collector, and author of the most famous printed world chronicle of the fifteenth century. After degrees at Leipzig, law under Pieter Luder, and a medical doctorate at Padua in 1466, he practised at Nördlingen, Amberg, and finally Nuremberg from 1481.

His Liber chronicarum of 1493, with a German version the same year, divides history into six medieval ages and follows earlier chronicles closely, above all Foresta's Supplementum of 1483. Its fame owes much to hundreds of fine woodcuts by Wolgemuth and Pleydenwurff. His manuscript hunting preserved monuments known today only through his copies, with a library later reaching Munich.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-frei:
Viennese architect Heinrich von Ferstel, born in 1828, stands with Hansen and Schmidt as a creator of modern Vienna. A bank clerk's son who wavered among the arts, he studied under Van der Null and Rösner and worked in his uncle's atelier on castles and a votive altar. He found his ideal, Renaissance beauty and proportion after Bramante, during a bursary year in Italy in 1854.

Still in Italy he beat seventy-four rivals for Vienna's Votivkirche in 1855, built from 1856 to 1879 as a marvel of symmetry. He followed it with the Austro-Hungarian Bank, the stock exchange, the Austrian Museum of 1871 with its arcaded court, and the university of 1871 to 1884. Professor from 1866 and Freiherr from 1879, he joined beauty to purpose without harming either.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hillel:
Hillel was a famous Jewish rabbi who lived about 70 BC to AD 10, known to us only from the Talmud. Born in Babylonia and descended from the family of David, he lived poor yet burned with zeal for God's law. At about forty he went to Jerusalem, where Shemaiah and Abtalion led the teachers, and he hired himself out as a day-labourer to pay for his own instruction and his family's keep.

After his masters died, Hillel was recognized as the best jurist of his day and headed the Sanhedrin with the title of Nasi, or prince, for his last forty years. He founded a lenient school, usually opposed to the stricter school of Shammai, framed seven rules of interpretation, and issued decrees that fitted points of law to changed times. His descendants led Palestinian Judaism for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ismael-ishmae:
Abraham's son by Hagar the Egyptian, Ishmael stands in Genesis 16 to 25 as a figure of promise and exile. His name, given before his birth and found also in early Babylonian and Minaean records, means “may God hear.” When Sarah proved barren she gave her handmaid Hagar to Abraham as concubine by the custom of the day, hoping for children through her.

Hagar's pregnancy led to flight into the wilderness. There an angel told her to return to her mistress. The angel fixed her son's name and character. Back at Beersheba she bore Ishmael to Abraham, then eighty-six, and the aged patriarch loved the boy dearly, pleading for him before God. Scholars split the Genesis account into three strands, J, E, and P, and the entry weighs them against the tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-israel:
Descendants of the patriarch Jacob, also called Israel, are the people this geography and ethnography entry describes. Israel matches the Hebrew “children of Israel,” the name the chosen people most often gave themselves in Old Testament times. Outsiders, and Israelites speaking to outsiders, said Hebrews. That name is commonly read as those from the other side of the Euphrates. Jews became another synonym. Classical writers, Josephus, and New Testament authors used it.

Leaving doctrine and famous figures to other articles, this one treats the people as a Semitic group in place and time: kinship, land, customs, and neighbors. Readers get the groundwork for the history that follows in entries on Judaism and on individual patriarchs, kings, and prophets. The entry is a map of a people before it is a story of their faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Duhamel, a French scientist, thinker, and theologian born at Vire in 1624 and dead in Paris in 1706. He published on geometry at eighteen and joined the Oratory the next year. After a parish at Neuilly and the chancellorship at Bayeux, Colbert made him first secretary of the new Academy of Sciences. That was in 1666.

Duhamel held that post until 1697, when Fontenelle succeeded him on his own advice. He travelled to peace talks at Aix-la-Chapelle and to England, meeting Boyle and other leading scientists. His books ranged from moral philosophy and astronomy to meteors, the mind, and the living body, and his school text weighed old Greek thought against Descartes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-dardel:
Jean Dardel, a fourteenth-century French Franciscan and chronicler of Armenia, is known only from his own Chronicle of Armenia. Born at Étampes, he joined the Friars Minor about mid-century and travelled as a pilgrim to Jerusalem and Sinai not earlier than 1375.

At Cairo Dardel found Leo, last king of Cilician Armenia, a prisoner after a nine-month siege, and became his adviser, confessor, and secretary. He said Mass for the captive king, drafted his letters to Europe seeking freedom. In 1379 set out as envoy with the royal seal to Aragon and the other Christian kings. His chronicle preserves that strange embassy first-hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-michel:
Jean Michel, a fifteenth-century French dramatist, is the likely reviser of Arnoul Gréban's Passion play, though three men share the name and proof is lacking. The bishop of Angers died in 1447, too early to revise a work first seen about 1450, and a king's physician named Jehan Michel died at Chieri in 1495.

Most likely author is a third Jean Michel, physician to the young dauphin, named in Angers university records and dead in 1501. Since the Passion in its new shape premiered at Angers in 1486, he fits the date. He also wrote a Resurrection play for King René's visit, with less dryness than Gréban but also less exactness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeremias-dres:
Jeremias Drexel, also called Dreschel or Drexelius, was a German Jesuit ascetic writer born at Augsburg in 1581 and dead at Munich in 1638. He joined the Society in 1598, taught rhetoric and humanities at Augsburg and Dillingen, and preached at the Bavarian elector's court for twenty-three years.

Drexel's books won immense vogue. His Thoughts on Eternity of 1620 ran to nine editions plus thousands of Latin and German copies, with English, Polish, French, and Italian versions. His Christian Zodiac, Guardian Angel's Clock, Nicetas, Trismegistus, and Heliotropium on conforming the will to God's followed, their odd titles matching a vivid, moralising imagination.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jezabel:
Jezabel, wife of Ahab king of Israel, was daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians and high priest of Astarte. Her marriage likely aimed to brace Ahab's house against Syria, but she brought Phoenician luxury to Samaria. She pressed Ahab to set up worship of Baal and Astarte, whose fanatical devotee she was.

Jezabel kept four hundred fifty priests of Baal and four hundred of Astarte. She hunted and killed prophets until Obadiah hid a hundred in caves, and hounded Elijah after Carmel's slaughter of Baal's priests. Her plot to seize Naboth's vineyard by false witness brought Elijah's doom upon her house: dogs would eat her in the field where Naboth died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joachim-bruel:
Joachim Bruel, a Flemish Augustinian theologian and historian of the early seventeenth century, born at Vorst and dead in 1653. He studied philosophy and theology at Bourges, where he became master of sacred theology. In 1638 Cologne chose him as prior, and twice later served as prior provincial.

Bruel matters most to students of Peru and China missions. His eighteen-book History of Peru for his order, printed at Antwerp in 1651, follows Calancha's Spanish chronicle as continued by Córdoba. He also turned Mendoza's great history of China, on its customs and realm, into Latin, giving European readers two mission frontiers in scholarly dress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joel:
Joel, son of Phatuel and second of the twelve Minor Prophets, is a figure about whose life nothing is known. His work belongs to Judah in the south, probably Jerusalem itself, since he returns again and again to temple and altar, His frequent calls to priests suggest he was priest-born.

The book's seventy-three verses form four chapters in Hebrew reckoning, three in Greek and Latin, where the last two Hebrew chapters join as one. Taken whole it is prophecy in miniature. Dark warnings of the Lord's day of judgment wake a drowsy people, and bright tidings of grace and salvation keep faith alive for God's coming kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-caspar:
Johann Caspar Barthel, a German canonist born at Kitzingen in 1697 and dead in 1771. He was a fisherman's son schooled at home and at Würzburg's Jesuit college, entering its seminary in 1715 and ordained in 1721. Prince-Bishop Hutten sent him to Rome in 1725 to study church law under Lambertini, later Benedict XIV.

Returning doctor of both laws in 1727, Barthel led Würzburg's seminary and taught canon law from 1728, rising to vice-chancellor in 1754. He settled the new Fulda diocese dispute in 1752. As teacher he broke with tradition, pioneering historical-critical canon law in Germany. His stress on state power drew Roman charges of unorthodoxy, but Benedict XIV answered his 1751 memorandum favourably.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-franz-:
Johann Franz Bessel, in religion Gottfried, was a Benedictine abbot and historian born at Buchen in 1672 and dead at Göttweig in 1749. Schooled at Aschaffenburg, Würzburg, and Bamberg, he entered Salzburg university in 1690, then Göttweig monastery in 1692, taking vows in 1693 and ordination in 1696.

Bessel taught philosophy and theology at Seligenstadt, then served Mainz's Archbishop Schönborn, studying Rota practice at Rome for two years and taking both laws' doctorate. Returning in 1703 as vicar-general and supreme judge of Mainz, he ran diplomatic missions, including Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel conversions. He made three Rome journeys to settle church differences, besides writing history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-georg-:
Johann Georg Reiffenstuel, in religion Anacletus, was a Franciscan theologian and canonist born at Kaltenbrunn in 1641 and dead at Freising in 1703. He joined the Reformed Franciscans in 1658, taught philosophy at Freising, Landshut, and Munich, and theology at Munich from 1671 to 1680.

Guardian at Weilheim and definitor of his province, Reiffenstuel taught canon law at Freising from 1683 until illness stopped him, then directed the town's episcopal schools and catalogued its libraries. His Moral Theology of 1692 ran to thirty editions, with additions on condemned views and crusade bulls. Later editors reshaped his views on moral doubt, a point the entry tracks with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-lohel:
Johann Lohel, archbishop of Prague born at Eger in 1549 and dead in 1622, was poor-born and piously raised. At fifteen he served as domestic at Tepl's Norbertine abbey, followed its school classes, outshone fellows, and took the habit in 1573 after two years' novitiate and Prague philosophy study.

Ordained in 1576, Lohel preached at Tepl against Lutheran inroads, winning many back, became prior of Strahov's Mount Sion in 1579, and abbot in 1586. With emperor and magnates aiding, he restored church and abbey, served as vicar-general for Austria, Bohemia, Hungary, and Poland, became auxiliary bishop in 1604. He became coadjutor in May 1612, and archbishop that September on Lamberg's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-mechte:
Johann Mechtel, a German chronicler born at Pfalzel near Trier in 1562, he lived past 1631 and died at Trier no later than 1653. He studied at home and at Trier's Jesuit university under historian Brote, whose sway lasted. Ordained about 1587, he served at Eltz, became Limburg canon in 1592, and ran troubled Camberg parish for two years.

Made dean in 1604, Mechtel clashed with canons and resigned at Trier's elector's request for peace, taking Saint Paulinus canonry at Trier. In both towns he gathered documents, records, and monument inscriptions with care, and since many sources are now lost his works hold near-original value. His Limburg Chronicle, begun 1610 and finished 1612, revises Tilemann's old town chronicle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-tetzel:
Johann Tetzel was the Dominican indulgence preacher whose work made him Martin Luther's first public antagonist. Born at Pirna in 1465, he studied at Leipzig and entered the Dominican Order. He served as prior at Glogau and as inquisitor for Poland and then for Saxony. He first preached indulgences in 1503 for the Teutonic Order in Livonia.

Further indulgence commissions took him to Strasburg, Nuremberg, Wurzburg, and Bamberg, and in 1516 he preached the indulgence for building St. Peter's at Rome, appearing at Juterbog just outside Saxony, near Wittenberg. The entry argues that this posting gave him an exaggerated importance and an unmerited odium. Careful research is only slowly lifting that odium. The entry traces his career through the documents rather than the legend that grew around his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-von-:
Johannes von Geissel was a cardinal and Archbishop of Cologne counted among the leading German bishops of the nineteenth century. Born in the Palatinate in 1796, he studied theology at Mainz, was ordained in 1818, taught at Speyer, and became Bishop of Speyer in 1837. His zeal there led to his appointment as coadjutor of Cologne in 1841, after Frederick William IV of Prussia came to the throne. He became archbishop in 1846 and cardinal in 1850.

Geissel settled the long Cologne conflict by working in harmony with the Prussian state. He ended the dissensions of the Hermesian school by suspending its refractory Bonn professors. He rebuilt the university's theological faculty with men of unsuspected orthodoxy. He reorganized his archdiocese and defended Catholic interests across Prussia and Germany. He served until his death at Cologne in 1864, leaving reforms of lasting value to the German Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-baptist-:
John Baptist Brondel was the first Bishop of Helena, Montana, and a trusted friend of the Indians of the Northwest. Born at Bruges in Belgium in 1842, he studied at the American College of Louvain and was ordained at Mechlin in 1864. He volunteered for the American missions two years later, serving at Heilacoon in Washington Territory and then at Walla Walla.

Consecrated in 1879 as third Bishop of Vancouver, he became administrator of Montana in 1883 and first bishop of the new diocese of Helena in 1884. Indians under his charge looked up to him as father and protector. The United States government often used his popularity to advance their political, material, and moral welfare. His death in 1903 was mourned as a great loss to the evangelization of the region, and he was buried beneath Helena cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-daniel:
John Daniel was Douai College's last de facto president, the English seminary swept up by the French Revolution. Born in 1745, great-nephew of the historian Dodd, he was educated at Fernyhalgh and Douai, where he was ordained and became professor of philosophy in 1778 and of theology after. When President Kitchen resigned in alarm in 1792, Daniel succeeded him.

Soon he and his professors and students were imprisoned, first at Arras and then at Dourlens, returning to Douai in 1794 and to England in 1795. He retired to Lancashire rather than take up the Crook Hall presidency, then went to Paris in 1802 to recover Douai's property. After 1815 France paid half a million pounds in compensation, but England confiscated it, and Daniel, who died at Paris in 1823, also wrote a church history of the Britons and Saxons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-james-ma:
John James Maximilian Oertel was a German-American journalist who became the leading voice of German Catholicism in the United States. Born at Ansbach in Bavaria in 1811 and raised a Lutheran, he studied theology at Erlangen and was ordained a minister. He came to New York in 1837 to serve his countrymen. Displeased by Lutheran unorthodoxy in New York and Missouri, and weakened in faith by denominational dissension, he became a Catholic in 1840.

His pamphlet account of his conversion, published in 1850, had quite a vogue in controversial literature. He taught German at Fordham and edited the Wahrheitsfreund at Cincinnati. He founded the Kirchenzeitung at Baltimore in 1846, moved it to New York in 1851, and made it the most prominent German Catholic paper in America. Pius IX knighted him in the Order of St. Gregory in 1875.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joost-van-den:
Joost van den Vondel was the great Dutch poet who converted to Catholicism in 1641 and devoted his pen to the Church. Born at Cologne in 1587 to Antwerp parents, he moved to Amsterdam as a boy, where his father worked in the hosiery trade. His first known poem dates from 1605, and classical studies soon widened his horizon among friends such as Hooft, Huygens, and Grotius.

His tragedies followed rapidly: Palamedes and the Amsterdam Hecuba in 1625, Joseph plays in 1635 and 1640, and Gijsbrecht van Aemstel in 1639. Between 1640 and 1641 he pondered higher things, as Protestant preachers already scented papal tendencies in him. In 1641 he openly joined the Catholic Church, converted, the Jesuit annals say, by Father Petrus Laurentius at the Krijtberg. He followed his daughter Anna and preceded his nephew Peter, and remained grateful to the Society of Jesus for life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-hilari:
Joseph Hilarius Eckhel was an Austrian Jesuit who became a founder of scientific coin study. Born at Enzesfeld in 1737, he studied at Vienna, joined the Society of Jesus in 1751, and was ordained thirteen years later. He taught poetry and rhetoric at Jesuit schools and handled Latin with ease and grace.

While teaching in Vienna he took charge of selecting unknown coins from the school cabinet and from private collections. Ill health ended his teaching, and in 1772 he traveled to Italy to study coin collections. At Florence he arranged the coins gathered by Cardinal Leopoldo de' Medici, a commission that won him the notice of Empress Maria Theresa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-sibbel:
Joseph Sibbel was a German-American sculptor of church art in New York. Born at Dülmen in 1850, he carved wood as a boy, trained under Friedrich Ewertz at Münster, and learned clay modeling from Achterman. He emigrated to Cincinnati in 1873, failed in two studios, and then set up his own studio in New York.

Sibbel fought the flood of machine-made pseudo-art filling churches with dull, uniform decoration. His bronze lectern for Garden City's Stewart Memorial Cathedral broke the mold with religious groups around the stand. His best-known work is the heroic, delicate St. Patrick in St. Patrick's Cathedral, alongside saints Anselm, Bernard, Alphonsus, and Bonaventure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-coronel:
Juan Coronel was a Spanish Franciscan who taught the Maya language in Yucatán. Born in Spain in 1569, he studied at Alcalá, joined the Franciscans of Castile, and reached Yucatán in 1590. There he mastered Maya so well that he taught it, counting the historian Cogolludo among his pupils.

Coronel published a Christian doctrine in Maya in 1620 and, the same year, sermons and spiritual treatises in Maya, both books now exceedingly rare. He ranks among the foremost teachers of Yucatán's Indians in the seventeenth century. A strict Observant for sixty-seven years, he always traveled barefoot, and his austerity blocked his election as provincial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kingisel:
Kingisel was the name borne by two abbots ruling Glastonbury in the seventh and eighth centuries. Almost all we know of them comes from charters in which their names appear, spelled in several different ways.

Kingisel I took office in 678. In his first year King Kentwine gave six hides to the abbey on condition the monks always freely elect their abbot under St. Benedict's Rule. King Baldred gave him Pennard manor in 681, and King Ina began generous gifts to the house. He died in 705. Kingisel II, fourth abbot after him, ruled from 729 to 744, receiving land grants from Ina's successor Edelard and a confirming charter from King Cudred.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lamuel:
Lamuel is a king named in Proverbs 31, otherwise unknown. The chapter opens with the words of King Lamuel, the vision his mother taught him, and verse 4 warns him against giving wine to kings.

The passage, an exhortation to chastity and temperance, is taken to end at verse 9. Some modern scholars read the opening as Lemuel, king of Massa, since Massa appears among Ishmael's sons in Genesis 25 and would place his kingdom in Arabia. In form the name is kin to Jamuel and Namuel, and in sense it matches Lael, meaning one consecrated to God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-libel:
Libel, from Latin libellus, is a malicious publication by writing, printing, picture, or sign, but not mere speech. It exposes the living, or the dead's memory, to hatred and ridicule. It tends to shame or avoid a person, or injure a business. The word's defamatory use seems to have arisen in the sixteenth century, as libellus famosus, a scurrilous pamphlet.

Every community has guarded against defamation. Mosaic and Solon's laws both punished it. A libel may be a civil injury or a criminal offence. Criminally, it tends to breach peace. Libel differs from slander: it may face civil and criminal action, while slander is no crime. Many statements are actionable per se when published, though spoken they need proof. Unwritten words imputing immoral conduct are actionable per se only if that conduct is a criminal offence. Published matter holding a person up to scorn is libellous per se.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenz-grasse:
Lorenz Grassel was a Bavarian priest chosen as coadjutor, or assistant with right of succession, to Bishop Carroll of Baltimore, but he died before taking office. Born at Ruemannsfelden in 1753, he entered the Jesuits just as the order was suppressed, and later was ordained a priest.

At Father Farmer's call he sailed for America in 1787, and took charge of the German members of St. Mary's in Philadelphia, plus Catholics scattered through New Jersey. Six years of zealous work won him a name for learning and piety. Rome granted his appointment in 1793, yet yellow fever killed him that October, before the brief naming him bishop reached him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-bancel:
Louis Bancel was a Dominican theologian of Avignon, born at Valence in 1628 and dead at Avignon in 1685. He joined the Dominicans young, taught philosophy before ordination, and later taught theology at Avignon.

Famed for a subtle mind and huge memory, he took the first chair of theology at Avignon University in 1654 and held it to his death. He served often as dean of the theology faculty, presided over thesis defences, and acted as synodal examiner and prefect of the legation. His works sum up Thomas Aquinas on morals and run a short course of all theology, finished after his death by Joseph Patin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludwig-engel:
Ludwig Engel was an Austrian Benedictine canonist, born at Wagrein castle and dead at Grillenberg in 1694. He took the habit at Melk in 1654, studied law at Salzburg at his abbot's command, and was proclaimed doctor of civil and canon law in 1657.

Ordained the next year, he soon taught canon law at Salzburg, and his learning and character won him high office, including the vice-chancellorship in 1669, chosen by unanimous vote. He left Salzburg in 1674 at Melk's abbot's wish, hoping he might succeed him there. His Collegium universi juris canonici of 1671 to 1674, praised for brevity, clarity, and solidity, reached a fifteenth edition in 1770.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luise-hensel:
Luise Hensel was a German poet and convert, born at Linum in 1798 and dead at Paderborn in 1876. Daughter of a Lutheran pastor, she returned with her widowed mother to Berlin in 1809, shone at school, and doubted Lutheran teaching even before confirmation in 1813.

Patriotic verse in 1813 gave way to friendship with Klemens Brentano in 1816, who called her his angel in the wilderness and returned to devout Catholicism through her. She herself entered the Church quietly on 8 December 1818 at Berlin's Hedwig church. Then came a wandering life: companion to Princess Salm, tutor to Stolberg daughters, head teacher at Aachen's St. Leonard Academy for six years, and nurse to her aging mother until 1835.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-military-orde:
The Military Orders of St. Michael comprise two foundations. The first, a Bavarian order, was founded in 1721 by Elector Joseph Clemens of Cologne, Duke of Bavaria, and confirmed by King Maximilian Joseph on 11 September 1808. Pius VII granted priests decorated with this order all the privileges of domestic prelates in 1802.

Under Louis I it became an order of merit in 1837, and under Otto I it was reorganized in 1887. The second order was founded in 1469 by Louis XI of France and remained the chief French military order until the Knights of the Holy Ghost were instituted. Afterwards the two together formed the ordres du roi, reception of the St. Michael cross being a condition for the other.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mont-st-miche:
Mont-Saint-Michel is a Benedictine abbey in the Diocese of Avranches, Normandy. It is called the finest example of French medieval building and of a fortified monastery. Its buildings pile around a cone of rock rising 300 feet straight from Atlantic waters. The great church crowns the rock. Since 1880 a causeway across the quicksands has made the mile from shore safe at low water.

Legend says Saint Aubert, Bishop of Avranches, founded it about 708. The Archangel Michael appeared to him in dreams three times. Benedictines from Monte Cassino replaced a lax community in 966. From 1017 Abbot Hildebert II drove a five-century building scheme. It levelled a platform around the rock and finished with the flamboyant choir in 1520. Commendatory abbots followed, then the Maurists in 1622, and the Revolution turned the abbey to other uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-carmel:
Mount Carmel is a well-known ridge in Palestine whose Hebrew name Hakkarmel means the garden or garden-land. Later Hebrew shortened it to Karmel, and modern Arabic knows it as Jebel Mar Elias, the Mountain of Saint Elias. Its northwestern end rises as a bold headland above the Mediterranean about nine miles southwest of Acre. From there the ridge runs southeast, climbing for ten miles to its crest.

Beyond the main range, lower hills stretch toward Jenin, though the entry argues these belong rather to the hills of Samaria. Carmel's story runs through Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal and the Carmelite order that took its name from the mountain. It covers its monasteries and hermits, and the shrines and churches that mark its slopes, with notes on its geology, flora and the views from its heights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nathanael:
Nathanael was one of the first disciples of Jesus, brought to him by his friend Philip, as John 1 relates. He is generally identified with the Apostle Bartholomew of the Synoptic writers. The Synoptists never mention Nathanael, but in their lists of the Twelve, Bartholomew always appears by his family name Bar-Tolmai, son of Tolmai. It is assumed the Fourth Gospel calls him by his personal name Nathanael.

The reasons are threefold. His call matches Peter's in solemnity, so he may be expected among the Twelve. He appears with other apostles after the Resurrection in John 21. He was brought by Philip, and Bartholomew always stands next to Philip in the Synoptic lists. The entry weighs that identification, Nathanael's confession of Christ, and the traditions that later grew around him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-viel:
Nicholas Viel, a Recollect friar who carried the Catholic mission to the Huron people of Canada, died in 1625 before he could return to Quebec. He reached Quebec in June 1623, pushed on to Huron country, and began learning the language while gathering the first pieces of a dictionary.

Left alone when his companions sailed back, Viel set out with a Huron party the next year and drowned in the rapids of the Rivière des Prairies. The entry notes that later reports blamed hostile Hurons rather than chance, and that the falls took the name Sault-au-Récollet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-noel-chabanel:
Jesuit missionary Noel Chabanel, born in southern France in 1613, gave his life to the Huron mission in Canada and died by violence there. He entered the Toulouse novitiate at seventeen, taught rhetoric in Jesuit colleges, and sailed for Canada in 1643.

After learning Algonquin, Chabanel joined the Huron mission beside Charles Garnier. Repelled by Huron ways and fearing he might quit, he vowed never to leave the mission, and kept that vow: a renegade Huron killed him on 8 December 1649. Father Ragueneau described the martyr deaths of Chabanel and Garnier in the Relation of 1649.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pasquier-ques:
Pasquier Quesnel, also called Paschase, was a French Oratorian born at Paris on 14 July 1634 and dead at Amsterdam on 2 December 1719. Of old noble stock, he shone at the Sorbonne in philosophy and theology, joined the Oratory at twenty-three, and directed young students. For them he wrote in 1671 an epitome of the evangelists' morals, which grew into his New Testament in French with Moral Reflections on each verse, printed from 1687 to 1692.

Steeped in Baius and Jansenist errors, he spread them skilfully through the Reflections, and added Gallican views on the papacy from de Dominis and Richer. His learned edition of Leo the Great, with notes attacking infallibility and Roman primacy, fell under ban. In 1708 Clement XI condemned his doctrines, and the 1713 bull Unigenitus censured 101 of his propositions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-powel:
Philip Powel was a Welsh Benedictine martyr, born at Trallong in Brecknockshire in 1594. Raised for the law by David Baker, later Dom Augustine Baker, he studied at the Temple in London at sixteen, then went to Douai, where he took the Benedictine habit at St. Gregory's, now Downside. Ordained in 1618, he left for the English mission in 1622.

About 1624 he settled with Mr. Poyntz in Somerset, retreated to Devon at the Civil War's outbreak, and served six months as chaplain to Catholic soldiers in Goring's Cornish army. His ship for South Wales was captured in February 1646, and he was denounced as a priest. Tried at Westminster Hall in June, he was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn on 30 June 1646. His crucifix, once Feckenham's, is kept at Downside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piel:
Peter Piel was a German pioneer of church music reform, born at Kessewick near Bonn in 1835. Trained at Kempen's teachers' seminary under Albert Michael Jopken, he became music professor at Boppard Seminary in 1868 and held the post until his death. All those years he laboured with extraordinary energy as composer, teacher, and critic.

His masses for equal and mixed voices, motets, and Marian antiphons for four and eight voices won great vogue. So did his Magnificats in all eight Gregorian modes and a Te Deum, showing a resourceful contrapuntist of classic purity. Organ trios, preludes, and postludes model finish and smoothness. Greatest was his influence as teacher, forming many distinguished musicians, and his Harmonielehre became a standard liturgical textbook. Prussia named him Royal Director of Music in 1887. He died at Boppard in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-tarise:
Pierre Tarisel was the master mason who saved Amiens Cathedral from collapse at the turn of the sixteenth century. He was born about 1442 and was already famous by 1475, when he was called to inspect the failing cathedral of Noyon. In 1483 he became master mason of the city of Amiens at higher pay than his predecessors.

From 1497 he shored up the choir pillars, rebuilt arches, and braced the transept with bands of Spanish iron. That work still holds the great iron chainwork running through the triforium. The entry also follows his inspections at Arras and Beauvais, and credits his skill, not ornament, with keeping the cathedral standing until his death in 1510.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rachel:
Rachel, whose name means a ewe, was the daughter of Laban and the younger sister of Leah. This encyclopedia entry retells her story from Genesis chapter 29. Jacob travelled to the east country, Mesopotamia, seeking a bride among his own kin, and met Rachel by chance at a well in open country. Jacob, loving Rachel, agreed to serve her father seven years, and the years seemed but a few days for the greatness of his love.

Laban deceived him. When the term ended, Laban gave him not Rachel, but her elder sister Leah, who was blear-eyed. Jacob won Rachel only by serving seven years more. Rachel long remained without offspring, the entry notes, before her sons were born. Tradition from at least the fourth century fixes her tomb four miles south of Jerusalem and one mile north of Bethlehem, and Vigouroux and Von Hummelauer supply the entry's biblical sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rainald-of-da:
Rainald of Dassel, born probably not before 1115, died in Italy on 14 August 1167. This encyclopedia entry presents a younger son of the Saxon count Rainald the First, destined for the Church and schooled at Hildesheim, with a probable stay at Paris. By 1130 he enjoyed high repute for classical learning and a place in the Hildesheim chapter. He was provost in 1148, and in 1154 he gained the provostships of Petersberg at Goslar and Saint Moritz at Hildesheim.

Soon after 1154 he also held Münster's provostship, turning down the See of Hildesheim. As a member of Frederick the First's embassy to Eugenius the Third at Rome in 1153, he first showed political ability, and in 1156 the emperor made him chancellor of the empire. The Diet of Besançon in October 1157 left no doubt of his standing, and he rose to become Archbishop of Cologne. Ficker, Hampe and Hauck supply the entry's German historical sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-arb:
Robert of Arbrissel was an itinerant preacher and founder of Fontevrault. Born about 1047 near Rhetier in Brittany, he studied at Paris. He was recalled to Rennes in 1089 as archpriest to reform simony, lay investiture, clerical concubinage, irregular marriages, and feuds. His zeal bred such enmity that on his bishop's death in 1093 he had to leave the diocese.

At Angers he took up ascetic practice, then became a hermit in the forest of Craon in 1095. Followers flocked to him. In 1096 he founded the monastery of La Roe as its abbot. That same year Urban II made him a preacher second only to himself, charged to travel widely. His theme was abandonment of the world and poverty, and his followers were known as the poor of Christ. Between 1097 and 1100 he resigned La Roe and founded Fontevrault, welcoming lepers and prostitutes among his disciples. He preached across western France until his death in 1117.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gabriel-th:
Gabriel, whose name means Fortitude of God, is the angel of the Incarnation and of consolation in this entry's reading. One of three archangels named in the Bible, he appears four times on record. In Daniel he explains the horned ram as Persia's fall to Alexander, whose divided kingdom yields Antiochus Epiphanes, and he bears the prophecy of seventy weeks before Christ's coming. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 counts a third Daniel passage doubtful.

In the New Testament he foretells John's birth to Zachary and the Saviour's to Mary. Christian tradition therefore makes Gabriel ever the angel of mercy, while Michael stands for judgment. The entry gathers those appearances into a single figure: messenger of empires' ends, of weeks counted toward redemption, and of two births that changed the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-michael-th:
Michael the Archangel, whose Hebrew name asks who is like God, ranks among the principal angels of Scripture and tradition. His name appears four times in the Bible. In Daniel he aids Gabriel and rises as great prince in the last days. In Jude he disputes with the devil over the body of Moses. In Revelation he leads heaven's army against the dragon.

From those passages the entry builds outward to his cult. He serves as guardian of the Church, patron of the dying, weigher of souls, and captain of the heavenly host. It surveys churches, apparitions, and feast days devoted to him, from Monte Gargano to Mont-Saint-Michel. In art he appears as a warrior angel with sword and scales. Readers get Scripture, legend, and devotion gathered in one survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-loui:
Peter Chanel, a French Marist priest, became the first martyr of Oceania on the island of Futuna. Born at Cuet in the diocese of Belley in 1802 and ordained in 1827, he served in parish ministry until missionary letters fired him with zeal for distant lands. He joined the Society of Mary in 1831 and sailed for Oceania in 1836.

Assigned to Futuna, he landed in November 1837, the first Christian missionary ever to set foot there. Amid great hardship he learned the language, treated the sick, and began to win converts. King Niuliki, jealous of the new faith and angered by his children's conversion, had Chanel assassinated on 28 April 1841. Within a year the whole island turned Christian, fulfilling his hope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-raphael-th:
Raphael, whose name means God has healed, appears in Scripture only in the Book of Tobit. He is absent from the Hebrew Scriptures and enters the Septuagint as the travelling companion of young Tobias, calling himself Azarias son of the great Ananias. The journey in Tobit 5 to 11 shows his protective care at every turn.

He binds in the desert of Upper Egypt the demon who had slain seven husbands of Sara, daughter of Raguel, and after the return he heals the blindness of elder Tobias. Then he reveals himself as the angel Raphael, one of the seven who stand before the Lord. With Gabriel and Michael he forms the trio named in canonical Scripture. The entry surveys his place in angelology, art, and devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teruel:
Teruel is a suffragan of Saragossa, covering the province except Bechi in Castellón. Some identify Teruel with ancient Turba, whose disputes with Saguntines gave Hannibal excuse to attack Saguntum. Teruel's annals place Turba not on the site but at its boundary. Sancho Sánchez Muñoz and Blasco Garcés Marcilla founded Teruel in 1176. It formed a community under the Fuero de Sepúlveda until 1598, when it came under Aragon.

Jaime I won its support for Valencia, and Teruel's standards waved in the Serranos gateway. In 1271 it joined war against Castile, invaded Huete and Cuenca, and backed Pedro IV. The king visited in 1348 and titled it exenta. Gregory XIII created the diocese in 1577 at Philip II's urging. The first bishop elected, Juan Pérez de Artieda, was never consecrated; the first installed, Andrés Santos, moved to Saragossa in 1579. Founders built nine churches, the central one becoming cathedral in 1577.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-arunde:
Thomas Arundel, sixtieth Archbishop of Canterbury, was born in 1353, the second son of the Earl of Arundel and Warren. Promoted to Ely while still in his early twenties, he became chancellor in 1386, moved to York in 1388, and reached Canterbury in 1396. Richard II soon attainted him for treason and sent him into exile in France and Rome.

Henry IV restored him to Canterbury in 1399, declaring his successor Roger Walden a usurper. Arundel is best remembered for his hard stand against the Lollards, pressing Rome to condemn their teaching and defending transubstantiation and papal authority. He died on 19 February 1414, after a career spent at the meeting point of church and crown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tower-of-babe:
The Tower of Babel is the building named in Genesis 11. Noah's descendants, spreading from the east into the plain of Shinar, resolved to build a city and a tower reaching heaven, to make their name famous before scattering. They used brick for stone and asphalt for mortar, but God confused their speech so they could no longer understand one another, and they left off building.

No Babylonian document yet found refers clearly to the tower, the entry notes. Smith, Sayce and others thought they had found allusions, but Delitzsch showed the key words too uncertain to prove it. The Talmud links Borsippa with the confusion of tongues, but the biblical account puts the tower inside city limits. Its form likely matched Babylonian staged towers, with shrinking blocks of masonry and stairs between storeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urgel:
Urgel is a Spanish diocese, suffragan of Tarragona. It is bounded on the north by France and on the east, south, and west by the provinces of Gerona, Barcelona, Lérida, and Huesca, with the valleys of Andorra. Its capital, Seo de Urgel, stands in northern Lérida between the Segre and Balira rivers and counts 4,000 inhabitants. The city ranks among Spain's most ancient, belonging to the Ilergetes and appearing on Iberian coins as Orgia or Orgelia.

Christianity reached Urgel very early. St Justus, its bishop, attended the Second Council of Toledo in 527 and the First Council of Lérida in 546, and wrote on the Canticle of Canticles for Sergius, Archbishop of Tarragona. The entry follows the see's bishops, its cathedral, and its mountain parishes through later centuries, a compact history of a Pyrenean diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentin-stan:
Valentin Stansel was an astronomer born at Olmütz in Moravia in 1621, who died at Bahia in Brazil on 18 December 1705. He joined the Society of Jesus on 1 October 1637 and taught rhetoric and mathematics at Olmütz and Prague. After ordination he asked to serve on the Jesuit mission in India and went to Portugal to await a ship, lecturing on astronomy with much success at the college of Évora meanwhile.

In Portugal he reshaped his name to Estancel, the form found on most of his published works. Obstacles blocked his passage to India, so he was sent to Brazil instead. He joined the Jesuit College and Seminary of San Salvador at Bahia as professor of moral theology and later of mathematics. The entry lists his astronomical writings, including observations of comets made from Brazil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-espin:
Vincent Espinel was a Spanish poet and novelist who lived from 1544 to 1634. Born at Ronda, he studied at Salamanca, served as a soldier in Italy and Flanders, took holy orders, and became chaplain of Ronda's hospital.

In 1618 he published at Barcelona a romance of Spanish manners, Relations of the Life and Deeds of Squire Marcos de Obregón. Admired at the time and later famous for its imitations and controversies, its hero's adventures thought largely drawn from Espinel's own life. Admirably written, full of wise maxims in pure, simple language, it was accused of supplying Le Sage with incidents and characters for Gil Blas. As poet he translated Horace's Art of Poetry, published his own verses in 1591, invented the ten-syllable décima stanza, and added a fifth string to the guitar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-tempe:
Wilhelm Tempel was a German sky-watcher who rose from lithographer to noted comet hunter without formal training. Born near Löbau in Saxony in 1821, he died near Florence in 1889. After a hard youth spent as sexton, gardener, and fee collector, he learned lithography, spent three years in Denmark, and settled in Venice around 1850, where he married and became a Catholic.

Venice friends stirred his love of the stars, and with a small comet-seeker he found a comet and the Merope Nebula in 1859. Paris shut its observatory to him for lack of schooling, but Marseilles took him on as an assistant in 1860. Working from windows and gardens, he went on to spot thirteen comets and four minor planets in ten years, and he published his sightings in the Astronomische Nachrichten.
christie-johnstone-a-novel:
Charles Reade built his novel Christie Johnstone around a bored lord whom pleasure has stopped pleasing. Viscount Ipsden, aged twenty-five with a large income, drifts through London and Europe hunting amusement. A doctor orders a cure: relieve one distressed person each day, and no more than one. The prescription sends the lord looking for work for his money and his heart.

Scotland gives the cure its setting, where Ipsden meets Christie Johnstone, a herring seller with a quick tongue and a creel to empty. Her plain speech and hard day's labor shame his soft hands and empty hours. Lady Barbara Sinclair, brilliant and political, offers the polished opposite pole of his old world. Reade, who dated the story to 1850 and refused to retouch it, mixes dialect comedy with social satire. Readers meet an early Reade here: energetic, funny, and preaching that labor dignifies life more than rank does.
darkness-and-daylight-a-novel:
Mary Jane Holmes opens Darkness and Daylight at Collingwood, a gloomy stone house empty for twelve years. Its owner wanders foreign lands, muttering of the darkness that fell when he lost his young wife. His son Richard has given up his youth to his father's whims. A fearful blight, blindness, is stealing upon noble Richard.

Edith Hastings comes to Collingwood as the story's daylight. Grace Atherton, Arthur, and the mystery at Grassy Spring fill the middle chapters. Nina, a strange childlike girl, carries the book's pathos. The darkness deepens, partings follow, and a fiery test prepares the sacrifice. A bridal and a leap of six years close the tale. Holmes was among America's best-selling domestic novelists, and this long novel shows her machinery of sentiment at full power.
democracy-an-american-novel:
Henry Adams published this novel anonymously in March 1880, and the prefatory note here records that his name reached the title page only in 1925. Readers of the first editions guessed at the author and at the real originals of the characters. The heroine needs no guessing: Mrs. Lightfoot Lee, a young New York widow, decides to pass a winter in Washington because New York has bored her into philosophy and philanthropy.

In Washington she sets out to understand the republic's working machinery at close range. A corrupt, charming senator from the West becomes her guide and her test. Adams builds the novel from drawing-room talk about power, money, and motive, and lets his widow ask the naive questions insiders avoid. It remains the sharpest short novel of Washington politics of its century.
doe-osti-2583535-wafer-free-crystalline-:
Leap Photovoltaics wants solar cells without wafers, and NREL helped it pin silicon particles into a working absorber. Report NREL/TP-5K00-92847, dated January 17, 2025, closes CRADA CRD-22-22482, with David Young and Pauls Stradins as contacts. Mainstream cells start as grown ingots, diamond-sawn into wafers; both steps burn money and silicon. Particles can come from sawing kerf, from ball-milled recycled wafers, or from gas-phase growth.

The project, run through the Solar Prize voucher program, developed methods to immobilize silicon particles permanently on an aluminum-coated substrate. The attachment had to do double duty, forming carrier-selective electrical contacts to each particle. An array of contacted particles becomes the absorber layer, catching photons and generating carriers without a wafer anywhere in the process. If the approach reaches reasonable efficiency, silicon solar gets a feedstock that the industry currently throws away.
doe-osti-2586541-enhancement-of-pyarc-fo:
Nicolas Stauff, Mike Smith, and Paolo Ferroni of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this final report, ANL/NSE-25/57, for Technology Commercialization Fund project TCF-21-24979. The project enhanced PyARC, Argonne's Python-based reactor analysis toolkit, for Westinghouse Electric Company's lead fast reactor design work. Lead-cooled fast reactors place modeling demands that older tools were not built for.

The enhancements span several codes in the toolkit. The team added a way to estimate displacement per atom, a measure of radiation damage in materials. It integrated the DASSH and NUBOW workflow, added correlations so DASSH can model lead fast reactors, and checked DASSH against high-fidelity fluid dynamics simulations. NUBOW-3D gained clearer input definitions and better output. Verification ran against a wide range of Monte Carlo simulations, the report's standard for trusting the faster deterministic tools.
doe-osti-2588839-megawatt-class-high-vol:
Geraldo Nojima of Eaton Corporation led this final technical report for cooperative agreement DE-EE0009135, covering October 2020 through April 2025. Carnegie Mellon University, North Carolina State University, Avago-Broadcom, and PWP partnered. The project built megawatt-class, high-voltage silicon carbide power converters for advanced manufacturing, designed to offer grid support services on the side.

Silicon carbide switches handle higher voltages and speeds than silicon, shrinking converters and cutting losses. The team developed the power conversion system and surveyed where it fits: cement factories, steel mills, and mining equipment all run huge motor drives. Those drives carry rotational inertia, and the report develops the idea of using it as stored energy, dispatchable for the grid. Multi-megawatt drive regeneration and flywheel-style applications are worked through with control designs. In the design case, the grid interface holds its total losses under one kilowatt.
doe-osti-2998142-game-theory-approaches-:
Wei Wang, Liping Li, Brittany Tarufelli, and co-authors at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory apply game theory to a practical grid problem in a September 2025 report. The problem: how to pay communities to build local energy gear that protects everyone. The framework is a Stackelberg game, where a leader sets incentives first and followers invest in response, and test cases use three linked communities.

Two failures were rehearsed: a line cut between communities, and full disconnection from the main grid. With no incentives, the first case built 217.1 megawatts of local capacity, while high incentives raised that to 432.5 megawatts. High incentives also cut total community costs by 63.8 million dollars, about 7.13 percent, and removed the need for a new transmission line. In the islanding case, incentives erased 24.3 megawatt-hours of unserved load and left up to 177.6 megawatt-hours of battery held in reserve. Planners get a priced menu of resilience.
doe-osti-2998441-data-driven-method-for-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38355, by Xuehang Song, Tse-Chun Chen, Grigoriy Kondyukov, and co-authors, dated September 2025, applies machine learning to Hanford's groundwater maps. Cleanup decisions ride on water level maps, yet wells measure only scattered points. The method rebuilds full water level fields over time and flags which wells earn their keep.

A diffusion model, a generative method trained on physics-based simulations, supplies the prior pattern of how water levels behave at the site. During reconstruction, a data assimilation step bends that pattern to honor the real well measurements. The output is a time sequence of water level maps consistent with both physics and data. Network optimization follows naturally: wells whose readings barely change the map are candidates for retirement, and gaps argue for new ones.
